# Row-Bot Docs Full Text

Concatenated public documentation for Row-Bot.

## Row-Bot Documentation

Route: /docs/

The Row-Bot user guide: install, first steps, everyday use, settings, connections, privacy and troubleshooting.

# Row-Bot Documentation

Row-Bot is a personal AI assistant that runs on your own computer. It chats, remembers what matters to you, works with your documents and apps, browses the web and uses the apps on your computer while you watch, runs workflows on a schedule, and makes designs and code. Your data stays on your machine, and you choose which models it uses, from a free local model to the ChatGPT, Claude or Grok plan you already have. Use it on your desktop, from your phone, or as a private server.

These pages describe Row-Bot 5.4.0.

## Start Here

1. [What's New In 5.3](/docs/getting-started/whats-new): the highlights, and what to know before upgrading.
2. [Install Row-Bot](/docs/getting-started/installation) on Windows, macOS or Linux, or with Docker.
3. [First Launch](/docs/getting-started/first-launch): choose how Row-Bot thinks.
4. [Your First Tasks](/docs/getting-started/first-tasks): five things to try in ten minutes.
5. [The Row-Bot Interface](/docs/app-shell/navigation): the sidebar, Home, a conversation, the command palette and Settings.

## Use Row-Bot

- [Chat](/docs/chat/): conversations, incognito chats, pages, questions, attachments and context.
- [Model Picker](/docs/chat/model-picker) and [Reasoning Controls](/docs/chat/reasoning-controls): choose a model and how hard it thinks.
- [Tools, Approvals And Background Work](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal): Ask, Auto, Hands-off and Block, background processes, Row-Bot's browser, video editing, sending files and the terminal.
- [Computer Use](/docs/computer-use/): Row-Bot works in an app on your computer with your mouse and keyboard while you watch.
- [Workflows](/docs/guides/workflows): work that runs again on a schedule, with approvals and delivery.
- [Profiles, Goals, And Agents](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/): agent profiles, goals that keep going, and helpers.
- [Knowledge](/docs/knowledge/): memory, documents and what Row-Bot has learned.

## Getting Started

Route: /docs/getting-started/

Install Row-Bot, complete first launch, and learn the first choices that matter.

# Getting Started

Start here if you are new to Row-Bot. You only need three things for a useful first session: the app installed, one working model path, and a basic understanding of where Row-Bot stores local data.

## The Short Path

1. Install Row-Bot from the release package for your platform, or [run it in your browser](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser) with nothing to install.
2. Launch the app and answer **How should Row-Bot think?**
3. Choose one model path: local Ollama, a hosted provider, a subscription account, or a custom endpoint.
4. Send a first chat message, or try [Your First Tasks](/docs/getting-started/first-tasks).
5. Open Setup Center or Settings later when you are ready for documents, workflows, designs, code folders, channels, apps, Skills, Buddy, or voice.

## Important Concepts

- **Local app** means Row-Bot runs on your machine and opens a local desktop or browser window.
- **Data directory** means the folder where Row-Bot keeps conversations, memories, documents, settings, workflows, logs, designs, code folder records, skills, plugins, and local integration state.
- **Model provider** means the service or local runtime that supplies a model. Ollama is local; API and subscription providers usually use the internet.
- **Tools** are actions Row-Bot can take, such as reading files, searching documents, using a browser, running commands in a code folder, or sending through a channel.
- **Approvals** ask you to approve or deny sensitive actions before Row-Bot proceeds. They wait until you answer.

## What's New In 5.3

Route: /docs/getting-started/whats-new

The highlights of Row-Bot 5.3 with links to each guide, and what to know before upgrading from 5.2.

# What's New In 5.3

Row-Bot 5.3 puts its browser inside the app and rebuilds computer use. It also adds pages and questions, incognito chats, Outlook, several X accounts, reviewed approvals and Hands-off, and background work. This page lists the highlights and links to the guide for each one. The full list is in the [release notes](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/releases).

## Row-Bot Does More Without Being Asked

You don't need to name a feature. Ask in your own words:
- a plan, checklist, comparison or numbers to track becomes a [page](/docs/chat/#pages);
- a choice only you can make comes as a [question](/docs/chat/#questions);
- research on several things goes to [helpers](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/#delegated-agents);
- a file server or watcher runs [in the background](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#background-processes);
- "keep me on track" gets a plan and a weekly check-in [workflow](/docs/guides/workflows).

A new chat also starts faster. Row-Bot sends about 40% less to the model before your first message, and with a ChatGPT plan the shared start of each chat comes from the provider's cache.

## Highlights

- **Row-Bot's browser, in the app.** A Browser pane beside the chat shows the page live, with tabs, Take control and Stop. See [Row-Bot's Browser](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#row-bots-browser).
- **Computer use, rebuilt.** Row-Bot works in an app with your mouse and keyboard while you watch. A Stop bar shows on screen, and Esc ends it. See [Computer Use](/docs/computer-use/).
- **Pages and questions.** Plans you approve step by step, checklists that remember ticks, and questions with options in a card. See [Pages](/docs/chat/#pages) and [Questions](/docs/chat/#questions).
- **Incognito chats.** Nothing in them is read for memory. See [Incognito Chats](/docs/chat/#incognito-chats).
- **Approvals: Ask, Auto, Hands-off, Block.** Auto's reviewer approves what you asked for, and Hands-off asks nothing. **Always ask me** keeps a step or an app asking you whatever the level. See [Approvals](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#approvals).
- **Outlook and several X accounts.** Outlook works through your own Microsoft app. Each X post names its account. See [Accounts](/docs/integrations/accounts).
- **Background work.** Servers and long jobs keep running and show in the chat. Video editing, sending files to your devices and code folders work from any device. See [Background Processes](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#background-processes).
- **Workflows.** Monthly schedules, timezones, missed-run handling, a code folder per workflow, and Always ask me steps. See [Workflows](/docs/guides/workflows).
- **Claude with your Claude plan,** through your own Claude Code. See [Settings › Providers](/docs/settings/providers).

## Before You Upgrade From 5.2

- **It arrives in the background.** Row-Bot 5.2.1 downloads 5.3 and offers **Restart now**. From 5.1 or 5.0, install 5.2 first with the full installer.
- **Claude needs setting up again.** The old Claude sign-in is removed on first start. Install and sign in to Claude Code, then choose your Claude plan in Settings › Providers.
- **Auto may ask a little more.** It now asks about anything that doesn't clearly match your request. Choose Hands-off for a chat or workflow that should never ask.
- **Workflow schedules keep their times,** in this computer's timezone. Runs missed while Row-Bot was closed are still skipped unless you change that.
- **Your X account** becomes your first account the next time Row-Bot reaches X.
- **Windows** may ask once about `Row-Bot Server` in Windows Firewall.
- **A job started with `&` inside a command** now stops when that command finishes. Ask Row-Bot to start a server instead.

## Installation

Route: /docs/getting-started/installation

Install Row-Bot on Windows, macOS or Linux, see where it keeps your data, move from 5.1, uninstall, or run it from source.

# Installation

Download the latest Row-Bot for your system from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/releases/latest) and install it. You do this once: after that, Row-Bot downloads its updates in the background (see [Updates](/docs/operations/updates)).

| System | Download | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit | `Row-Bot-X.Y.Z-Windows-x64.exe` | about 420 MB |
| macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer, Apple silicon | `Row-Bot-X.Y.Z-macOS-arm64.dmg` | about 930 MB |
| Linux x86_64 (glibc) | the one-line installer, or `Row-Bot-X.Y.Z-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz` | about 790 MB |

Ollama is optional; you only need it for models that run on your own computer.

## Windows

1. Download the installer and open it.
2. It installs without questions and without administrator rights, for your Windows account only. When it finishes, Row-Bot opens.

Row-Bot installs into `%LocalAppData%\Programs\Row-Bot` and adds a Start menu shortcut (and, the first time, a desktop shortcut). While it runs, its icon sits in the system tray.

## macOS

Row-Bot needs macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer on a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later).

1. Open the downloaded DMG and drag **Row-Bot** to **Applications**.
2. Open Row-Bot from Applications. The first time, macOS asks whether to open an app downloaded from the internet: choose **Open**.

If you open Row-Bot straight from the disk image or the Downloads folder, it offers **Move to Applications**. Choose it, so Row-Bot always starts from the same place. While it runs, Row-Bot sits in the menu bar. The first time it uses the microphone or camera, macOS asks you to allow Row-Bot.

## Linux

Install the latest release for your user with:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/main/installer/install-linux.sh | bash
```

It checks the download's SHA-256, installs under `~/.local/share/row-bot`, creates the `row-bot` command in `~/.local/bin` and adds Row-Bot to your app menu. Run `row-bot`; it opens in your browser. To install a specific release, add its version: `... | bash -s -- X.Y.Z`.

Or install the tarball by hand:

```bash
tar -xzf Row-Bot-X.Y.Z-Linux-x86_64.tar.gz
cd Row-Bot-X.Y.Z-Linux-x86_64
./install.sh
row-bot
```

A native window and tray icon need GTK or Qt and AppIndicator from your distribution; without them Row-Bot uses your browser.

### Run As A Server

`row-bot serve --port 8080` runs Row-Bot as an authenticated server, without a window or tray. Connect your browser with an invitation, as [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access) explains.

To keep it running with systemd, create `~/.config/systemd/user/row-bot.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Row-Bot server

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/row-bot serve --port 8080
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

Then start it, and let it keep running after you log out:

```bash
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now row-bot
loginctl enable-linger "$USER"
```

When Row-Bot restarts itself to install an update, it exits with code 75 and leaves the restart to systemd. Use `Restart=always`, or add `RestartForceExitStatus=75` to your own restart policy. `systemctl --user stop row-bot` installs an update that is ready, and the next start runs it.

## Browser Automation And Exports

No installer includes a browser. Browser Automation uses Chrome or Edge already on your computer (Edge comes with Windows). Exporting a design to PDF, PNG or PowerPoint needs Row-Bot's own browser runtime instead: the first time, the export says **Exports need Browser Automation** with **Set up Browser Automation**. Choose it, then **Install** the **Browser runtime** in **Settings › System › Browser and computer use**. It is a one-time download into your data folder, so updates keep it, and Row-Bot never downloads it by itself.

## Where Row-Bot Keeps Things

| System | App files | Your data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | `%LocalAppData%\Programs\Row-Bot` | `%USERPROFILE%\.row-bot` |
| macOS | `Row-Bot.app` in Applications, and updates in `~/Library/Application Support/Row-Bot` | `~/.row-bot` |
| Linux | `~/.local/share/row-bot`, and the `row-bot` command in `~/.local/bin` | `~/.row-bot` |

Your data folder holds conversations, memories, model and provider settings, workflows, designs, code folder records, documents, logs, skills, plugins, Buddy assets, channel settings and MCP settings. Keys and sign-ins are kept in Windows Credential Manager, the macOS Keychain or the Linux Secret Service. Updates, Repair and uninstalling never touch your data.

Advanced users can set `ROW_BOT_DATA_DIR` before launch to use a separate data folder for testing or portable runs. Row-Bot then treats that folder as its data for the whole run.

## Moving From 5.1

Row-Bot 5.1 updates to 5.2 the way it always has, once, with the full installer. After that, updates download in the background.

- **Windows:** 5.1 was installed for all users in Program Files. The 5.2 installer moves Row-Bot to your account and asks once for administrator approval to remove the old copy. If you decline, or your account isn't an administrator, Row-Bot 5.2 installs and opens anyway, and **Settings › Updates** offers **Remove the old Row-Bot** later. That button appears only in the Row-Bot desktop app on that computer, because Windows asks for approval on its own screen.
- **macOS:** 5.1 opens the new DMG. Drag Row-Bot to Applications one last time and replace the old copy.
- **Linux:** nothing to do; 5.1 installs 5.2 by itself.

Your data, settings and sign-ins carry over. **Repair** can go back to an earlier 5.2 version, not to 5.1.

## Uninstall

- **Windows:** open Windows Settings › Apps › Installed apps (Apps & features on Windows 10), choose Row-Bot and **Uninstall**. It asks you to quit Row-Bot first if it is running, and removes `%LocalAppData%\Programs\Row-Bot`.
- **macOS:** quit Row-Bot from the menu bar, drag Row-Bot from Applications to the Bin, and delete `~/Library/Application Support/Row-Bot`, which holds the updates it downloaded.
- **Linux:** run `~/.local/share/row-bot/current/uninstall.sh`. It removes the app files, the `row-bot` command and the app menu entry.

Uninstalling keeps your data folder, so reinstalling picks up where you left off. To remove your data too, delete the data folder after uninstalling (back it up first if you might come back), and remove Row-Bot's saved keys from the system's key store.

## Run From Source

Use the source path if you are developing Row-Bot or testing changes:

1. Clone the repository.
2. Create a Python environment.
3. Install uv and sync the locked Python dependencies with `uv sync --locked --all-extras --group test`.
4. Install the docs-site dependencies only if you are working on documentation.
5. Run the app entry point from the repository.

`requirements.txt` is a generated pip export from `uv.lock` for installer compatibility. It is available as a fallback for environments that cannot use uv, but source dependency changes should be made in `pyproject.toml`.

Source runs use the same local data as the installed app and never update themselves. Keep test data separate from personal data when experimenting.

## After Installing

Continue to [First Launch](/docs/getting-started/first-launch): answer **How should Row-Bot think?** to choose your first model. You can finish optional setup later from the Setup Center and Settings.

The installed app starts a local Row-Bot process and opens it in a desktop window or your browser, depending on your system. If the usual port is busy, Row-Bot chooses another local port.

The standard desktop install stays on local loopback. To connect another trusted computer or phone, finish local setup first and then follow [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access). For a headless or container deployment, read that guide before publishing a port or creating the first owner invitation.

## Row-Bot In Your Browser

Route: /docs/getting-started/in-your-browser

Run your own Row-Bot on a hosting service and use it from any browser or your phone: start it, sign in, choose a model, and see what's different from the desktop app.

# Row-Bot In Your Browser

A hosting service can run your own private Row-Bot for you on a small server. There's nothing to install: you open it from any browser, on a computer or a phone, and it keeps working while your devices are off, so schedules and channels keep running.

It's the same Row-Bot as the desktop app, and it's yours alone: one owner, signed in from as many devices as you like. You bring the model: a ChatGPT or Claude plan, an API key, or your own model server.

Your host runs the server; Row-Bot runs on it. [What Your Host Can See](/docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see) says plainly what that means for your data.

## Start

- **On Railway:** **Continue with Railway** at [row-bot.ai/railway](https://row-bot.ai/railway/) creates your Row-Bot in your own Railway account in about 3 minutes and opens it signed in. [Row-Bot On Railway](/docs/getting-started/on-railway) has the steps, the template you can deploy by hand instead, and what it costs.
- **On another host:** any service that runs Row-Bot's container image can host it. [Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting) has what the image needs.

## Enter The Setup Code

The setup code makes your browser the owner, so nobody else can use your Row-Bot. **Continue with Railway** uses it for you and opens Row-Bot signed in. Otherwise:

1. Find the code. On Railway, it's the sign-in link in the service's deploy log, or `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE` in its **Variables** ([Sign In](/docs/getting-started/on-railway#sign-in)). On another host, it's on the line that starts `Row-Bot setup code:` in the server's log.
2. Open your Row-Bot at its address. It says **Welcome to your Row-Bot**.
3. Paste the code into **Setup code** and choose **Continue**. Dashes, spaces and capitals don't matter.

Row-Bot says "This browser is signed in." and asks how it should think. The code works once: from then on, anyone else who opens your address sees **This Row-Bot already has an owner**, and you add your other devices from Row-Bot itself ([Add Your Phone](#add-your-phone)).

Keep the code private until you've used it. If you can't find it, or later lose access, see [Lost The Setup Code](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted#lost-the-setup-code).

## Choose A Model

Row-Bot asks **How should Row-Bot think?** with two big buttons:

- **Sign in with ChatGPT**: one click copies a code and opens OpenAI's page in a new tab. Paste the code there and approve; Row-Bot notices when you're done.
- **Use my Claude plan**: Row-Bot installs Claude Code, Anthropic's program, on your server, then opens Claude's own sign-in in a small panel. Open the link it shows, sign in to Claude, and paste the code Claude gives you into the panel. Your plan's limits apply, and Row-Bot never sees, stores or relays your Claude sign-in.

**Other ways** holds **Use an API key** (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter and more), **Use my own model server** and **Sign in with Grok**.

After you sign in, Row-Bot picks that provider's first model, checks that it answers, and opens a chat with one suggestion to tap: **What can you do for me?** Change the model any time in the model picker. [First Launch](/docs/getting-started/first-launch#on-a-hosted-row-bot) explains each choice.

Your server has no graphics card, so it can't run chat models itself. To use models on hardware of your own, connect it as [your own model server](/docs/guides/own-model-server), or use the desktop app.

## Add Your Phone

Opening your Row-Bot's address on another device isn't enough: Row-Bot doesn't know that browser yet. Sign the new device in from one that's already signed in:

- **After your first answer,** a card in that chat offers **Add Row-Bot to your phone**. On a computer, choose **Show the code** and scan it with your phone's camera. The phone signs in once and stays signed in.
- **Any time later,** open **Settings › Devices & remote access** and choose **Connect a phone or computer**. **Copy link** gives the same one-time sign-in as a link, for a device without a camera.

Then add Row-Bot to your phone's home screen, so it opens like an app:

- **iPhone:** in Safari, tap Share, then **Add to Home Screen**.
- **Android:** in Chrome, tap ⋮, then **Add to Home screen** or **Install app**.

**Settings › Devices & remote access** also lists every signed-in device, and signs one out.

## What's Different

A hosted Row-Bot is the full Row-Bot, without the parts that need your own computer or a graphics card.

### Works The Same

- Chat, agents, workflows and schedules, always on: they keep running while your devices are off.
- Memory, knowledge and documents, with Row-Bot's own search model.
- Row-Bot's browser: watch it work, take control, and sign in to a site once, from your phone too.
- Commands and Python, Developer Studio and Designer Studio.
- Apps, MCP servers, and channels such as Telegram and Slack.
- Row-Bot on your phone's home screen.
- ChatGPT sign-in and API keys.

### Different On A Hosted Row-Bot

- **Your files live on the server,** not on your computer. Attach a file in a chat to give it to Row-Bot.
- **Row-Bot says "your Row-Bot server"** where the desktop app says "this computer".
- **Websites see a datacenter's address** when Row-Bot's browser visits them, so some may ask for extra checks.
- **Your host installs updates.** On Railway, new versions install each night ([Updates](/docs/getting-started/on-railway#updates)). **Settings › Updates** shows your version and a **What's new** link.
- **Local speech-to-text needs a 4 GB server.** On a smaller one, **Settings › Voice** marks it **Needs a 4 GB server**: use cloud speech-to-text there.
- **Your Claude plan** works through Claude Code, which Row-Bot installs on your server when you choose **Use my Claude plan**.
- **Models on your own hardware** work through a custom endpoint your server can reach over the internet, with a key or a tunnel in front: see [Use Your Own Model Server](/docs/guides/own-model-server).
- **Keep a backup of your own.** Not every host backs up the server (Railway does only on its Pro plan): download a backup from **Settings › Data** from time to time ([Moving To Your Computer And Back](#moving-to-your-computer-and-back)).

### Not On A Hosted Row-Bot

- Chat models running on the server itself, since it has no graphics card. Your own model server elsewhere works.
- Computer use of your own screen, and your own browser with its sign-ins. Row-Bot's own browser works.
- The desktop window, your computer's file pickers, and a terminal window on your computer.

For those, use the [desktop app](/docs/getting-started/installation). You can move between the two whenever you like.

## Costs

- **The server:** billed by your host for what it uses ([Railway's costs](/docs/getting-started/on-railway#costs)). Row-Bot needs 4 GB for local speech-to-text; 2 GB also works if you use cloud speech-to-text.
- **The model:** billed by whoever provides it. A ChatGPT or Claude plan is the subscription you already pay for, with its limits. An API key is billed by its provider for what you use. Your own model server costs whatever running it costs you.
- **Row-Bot itself** is free and open source, and bills you for nothing.

## Moving To Your Computer And Back

Your Row-Bot isn't tied to its host. A backup carries your conversations, memories, workflows, designs and settings between a hosted Row-Bot and the desktop app, either way.

To move to your computer:

1. On your hosted Row-Bot, open **Settings › Data** and choose **Download backup**.
2. [Install Row-Bot](/docs/getting-started/installation) on your computer. At first launch you can choose **Set up later**.
3. Open **Settings › Data**, choose **Restore from backup…**, pick the file, and choose **Restore on restart**. The restore applies the next time Row-Bot starts.
4. Sign in to your model again, and set up whatever the backup lists under "After restoring it, set these up again".

To move back, choose **Back up now** in the desktop app's **Settings › Data**. Then, on your hosted Row-Bot, choose **Restore from backup…** in **Settings › Data**, pick the file, choose **Restore on restart**, and restart Row-Bot on your host (on Railway, redeploy the service from its **Deployments** tab).

A backup never holds passwords, API keys or sign-ins, your Claude plan's included, so you sign in again after moving. It also leaves out Row-Bot's browser sessions, your signed-in devices, and downloaded models and runtimes, which you download again where you need them. Once everything has arrived, you can remove the old server from your host.

## Getting Help

- **Your host** helps with the server: billing, its size, its backups, and whether it's up. In Row-Bot, **Settings › System** shows who hosts it, with links to manage the server and to the host's support. On Railway, see [Getting Help](/docs/getting-started/on-railway#getting-help).
- **Row-Bot** helps with everything inside Row-Bot: chats, models and sign-ins, workflows, memory, apps, the setup code and the out-of-memory notice. Start with [Fix A Hosted Row-Bot](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted). Ask in [Discussions](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/discussions), or [report a bug](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/issues/new/choose): under "Where does Row-Bot run?" choose a hosting service, and name your host and your server's size. Monitor's **Copy diagnosis report** gives a summary to paste in.

## Row-Bot On Railway

Route: /docs/getting-started/on-railway

Run your own Row-Bot in your own Railway account and open it from any browser: Continue with Railway or the template, sign in, updates, spending, backups, and what it costs.

# Row-Bot On Railway

Railway, a cloud platform, can run your own private Row-Bot in your own Railway account. You open Row-Bot from any browser, on a computer or a phone, and it keeps working while your devices are off, so schedules and channels keep running.

It's the same Row-Bot as the desktop app and as any [hosted Row-Bot](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser), and it's yours alone: one owner, signed in from as many devices as you like. You bring the model: a ChatGPT or Claude plan, a Grok sign-in, an API key, or your own model server.

Railway runs the server and bills you for what it uses. New versions install by themselves each night. You keep your own backups and, if you like, a spending limit. [What Your Host Can See](/docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see#railway) says plainly what Railway can reach.

There are two ways to start: **Continue with Railway**, which sets everything up and signs you in, or Railway's **template**, which you set up by hand.

## Before You Start

- **A Railway account.** You can make one on the way, with GitHub, Google or an email address.
- **Railway's Hobby plan** is the one to use: $5 a month, with $5 of usage included, and it asks for a card. Railway may also ask to verify your account before Row-Bot can reach the internet.
- **Railway's trial** gives Row-Bot 1 GB: chats, memory and schedules work. Browser tasks and local speech-to-text need Railway's Hobby plan. Row-Bot says so on its first screen and in **Settings › System**, with **Upgrade in Railway**.

## Continue With Railway

The quickest way: about 3 minutes, with no setup code to copy.

1. Open [row-bot.ai/railway](https://row-bot.ai/railway/) and choose **Continue with Railway**.
2. Sign in to Railway, or make an account, and choose **Allow**. That lets the page create Row-Bot in your workspace.
3. Pick the **workspace** and the **region**. The region is guessed from your time zone; change it if you like.
4. Choose **Create my Row-Bot**. Railway downloads and starts Row-Bot, which takes about 1½ minutes. Keep the page open.
5. Your Row-Bot opens, already signed in: "This browser is signed in." Row-Bot then asks how it should think ([First Run](#first-run)).

The page makes one project, **Row-Bot**, with one service, **row-bot**:

- a volume at `/data` for your data, and its own address ending in `up.railway.app`;
- memory and CPU limits of **8 GB** and **8 vCPU**, the Hobby plan's ceiling. Railway bills only what Row-Bot uses;
- **nightly automatic updates** ([Updates](#updates));
- a setup code, made in your browser, which the page uses once to sign you in.

**What the page sees.** It talks only to Railway. Railway's API doesn't accept calls from web pages, so they pass through a small relay Row-Bot runs on Cloudflare, which keeps and logs nothing. Row-Bot never stores your Railway sign-in; the page forgets it once your Row-Bot opens.

If something stops it, the page says what to do:

- **Verify your account:** **Verify at Railway**, then come back. The page checks again by itself.
- **You can't create projects in this workspace:** pick another workspace.
- **You already have a Row-Bot in this workspace:** **Open it**, or **Create another**.
- **Still starting after a few minutes:** Railway is still downloading Row-Bot. You can leave the page; your Row-Bot's address and its setup code (in Railway's **Variables**) are on the page.
- **Railway couldn't start Row-Bot:** **See Railway's log**, or **Try again**, which carries on where it stopped.

## Or Deploy The Template

The same Row-Bot, set up in Railway's own pages.

1. Open Row-Bot's template in Railway's template marketplace (search for **Row-Bot**) and choose **Deploy Now**. Sign in to Railway, or create an account.
2. Deploy. Railway creates a project with one service, **row-bot**, its volume for your data, and its own address ending in `up.railway.app`. Leave the variables as they are: the template fills them in, your setup code included. It also sets the memory and CPU limits (**8 GB** and **8 vCPU**; Railway bills only what Row-Bot uses) and turns on nightly automatic updates ([Updates](#updates)).

The deploy log ends with `Row-Bot is running at`. If it shows `Row-Bot didn't start:` instead, the rest of that line says why.

### Sign In

The setup code makes your browser the owner, so nobody else can use your Row-Bot. Either:

- **Click the sign-in link** in the service's deploy log: the line `Open this link to sign in: https://…/setup#code=…`. Your Row-Bot opens and signs this browser in. Or:
- **Enter the code.** Open your Row-Bot at its address (the link on the service, or **Settings › Networking**); it says **Welcome to your Row-Bot**. Under **Where's my code?**, choose **Open your Variables in Railway** and copy the value of `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE`. Paste it into **Setup code** and choose **Continue**. Dashes, spaces and capitals don't matter.

Row-Bot says "This browser is signed in." The code works once: from then on, anyone else who opens your address sees **This Row-Bot already has an owner**, and you add your other devices from Row-Bot itself ([Add Your Phone](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser#add-your-phone)). The sign-in link is printed only while nobody owns your Row-Bot.

## Lost Access?

Set a new `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE` of at least 12 letters or digits in the service's **Variables** and deploy the change. Then open your Row-Bot, choose **Lost access?** and enter the new code. It works once, and signs out every other browser. [Lost The Setup Code](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted#lost-the-setup-code) has more.

## First Run

Row-Bot asks **How should Row-Bot think?**, exactly as on any hosted Row-Bot: **Sign in with ChatGPT**, **Use my Claude plan**, and **Other ways** for an API key, your own model server or **Sign in with Grok**. [Choose A Model](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser#choose-a-model) explains each one.

After you sign in, Row-Bot checks that the model answers and opens a chat with one suggestion to tap.

## Your Subscriptions And Accounts

Everything you sign in to on Railway works as in the desktop app, through your browser:

- **ChatGPT:** Row-Bot copies a code and opens OpenAI's page; paste the code there and approve. If ChatGPT won't take the code, enable device code login in your ChatGPT security settings ([OpenAI's steps](https://developers.openai.com/codex/auth)), then try again.
- **Your Claude plan:** Row-Bot installs Claude Code, Anthropic's program, on your server, then opens Claude's own sign-in; paste the code Claude gives you. Row-Bot never sees, stores or relays your Claude sign-in.
- **Grok:** xAI's sign-in ends on a page that doesn't load; paste that page's address back into Row-Bot ([A Sign-In That Won't Finish](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted#grok)).
- **Outlook:** Microsoft signs you in with a code you enter at Microsoft's own page; nothing to set up.
- **X and Google** use an app or client of your own, which sends you back to your Row-Bot's own address, so it must list it:
  - X: `https://<your address>/api/v1/accounts/x/auth/callback`
  - Google, in a **Web application** client: `https://<your address>/api/v1/accounts/google/auth/callback`

  where `<your address>` is the service's address, such as `row-bot-production-1a2b.up.railway.app`. Each account's setup guide, in **Settings › Apps**, shows the exact address to copy. [Accounts And Authorisation](/docs/integrations/accounts#sign-in-from-another-device) explains the rest.

If you give the service a domain of your own, set `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL` to it (`https://` and the domain, nothing else), deploy the change, and list the new callback addresses too.

## Updates

New versions install by themselves each night when automatic updates are on in Railway. **Continue with Railway** and the template both turn them on. Railway then installs each new stable version of Row-Bot between 02:00 and 06:00 UTC, with your data and sign-ins kept.

**Settings › Updates** says **Updates come from Railway**, with your version, **Check in Railway** (your service's settings, where automatic updates are) and **What's new**. Row-Bot can't see Railway's settings, so if you turn automatic updates off, update from the service's settings yourself.

Each version's notes in [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/releases) end with a **For Hosts** section: on Railway you're the host, so it's for you.

## Costs

Railway bills by what your service uses, at the prices it publishes ([Railway's pricing](https://railway.com/pricing)):

| What | Price |
|---|---|
| Hobby plan | $5 a month, which includes $5 of usage |
| Memory | $10 per GB a month |
| CPU | $20 per vCPU a month |
| Volume | $0.15 per GB a month |
| Data out | $0.05 per GB |

Row-Bot uses about 0.4 GB of memory just started, more while it works, and very little CPU when idle. The 8 GB and 8 vCPU limits are a ceiling, not a charge. For light use, expect the $5 minimum to about $10 a month; heavy use, such as local speech-to-text or long browser sessions, costs more.

**Set a spending limit.** In Railway, open your workspace's **Usage** page and set a hard limit under **Usage Limits**; $10 or more leaves room for a busy month. After your first answer, **Settings › System** suggests it too: **Set a spending limit in Railway**, with a ✓ to hide the line once it's done (Row-Bot can't see Railway's billing).

The model is billed by whoever provides it: a ChatGPT or Claude plan is the subscription you already pay for, and an API key is billed by its provider. Row-Bot itself is free and open source.

## Memory And Space

- **Memory:** with an 8 GB limit, everything fits, local speech-to-text included. **Settings › System** shows **Memory … of 8 GB**. If Row-Bot ever restarts for lack of memory, Home and Monitor say so, with **Raise the memory limit**. [Row-Bot Restarted: Out Of Memory](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted#row-bot-restarted-out-of-memory) explains.
- **On Railway's trial (1 GB):** chats, memory and schedules work; browser tasks and local speech-to-text need the Hobby plan. Row-Bot says so, with **Upgrade in Railway**.
- **Space:** a Hobby volume holds up to 5 GB. Row-Bot's search model (641 MB) and local speech-to-text (464 MB) come to about 1.7 GB in the first hour with the rest of Row-Bot's data, which leaves about 3 GB for your conversations, documents and workspaces. Railway's volume view shows how full it is.

## Backups And Moving

**Railway backs up your server only on its Pro plan.** So download a backup from time to time: in **Settings › Data**, choose **Download backup**. It saves a copy on your device. **Back up now** only keeps a copy on your Row-Bot server, on the same volume. A backup holds your conversations, memories, workflows, designs and settings, without passwords or sign-ins.

The same backup moves your Row-Bot to the desktop app, to another host, or to a new Railway service, and back: see [Moving To Your Computer And Back](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser#moving-to-your-computer-and-back). To restore on Railway, choose **Restore from backup…** in **Settings › Data**, choose **Restore on restart**, then redeploy the service from its **Deployments** tab. Once everything has arrived, you can delete the old service.

## Railway's October Incident

On 21 October 2026 Railway [disclosed](https://blog.railway.com/p/security-disclosure-wednesday-october-21st) that an attacker may have reached the systems that keep customers' environment variables, and decrypted some of them. Its [preliminary report](https://blog.railway.com/p/preliminary-report-october-security-incident) covers what happened and asks customers who signed up before 21 October to replace keys kept in Railway.

What Row-Bot does about it:

- **No key in Railway's variables.** The key that encrypts your saved sign-ins isn't one of the service's variables. Row-Bot makes it on your volume at its first start, readable only by Row-Bot, and its backups leave it out.
- **A setup code that works once.** The code in your variables is useless once you've signed in. A new code you set to get back in works once too, so use it soon after setting it.
- **Your sign-ins stay on the volume,** encrypted, never in Railway's variables.

What it doesn't change: like any host, Railway runs the computer and can reach your volume, the key on it included. [What Your Host Can See](/docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see#railway) says what that means and how to protect yourself, such as spending limits on API keys.

## Getting Help

- **Railway** helps with your account, billing, the service and whether it's up. In Row-Bot, **Settings › System** shows **Hosted by Railway** with links to your service, your workspace's usage, Railway's support ([Central Station](https://station.railway.com/)) and its [status page](https://status.railway.com/).
- **Row-Bot** helps with everything inside Row-Bot. Start with [Fix A Hosted Row-Bot](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted), ask in [Discussions](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/discussions), or [report a bug](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/issues/new/choose): under "Where does Row-Bot run?" choose a hosting service, and name Railway and your memory limit.

[Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting#railway) has the technical details of how the template runs the image.

## First Launch

Route: /docs/getting-started/first-launch

Answer "How should Row-Bot think?" to choose your first model, then finish the rest at your own pace in Setup Center.

# First Launch

The first time you open Row-Bot, it asks one question: **How should Row-Bot think?** Your answer connects one working model, which becomes the default for new conversations. Everything else can wait for Setup Center. Every desktop, source, and official Docker install uses the same first launch. A Row-Bot that a hosting company runs for you asks the same question more simply: see [On A Hosted Row-Bot](#on-a-hosted-row-bot).

## How Should Row-Bot Think?

Pick one of four cards. You can add other providers later.

| Choice | What it means | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **On this computer** | Private and free. No account needed. | Uses a model server already running here (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp), or sets one up, Row-Bot's own download among them; larger models need more memory and disk space. |
| **With my subscription** | ChatGPT, Claude or Grok. | Uses a plan you already pay for and follows that provider's terms. ChatGPT and Grok sign in from Row-Bot; Claude works through Claude Code, which **Use my Claude plan** installs from Anthropic if needed before Claude's own sign-in. |
| **With an API key** | OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter and more, or your own endpoint. | Needs an API key and internet access; the provider bills per use and receives the prompts you send it. |
| **Try it free** | No plan or key: OpenRouter's free models. | Needs a free OpenRouter account and internet access; about 50 messages a day; your messages go to OpenRouter and the free model's host, and some free hosts may keep what you send. Free models don't make pictures. |

- **On this computer** opens one page. **Found on this computer** lists the model servers already running here (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or a llama.cpp server on its usual port), each with its models and **Use**; Row-Bot asks this computer only (127.0.0.1), and only when the page opens or you choose **Check again**. Below, every way to run models locally is a row of equal weight: Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, a llama.cpp server of your own, and **Download with Row-Bot (llama.cpp)**, each with one line, **Set up** and, for the others, **Get it**. Row-Bot's download suggests the model that fits this computer (Qwen3.8 27B at the build that fits the graphics card, or Qwen3.5 9B or 4B, "a smaller model for this computer (older generation)"), and downloads it when you press **Download** (the button names the size). The bar shows how much has arrived and about how long is left; the pause icon stops it, and it carries on from there next time. The sliders icon (**Choose another model**) lists every model with how it would run here. When it's ready, **Use** makes it the default and sends the test message. From a phone, the download is offered only in Row-Bot on the computer. See [Local](/docs/settings/models#local).
- **Set up Ollama** walks you through Ollama: **Install Ollama** if it is missing, **Start Ollama** if it isn't running, **Download a model**, then **Pick a model** from the models on this computer. Up to three are tagged **Recommended**: your saved choice first, then the largest models that use tools. A variant with its safety training removed ("abliterated" or "uncensored") is never recommended, but stays under **Show all models**.
- **With my subscription** lets you choose ChatGPT, Claude or Grok. ChatGPT and Grok sign in in your browser. Claude offers **Use my Claude plan**: Row-Bot installs Claude Code from Anthropic if it isn't there yet, then opens Claude's own sign-in in a small panel. Row-Bot never handles your Claude sign-in. See [Claude (Your Claude Plan)](/docs/settings/providers#claude-your-claude-plan).
- **Try it free** says what happens before anything is sent: about 50 messages a day (each step of a longer task counts as one), who sees your messages, and that free models don't make pictures. **Sign in with OpenRouter** opens OpenRouter's page in your browser; it makes you a free account if you don't have one. When you approve, OpenRouter gives Row-Bot a key of your own, saved like a pasted one, and Row-Bot lists the free models with one marked **Recommended**. **Use an API key** is there if you have one. When the day's free messages are used up, the chat says when they come back and offers **Use this computer**, **Sign in with a plan** or **Add credits** (once you've ever bought credits, OpenRouter allows about 1,000 free messages a day).
- **With an API key** lists the recommended providers first and the rest under **More providers**. Choose one, paste its key, and pick a model. Advanced users can add an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp, LocalAI, LiteLLM or SGLang.

After you pick a model, Row-Bot sends it a short test message. A local model can take a minute to load the first time. If the model doesn't answer, choose **Try again** or **Choose another model**.

If Row-Bot finds Hermes Agent or OpenClaw on this computer, it then offers to bring that assistant along: its memories (which wait for you to check them), past chats if you tick them, persona, skills, MCP servers (turned off) and main model, and its keys only if you tick them. Choose **Import from …** or **Not now**; you can import later from **Settings › Data**. See [what comes over](/docs/operations/#import-from-another-assistant), and for Hermes, [Coming From Hermes?](/docs/getting-started/coming-from-hermes).

Choose **Set up later** to look around first. Home then stops opening setup for the rest of this window, and Overview reminds you to choose how Row-Bot thinks.

In an installed Row-Bot, the first screen also says that Row-Bot downloads updates in the background, with a link to **Settings › Updates**, where you can turn that off. See [Updates](/docs/operations/updates).

## On A Hosted Row-Bot

When a hosting company runs Row-Bot for you (its server is set up with `ROW_BOT_HOSTED_BY`, as Row-Bot on Railway is), the server has no graphics card for running models, so the first launch asks with big buttons instead of cards:

- **Sign in with ChatGPT**: one click starts ChatGPT's sign-in, copies its code and opens OpenAI's page in a new tab. Paste the code there and approve; Row-Bot notices when you're done. If your browser doesn't allow the copy, or doesn't open the tab, the code and an **Open sign-in page** button stay on screen. If the code runs out, **Get a new code** starts again.
- **Use my Claude plan**: Row-Bot installs Claude Code from Anthropic on your server and opens Claude's own sign-in, as described in [Claude (Your Claude Plan)](/docs/settings/providers#claude-your-claude-plan).
- **No plan? Try it free**: the same as **Try it free** above. OpenRouter's page opens in a new tab and returns to your Row-Bot's own address, so it works from a phone too.
- **Other ways**:
  - **Use an API key**: the same providers as **With an API key**.
  - **Use my own model server**: opens the custom endpoint form with Ollama picked, for a model server you run elsewhere, such as Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM or LM Studio. See [Use Your Own Model Server](/docs/guides/own-model-server) for reaching it safely from the internet.
  - **Sign in with Grok**: xAI's page sends your browser to an address on the server's own computer, which your browser can't open. Copy the address of that page from the address bar and paste it into Row-Bot.

A line below says that running models on the server needs a GPU, with a link to the desktop app.

After you sign in, Row-Bot picks the provider's own first model, sends it a short test message and opens a new conversation with one suggestion, **What can you do for me?**, which sends with one tap. You can change the model any time in the model picker. With an API key or your own model server, you pick the model yourself as usual.

After the first answer, a small card in that conversation offers **Add Row-Bot to your phone**; it doesn't follow into new conversations. On a computer, **Show the code** shows a QR code that signs your phone in once; on a phone, the card shows how to add Row-Bot to the home screen. Close the card with **×** and it doesn't come back; **Settings › Devices & remote access** connects a phone any time.

To start a hosted Row-Bot, and for what's different there, see [Row-Bot In Your Browser](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser).

## Setup Center

Setup Center is where you finish the rest whenever you like. Open it from Overview's **Finish setup** card or from the command palette (**Setup Center**).

1. **What would you like to use?** Pick any of: chat assistant, research and documents, workflow automation, designs, code, messaging channels, or local and private AI. Recommended areas move to the top.
2. **Continue setup** lists each area with one button that goes where it is set up: Models, Knowledge, Workflows, Designer (starts a design in a chat), Developer, Apps (the services you use, including your accounts and messaging channels, in Settings › Apps), Skills, Tools, Voice, and a Final Check that opens Monitor to run the diagnosis. Picking messaging channels moves Apps to the top. A hosted Row-Bot adds **Add your phone** (to **Settings › Devices & remote access**; it ticks itself once another device is signed in) and **Back up** (to **Settings › Data**), says that local and private AI there means your own model server or Row-Bot on your own computer, and its diagnosis starts with a **Hosted by …** row that reads **Reachable** when your server answers. It leaves out the public link's row: your host gives the server its address.
3. Each area's **⋯** menu marks it done or skips it. Areas Row-Bot can check tick themselves once you have set them up: a model you chose, a workflow you made, turned on or ran, a code folder you connected. What Row-Bot comes with, such as the starter workflows, doesn't count.

The links at the bottom import from Hermes or OpenClaw, or set up private knowledge search.

## Install Private Knowledge Search

Row-Bot can search your memories and documents by meaning with **Mixedbread Embed Large v1**, a separate local model for semantic memory and document search. It is a 675 MB download from Hugging Face and is not the model that writes chat responses.

Install it from **Settings › Documents** (Setup Center's **Set up private knowledge embeddings** link goes there). Under **Index health and maintenance**, **Search model files** offers **Download** for the first install, **Retry** to load an already cached model again, and **Repair** to replace a damaged download. Files go into Row-Bot's private cache; documents and memories are not uploaded, and normal recall stays offline after the download. Docker keeps this cache in its named `/data` volume.

Until it is installed, Row-Bot continues with bounded lexical and graph fallback, so chat and memory do not stop working. Rebuild the document and memory vectors after changing the search model.

## Privacy, Cost, And Credentials

Local model runs can stay on your computer. Hosted, subscription, Live voice, cloud speech, web search, account, channel, and app features can contact outside services when configured and used. Enter provider keys and account sign-ins only through first launch or the relevant Settings page. Cost depends on the provider or service you choose.

## Troubleshooting

- If Row-Bot can't find Ollama, install or start it, then check again from the same card.
- If a provider connects but no models appear, refresh its model list in its sheet in Settings › Models.
- If the test message fails, try again or choose another model; a small local model may need a minute to load.
- If the private knowledge model download fails, check internet access to Hugging Face and try **Download** again later.
- If you skipped setup, open Setup Center from Overview or the command palette.

## Coming From Hermes?

Route: /docs/getting-started/coming-from-hermes

Bring your Hermes Agent memories, persona, skills, MCP servers and model into Row-Bot, see what doesn't come over, and how Hermes's ideas map to Row-Bot's.

# Coming From Hermes?

If you use [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent), Nous Research's open-source agent, Row-Bot can bring over what it knows about you and how you set it up. The import reads Hermes's folder and never changes it, and nothing leaves your computer. This page describes Hermes Agent v0.23 (November 2026).

## In One Minute

1. [Install Row-Bot](/docs/getting-started/installation) and answer **How should Row-Bot think?** on [first launch](/docs/getting-started/first-launch).
2. When Row-Bot finds Hermes on this computer (in the folder `HERMES_HOME` names, in `~/.hermes`, or in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` on Windows), it offers to bring it along. **Import from Hermes Agent** opens **Settings › Data › Import from another assistant**; **Not now** leaves it for later.
3. Choose **Scan folders**. Row-Bot lists what it found and where each item goes, and changes nothing yet.
4. Tick what you want, choose **Apply selected items**, then **Confirm import**.
5. When it's done, choose **Review memories** to check the memories before they're saved. They wait for you if you'd rather do it later, even after Row-Bot restarts: open **Settings › Memory › Import memories** and choose **Review** beside **From Hermes Agent**. They wait for 7 days.

If your Hermes home is somewhere else, enter that folder as **Source folder** in **Settings › Data**. Leave **Target folder** empty, so everything comes into the Row-Bot you're using.

## What Comes Over

- **Memories** (`memories/MEMORY.md` and `memories/USER.md`) wait in **Import memories** for you to check. Nothing is saved to Row-Bot's memory until you import them there.
- **Past chats** (`state.db`) are offered but not ticked. Tick them to have them wait in **Import memories** with your memories, where Row-Bot can look in them for things worth remembering (see below).
- **Persona** (`SOUL.md`) becomes your personality in **Settings › Preferences**: its prose, shortened to fit.
- **Agent instructions** (`AGENTS.md`) become a skill, *Instructions from Hermes*, in **Settings › Skills**. It isn't pinned, so it isn't part of every chat.
- **Skills**: each skill's `SKILL.md` is copied to **Settings › Skills**.
- **MCP servers** (`mcp_servers` in `config.yaml`) come over when you tick them in the list. They arrive in **Settings › Apps** turned off, without their `env` or header values: fill those in, check the server, then turn it on.
- **Main model** (`model` in `config.yaml`) becomes the main model in **Settings › Models** when its provider is one Row-Bot has, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Google, xAI or Ollama.
- **Your own model servers** (custom providers) become **Custom endpoints** in **Settings › Models**. Row-Bot contacts one only when you use it.
- **API keys** (`.env`) come over only if you turn on **Include API keys and tokens** before you scan, into the system keychain.

What you already have stays as it is: an item that would replace your personality, main model or a skill is shown as a conflict, and comes over only if you turn on **Replace what you already have**, which keeps a backup first. An app or custom endpoint with the same name as one of yours is left alone.

### Memories From Your Past Chats

Hermes's chats aren't turned into Row-Bot conversations, but Row-Bot can look in them for things worth remembering. Tick **Past chats from state.db** in the import, then choose **Review memories** when it's done. (Or open **Import memories** in **Home › Knowledge** and add Hermes's `state.db`, or a file from `hermes sessions export`, yourself.) Turn on **Also look for memories in … past conversations**: it reads only what you wrote, newest first, up to the limit the dialog shows, using your chat model (on this computer, or through its provider). Nothing is read until you turn it on. You check what it finds like any other memory, and **Undo import** takes an import back for 7 days.

The import copies `state.db` into Row-Bot's own data first, newest chats included, so it works while Hermes is running and never changes Hermes's folder.

## What Doesn't Come Over

- **Scheduled (cron) jobs** aren't converted, and the import says so: make a [workflow](/docs/guides/workflows) for each one. A workflow is a scheduled chat, and can also start from a webhook or when another workflow finishes.
- **The messaging gateway**: set up [Channels](/docs/integrations/channels) for Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp or SMS.
- **Sign-ins** (`auth.json`, MCP tokens): sign in again in Row-Bot.
- **Hermes plugins**: they aren't run. Row-Bot can browse the Hermes catalog in [Settings › Apps](/docs/settings/apps); a package made only for the Hermes app can't be added there.
- **Nous Portal models**: Row-Bot doesn't connect to the Nous Portal, so the import lists such a model as not brought over. Choose a model in **Settings › Models**.
- **Kanban and `/loop`**: Row-Bot has neither. A [goal](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/#goals) keeps working until something is done, and a workflow repeats on a schedule.

Hermes's sessions, logs, cron jobs and plugins can be copied into the import's report for you to look at (tick them in the list), with secrets removed from text files. Binary files are only noted there, not copied.

## How Things Map

| In Hermes | In Row-Bot |
| --- | --- |
| `/goal` | [Goals](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/#goals) |
| Cron jobs | [Workflows](/docs/guides/workflows) |
| `delegate_task` | [Delegated agents](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/#delegated-agents) (helpers) |
| The messaging gateway | [Channels](/docs/integrations/channels) |
| Manual approvals | **Ask** |
| Smart approvals | **Auto**: its reviewer reads only your own messages |
| YOLO | **Hands-off**, turned on by you, per conversation |
| `config.yaml` | Settings: there is no file to edit |
| Memory files | Memory in [Knowledge](/docs/knowledge/) |

## What's Different On Purpose

- **Approvals decide what an action may do.** Changing, sending, deleting and paying go through your approval level, and Auto's reviewer never sees web pages, files or tool results, so outside text can't approve its own action. See [How Row-Bot Keeps An Agent In Bounds](/docs/privacy-safety/agent-in-bounds).
- **Imported memories are checked first.** Hermes's memory files can hold notes the agent wrote itself, so they wait for you in **Import memories**.
- **Settings, not a config file.** Everything you set up lives in **Settings**, and Row-Bot keeps its data in its own folder.

## Using Your ChatGPT Or Claude Plan

Row-Bot signs in to ChatGPT and Grok plans directly. A Claude Pro or Max plan works through your own Claude Code, which Row-Bot installs from Anthropic if needed; Row-Bot never handles your Claude sign-in. See [Settings: Providers](/docs/settings/providers#claude-your-claude-plan).

## Questions

- **Can I keep using Hermes?** Yes. The import only reads Hermes's folder, and Row-Bot keeps its own data in its own folder, so both can run.
- **Can I import again?** Yes. Items you already have are skipped, or shown as conflicts.
- **How do I undo it?** Anything the import replaced is backed up first, in the `migration-backups` folder of Row-Bot's data. Imported memories have **Undo import** in **Import memories** for 7 days. Remove a skill or an app in its Settings page.
- **I also use OpenClaw.** The same import brings OpenClaw over: choose it as **Source app** in **Settings › Data**. See [Import From Another Assistant](/docs/operations/#import-from-another-assistant).

## Your First Tasks

Route: /docs/getting-started/first-tasks

Five things to try in your first ten minutes with Row-Bot, each in plain words.

# Your First Tasks

Once Row-Bot can think (see [First Launch](/docs/getting-started/first-launch)), try these from **New chat**. Each one shows a different part of Row-Bot. Type them in your own words: you don't need to name a feature.

## 1. Plan Something

> "I want to redo my small garden this spring on a £300 budget. Lay out what I should do and when."

Row-Bot may first ask a question or two in a card. Then it makes a **page** beside the chat, a plan you can approve, change or skip step by step. **Send to Row-Bot** sends your decisions back. See [Pages](/docs/chat/#pages).

## 2. Ask About Today

> "What's the weather in Leeds today?"

Anything that changes, such as weather, news or prices, is looked up live and never guessed. The step shows what Row-Bot checked.

## 3. Let Row-Bot Remember

> "By the way, I'm vegetarian and my partner is called Sam."

Row-Bot saves both and says so. In a new chat, ask "What should I cook tonight?" and it uses what it knows. See what it remembers in **Home › Knowledge**, or keep a chat out of memory with [incognito](/docs/chat/#incognito-chats).

## 4. Set Something Up To Run By Itself

> "Every weekday at 8am I'd like a short summary of the BBC technology headlines."

Row-Bot creates a [workflow](/docs/guides/workflows) and shows its steps. Find it in **Home › Workflows**, where **Run** tries it now. A reminder works the same way: "Remind me to call the dentist tomorrow at 10."

## 5. Use It From Your Phone

Open **Settings › Devices & remote access › Connect a phone or computer** and scan the code. Your phone gets the same chats, approvals and pages. See [Phone And Native Desktop](/docs/mobile-native/).

## Next

- [Chat](/docs/chat/) covers the composer, models, attachments and approvals.
- [How Row-Bot Works](/docs/concepts/) explains what happens behind a request.
- [Keyboard Shortcuts](/docs/reference/keyboard-shortcuts) and [Slash Commands](/docs/reference/slash-commands) make everyday use quicker.

## Models And Providers

Route: /docs/configuration/models-and-providers

Configure providers, discover models, choose defaults, and pin quick model choices.

# Models And Providers

Providers are where models come from. Models are the specific choices you use in conversations, workflows, designs, code folders, voice, and other Row-Bot surfaces.

To understand what leaves the app, when tools run, and where approvals fit, read [How A Request Runs](/docs/concepts/request-lifecycle).

## Recommended Setup Order

1. Open Settings -> Providers (or answer **How should Row-Bot think?** at first launch).
2. Connect one provider path.
3. Refresh provider health.
4. Open Settings -> Models.
5. Refresh the catalog.
6. Choose the **Brain** model, and Vision, Image and Video models if you want those jobs.
7. Pin the models you use most.
8. Test in a chat.

## Choosing A Provider Path

Use local Ollama for local-first privacy and no provider billing. Use an API provider for strong hosted models. Use a subscription account when you already have the supported provider account. Use a custom endpoint for advanced local or self-hosted OpenAI-compatible runtimes.

## Choosing Models

Keep at least one everyday chat model and one stronger tool-capable model pinned. For code folders, designs, workflows, and complex tools, choose a model that can handle tool calls and enough context.

For models with exact reasoning capabilities, Row-Bot exposes a per-thread [Reasoning control](/docs/chat/reasoning-controls) with only the efforts, toggle, or token-budget choices that model supports. Provider default remains available as the compatibility-safe option.

For Ollama, Row-Bot prefers explicit tool-calling metadata, then the daemon's reported capability list. A reported `tools` capability enables agent use even for a model family newer than Row-Bot's maintained fallback catalogue; an explicit capability list that omits `tools` remains authoritative. Family fallbacks are used only when the daemon provides no capability metadata.

## Troubleshooting

- If a provider connects but has no models, refresh Models.
- If a model fails with tools, choose a tool-capable model.
- If an Ollama model is unexpectedly excluded from agent use, refresh the local catalogue and inspect the capabilities reported by the installed Ollama daemon.
- If a custom endpoint fails, check base URL, model name, API compatibility, and context window.

## Use Your Own Model Server

Route: /docs/guides/own-model-server

Connect Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM or LM Studio as a custom endpoint, and reach a model server at home safely from a Row-Bot on another network.

# Use Your Own Model Server

Row-Bot can use models that run on a computer you control, such as a desktop with a good graphics card, through a **custom endpoint**. Row-Bot talks to it the way it talks to OpenAI, through the server's OpenAI-compatible API. Ollama, llama.cpp (`llama-server`), vLLM and LM Studio all have one, and so do LocalAI, LiteLLM, SGLang and oMLX.

On this page, **your model server** is the computer that runs the models. **Your Row-Bot** may run somewhere else: the desktop app on a laptop, Docker on a home server, or a hosted Row-Bot on the internet.

If Ollama runs on the same computer as Row-Bot, you don't need this page: choose **On this computer** at first launch, or use its tile in **Settings › Models**.

## What You Need

- A model server with an OpenAI-compatible address. Its base URL ends in `/v1`.
- A model that can call tools. Agents, workflows and Row-Bot's own tools work through tool calls; a model without them can only chat.
- Enough context. When the server doesn't say how much a model has, Row-Bot assumes 32,768 tokens, so start the server with at least that much if your graphics card has room.

## Add The Endpoint In Row-Bot

1. Open **Settings › Models**, choose **Add a provider › Your server**, or under **Custom endpoints** choose **Add custom endpoint**.
2. Fill in the form:

   | Field | What to enter |
   |---|---|
   | **Endpoint id** | A short name in lowercase letters, numbers, `-` or `_`, such as `home-gpu`. |
   | **Display name** | The name the model picker shows, such as "Home GPU". |
   | **Base URL** | The server's address, ending in `/v1`. Each server's address is below. |
   | **Server type** | **Ollama**, **llama.cpp**, **vLLM** or **LM Studio** for those servers; **OpenAI-compatible** for anything else. |
   | **Execution location** | **Local/private** when the model server is on your own network next to Row-Bot; **Remote/proxy** when Row-Bot reaches it over the internet. |
   | **API key required** | On whenever the server checks a key, and always for a server the internet can reach. |

   **Endpoint id**, **Server type** and **Execution location** can't be changed later: remove the endpoint and add it again.

3. Choose **Save**. With **API key required** on, Row-Bot asks for the key next: paste it under **API key** and choose **Save key**. Row-Bot keeps the key with its other secrets, not in its settings file, and sends it with every request as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.
4. Row-Bot reads the server's list of models. They appear in the model picker under the display name.
5. To check that a model can do agent work, open the endpoint's **More actions** menu and choose **Probe**. The row then says **Agent ready** (chat, streaming and tool calls work), **Chat only** (it answers, but tool calls don't work) or **Unavailable**. **Show probe details** lists each check.

To change the key later, choose **Manage _name_ API key** in the same menu. **Edit** changes the other fields, and **Advanced** there holds the context size, vision, tool calling and reasoning settings.

## Start Your Model Server

Each server's base URL below is for the Row-Bot desktop app on the same computer. From another computer on your network, use the model server's network address instead of `127.0.0.1`, such as `http://192.168.1.20:11434/v1`. From outside your network, read [Reach It From Anywhere](#reach-it-from-anywhere).

### Ollama

- **Base URL:** `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`. **Server type:** **Ollama** (Row-Bot saves it as **OpenAI-compatible**, which is how it talks to Ollama).
- Ollama listens only on its own computer. For other computers on your home network, set `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` before starting it.
- Ollama gives a model 4,096 tokens of context unless you set more. Set `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768` (or what fits your graphics card) before starting Ollama, and enter the same number as **Native context limit** under **Advanced**: Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API doesn't report it.
- Ollama has no sign-in or keys of its own. To reach it from outside your home network, put [the key check](#a-key-check-in-front-of-ollama) in front of it.

### llama.cpp

```bash
llama-server -m /path/to/model.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 -c 32768 --jinja --api-key YOUR-KEY
```

- **Base URL:** `http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1`. **Server type:** **llama.cpp**.
- `--jinja` uses the model's own chat template, which tool calls need. `--api-key` refuses every request without the key. Row-Bot reads the context size from the server.

### vLLM

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --max-model-len 32768 --api-key YOUR-KEY --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes
```

- **Base URL:** `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1`. **Server type:** **vLLM**.
- Tool calls need `--enable-auto-tool-choice` and the parser for your model's family; vLLM's tool-calling docs list them (`hermes` suits Qwen models). Row-Bot reads the context size from the server.
- vLLM listens on every network address unless `--host` says otherwise.

### LM Studio

- Start the server from LM Studio's **Developer** tab. **Base URL:** `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1`. **Server type:** **LM Studio**.
- For other computers on your network, turn on **Serve on Local Network** in the server settings.
- To require a key, turn on **Require Authentication**, create a token with **Manage Tokens**, and paste the token into Row-Bot as the API key.
- Row-Bot reads each model's context size from LM Studio, as it loaded the model. To load it at another size, open the model's settings in Row-Bot (the sliders icon) and choose **Reload in LM Studio at _size_** (LM Studio 0.4 or later), or change **Context Length** in LM Studio.

## Reach It From Anywhere

A Row-Bot on another network can't see addresses inside your home: a hosted Row-Bot, a Row-Bot on a server, or the desktop app on a laptop away from home. It needs an HTTPS address the internet can reach, with a key check in front of the model server.

**Note: On a hosted Row-Bot**
Private addresses such as `10.x`, `192.168.x` or `169.254.x` are on the hosting company's network, not yours. A hosted Row-Bot asks before an endpoint uses one: choose **Allow and save** only if your model server really runs there. It never connects to a cloud metadata address such as `169.254.169.254`.

| Way | When it fits | What you need |
|---|---|---|
| [Your own HTTPS address](#your-own-https-address) | You can open a port on your router, or the model server has a public address | A domain name and Caddy |
| [Cloudflare Tunnel](#cloudflare-tunnel) | You'd rather not open ports | A domain on Cloudflare and `cloudflared` |
| [Tailscale Funnel](#tailscale-funnel) | No domain and no open ports | A Tailscale account with Funnel turned on |

In every case the model server keeps listening only on its own computer (`127.0.0.1`), and nothing reaches it without the key.

**Danger: Never put Ollama on the internet without a sign-in**
Ollama has no sign-in of its own. Anyone who finds an open Ollama can use your graphics card, download models onto your disk and delete the ones you have. Never forward port 11434 on your router, and never point a tunnel straight at Ollama: put [the key check](#a-key-check-in-front-of-ollama) in front of it. The same goes for any model server started without a key.

### A Key Check In Front Of Ollama

llama.cpp, vLLM and LM Studio check a key themselves when you start them with one. Ollama doesn't, so a small proxy does it: [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com) passes a request to Ollama only when it carries your key.

1. Make a long random key, for example with your password manager or `openssl rand -hex 32`.
2. Save this as `Caddyfile` in a folder of its own, with your key in place of `YOUR-KEY`:

   ```text
   :8090 {
       bind 127.0.0.1
       @key header Authorization "Bearer YOUR-KEY"
       handle @key {
           reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:11434 {
               header_up Host localhost:11434
           }
       }
       handle {
           respond 401
       }
   }
   ```

3. Run `caddy run` in that folder. A tunnel now points at `http://localhost:8090`, not at Ollama.

Ollama refuses requests addressed to another name, so the `header_up` line passes them on as `localhost`. The file holds your key: keep it private.

### Your Own HTTPS Address

Point a name such as `models.example.com` at your home (or the server), forward ports 80 and 443 on your router to the computer that runs Caddy, and Caddy gets an HTTPS certificate by itself. Use the name in place of `:8090`, without the `bind` line:

```text
models.example.com {
    @key header Authorization "Bearer YOUR-KEY"
    handle @key {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:11434 {
            header_up Host localhost:11434
        }
    }
    handle {
        respond 401
    }
}
```

For llama.cpp, vLLM or LM Studio, use their port instead of `11434` and leave out the `header_up` lines. In Row-Bot, the base URL is `https://models.example.com/v1`.

### Cloudflare Tunnel

`cloudflared` on the model server connects out to Cloudflare, and Cloudflare gives it an HTTPS address, so no port opens on your router.

- **To try it:** `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8090` prints a temporary `https://….trycloudflare.com` address. It changes every time it starts.
- **To keep it:** create a tunnel in Cloudflare's Zero Trust dashboard, install its connector on the model server, and route a name on your domain, such as `models.example.com`, to `http://localhost:8090`. For llama.cpp, vLLM or LM Studio started with a key, route it to their own port.
- In Row-Bot, the base URL is `https://models.example.com/v1`.

Row-Bot sends its key in one header, so it can't use Cloudflare Access service tokens, which need two of their own (`CF-Access-Client-Id` and `CF-Access-Client-Secret`). Leave the address outside Cloudflare Access, and let the key check on your model server do the job.

Cloudflare decrypts the traffic on its way through, so it can read your prompts and the model's answers.

### Tailscale Funnel

Funnel gives a computer on your tailnet a public HTTPS address, `https://<computer>.<tailnet>.ts.net`, and passes requests to a port on it. The encryption ends on your computer, so Tailscale's relays can't read the traffic.

- On the model server, run `tailscale funnel 8090` for Ollama behind the key check; for llama.cpp, vLLM or LM Studio started with a key, use their port instead. Add `--bg` to keep it running after you close the terminal. The first time, Tailscale asks you to turn on HTTPS and Funnel for your tailnet.
- In Row-Bot, the base URL is `https://<computer>.<tailnet>.ts.net/v1`.
- Funnel is open to the whole internet: anyone with the address reaches the port, so the key check matters just as much.

If your Row-Bot runs on a computer in the same tailnet, such as the desktop app on your laptop or your own server, you don't need Funnel: use the model server's tailnet name, such as `http://<computer>:11434/v1`, with the server listening on the network (for Ollama, `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0`). A hosted Row-Bot isn't on your tailnet, so it needs Funnel.

### Check It From Outside

From a computer outside your home network, with your address and key:

```bash
curl https://models.example.com/v1/models
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR-KEY" https://models.example.com/v1/models
```

The first must be refused with `401`; the second lists your models. If the first lists them too, anyone can use your model server: fix the key check before you go on.

## Privacy

Every request sends your prompt, files you attach and tool results to your model server, through whatever carries the traffic there: nothing else sees it on your own HTTPS address or Tailscale Funnel, and Cloudflare can read it on Cloudflare Tunnel. Read [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/) for every connection Row-Bot makes.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Row-Bot couldn't reach https://…":** check that the base URL ends in `/v1`, the server is running, and it can be reached from where your Row-Bot runs (from the internet, for a hosted Row-Bot). Try the [`curl` check](#check-it-from-outside). The row says **Unavailable** until a refresh works.
- **"The model server refused the API key":** the server turned the key down. Choose **Enter API key**, paste the key again, and Row-Bot refreshes the endpoint. **"This endpoint needs an API key"** means none is saved yet.
- **Ollama refuses the key although it's right:** Ollama answers 403 Forbidden when a request reaches it under your public name. Send it through [the key check](#a-key-check-in-front-of-ollama), which rewrites the name.
- **The row says Chat only:** the model or the server isn't set up for tool calls. Choose a model that supports tools, start `llama-server` with `--jinja`, or start vLLM with `--enable-auto-tool-choice` and the right `--tool-call-parser`, then **Probe** again.
- **Answers lose track of the conversation or stop early:** the server has less context than Row-Bot thinks. Start it with more, or set **Native context limit** under **Advanced** to what the server uses. A model's settings sheet in **Settings › Models** shows what the server loaded and, under **More**, a **Reply length** limit for replies that run on.
- **The first answer is slow:** the server loads the model on first use; the next answers come faster.

Related: [Settings: Providers](/docs/settings/providers), [Models And Providers](/docs/configuration/models-and-providers) and [Reasoning Controls](/docs/chat/reasoning-controls) for a custom endpoint's reasoning settings.

## Row-Bot Interface

Route: /docs/app-shell/navigation

Find your way around Row-Bot: the sidebar, Home, a conversation and its details card, panels, the terminal, the command palette and Settings.

# Row-Bot Interface

Row-Bot has one window with three parts: the **sidebar** on the left, the main area in the middle (Home, a conversation, the conversation library, or Settings), and, in a conversation, the **panels** for its designs and code folders on the right, with the **terminal** docked underneath when you open it.

## The Sidebar

- The top row holds **Home** (the house icon, also the Row-Bot logo), which opens the Home tabs: Overview, Workflows, Knowledge, Monitor and Insights, and Learning while it's on (see [Home](/docs/home/)); **Search**, which opens the command palette; and the button that collapses the sidebar.
- **New chat** starts a conversation. Its **▾** starts a chat with one of your favourite agents, or **All agents…** opens the Agents dialog.
- **Conversations** lists your conversations, pinned ones first. The icons beside the heading filter by type: All, Chats, Designs, Code and Workflows. A conversation's row shows when it is replying, waiting for approval, or has agents working.
- A row's pin button keeps it at the top; its **⋯** menu renames it, exports it as Markdown or PDF, or deletes it. After you confirm a delete, the chat leaves the list and **Undo** stays in the notice for a few seconds; the delete happens when the notice goes. A chat you started and never used isn't listed here or on Home (unless it's open); the Conversation library still lists it, and **New chat** reuses an empty chat it just made in this window instead of making another.
- **Show all** lists every conversation in the sidebar; **Conversation library** opens the full library to search, filter, export and clean up. See [Chat](/docs/chat/#find-export-and-clean-up).
- **Agents**, below the conversations, shows your favourite agents with each one's face and name (one click starts a chat with that agent; until you pin some, the built-in Everyday agents stand in) and **All agents**, which opens the Agents dialog with the whole profile library. See [Profiles, Goals, And Agents](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/).
- The **attention indicator** at the bottom appears only when something needs you: waiting approvals (with **Approve** and **Deny** in place), problems (opens Monitor), or an update: available, or **Restart to update** once it is downloaded and ready (opens Updates; see [Updates](/docs/operations/updates)).
- **Buddy** sits above **Settings**. In the native Windows and macOS apps, drag Buddy itself out of the sidebar to undock its desktop overlay. See [Settings: Buddy](/docs/settings/buddy).
