- An X sign-in from before 5.3 becomes your first account the next time Row-Bot reaches X. Until then it shows as "Your X account · Signed in before Row-Bot 5.3".

## Sign In From Another Device

In the Row-Bot desktop app, signing in to Google or X opens the browser on the computer Row-Bot runs on. From any other signed-in device, such as your phone, another computer's browser or a Row-Bot server, signing in works when Row-Bot has exactly one public HTTPS address, set up in **Settings › Devices & remote access**: Row-Bot opens the service's sign-in page in that device's browser, and the service sends you back to Row-Bot at that address. If the page doesn't open, choose **Open Google's sign-in page** (or X's). Finish within five minutes, on the device that started it.

- **Google** returns only to addresses the client lists. A Desktop app client lists only the computer Row-Bot runs on, so another device needs a **Web application** client whose **Authorised redirect URIs** include the address the guide shows there: Row-Bot's public address followed by `/api/v1/accounts/google/auth/callback`. Row-Bot checks the file lists it before saving it.
- **X** returns to the callback address the guide shows on that device, which must be listed in your app's sign-in settings.

Without a public HTTPS address, or with a Google client that doesn't list it, the account's settings say what's missing. **Check** and **Disconnect** work from every device.

## Tokens And Scopes

Secrets use the configured operating-system secret store when available. Settings show status, not the secret value. A service may still retain its own authorisation grant until you revoke it there. Use the narrowest scopes that support the feature and disconnect access you no longer use.

## When A Sign-In Expires

Overview's **Needs you** shows the app, such as **Sign in to Google**, with a button that opens the account's own settings at its fix. Monitor offers **Reconnect Google** or **Reconnect X**, which starts the sign-in again: in the Row-Bot desktop app through a browser on the computer Row-Bot runs on, and on another device through Row-Bot's public address (see [Sign In From Another Device](#sign-in-from-another-device)). Where a device can't sign in, the fix opens the account's settings instead, where Check and Disconnect work.

## Troubleshooting

- Confirm the system browser returned to the same Row-Bot instance that started the flow.
- For GitHub CLI, refresh CLI authorisation after signing in or changing accounts.
- If Row-Bot says the Google file isn't a valid Google OAuth client file, create a client of type **Desktop app** (or **Web application**, to sign in from another device) and download its file again.
- If Google shows `redirect_uri_mismatch`, or Row-Bot says the client doesn't list its sign-in address, add the redirect URI the guide shows to the Web application client in Google Cloud, download its file again and choose it. Google accepts only an `https` address on a domain name, not an IP address.
- If a sign-in from another device says it has expired or isn't valid, start it again from that device: each one works once, for five minutes.
- If Google asks you to sign in again every week, your Google app is still in Testing; publish it in **Audience** (see [Google Sign-Ins In Testing Last 7 Days](#google-sign-ins-in-testing-last-7-days)).
- If a callback fails, repeat the supported flow instead of copying browser storage.
- If an action is denied after connection, review both the service scopes and the Row-Bot approval policy.

## Channels

Route: /docs/integrations/channels

Connect Row-Bot to messaging channels as apps: setup steps, pairing, public addresses, conversations and threads, delivery, and safe external behavior.

# Channels

Channels connect Row-Bot to external messaging platforms: Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, and SMS through Twilio. Use channels when you want to message Row-Bot outside the desktop app or send workflow results somewhere specific.

Each channel is an app in **Settings › Apps**, under the **Communication** category: **Telegram**, **WhatsApp**, **Discord**, **Slack** and **Text messages** (SMS). On the app's page the channel is a **Built in** way to connect. Slack's page also lists Slack's own hosted server, which lets Row-Bot work in your Slack workspace rather than talk to you through it. A package can bring a channel too; it is listed with its package.

## Setup Workflow

1. Open **Settings › Apps** and choose the channel's app, or type "connect telegram" (or the channel you want) in the command palette.
2. Choose **Set up** (or **Open** once it is set up). The channel's own settings open, showing only that channel.
3. Follow **Connect _channel_**. Each step says what to do where, links to the platform's page (such as **Open @BotFather** for Telegram), and has its field in place: paste a value and choose **Save** for it.
4. Choose **Start _channel_**. A channel that needs a public address, such as SMS, opens your tunnel by itself; its setup is the public link in **Settings › Devices & remote access**. WhatsApp's first start installs its bridge, then shows a code to scan with your phone.
5. Pair or approve your account before trusting private messages: **Get pairing code for _channel_**, then send the code to the bot from the account you want to approve.
6. **Send a test message to me** to check it works with a low-risk message.

## Controls

- **Save** and **Clear** beside each field store or remove that value. Saved values are never shown again.
- **Start _channel_** begins the channel; it starts again with Row-Bot until you stop it. **Stop _channel_** shuts it down.
- **Reachable at** shows the public address a channel uses, with **Copy**.
- **Get pairing code for _channel_** shows a code that approves the account that sends it; it expires after one hour. Some channels approve people their own way and say so.
- **Paired accounts** lists who is approved, with **Revoke** for each.
- **Reset session** (WhatsApp) unlinks your phone and shows a new code to scan.
- **Reply to voice notes with a voice note** (Telegram and WhatsApp, on until you turn it off): when you send a voice note, Row-Bot answers for listening and sends its reply as a voice note too, right after the text, so code, links and tables still arrive as text. It speaks with the voice chosen under **Read aloud** in **Settings › Voice**: Kokoro on the computer running Row-Bot, or a cloud voice you chose, which is then sent the reply's text. With no voice that can speak (Kokoro not installed, and no cloud voice with its key saved), the reply is text only. A reply too long for one voice note (about an hour of speech on WhatsApp), or in a language the voice can't speak, goes as text only. The voice note you send is transcribed on the computer running Row-Bot, in the language set in **Settings › Voice**.
- **More settings** holds the channel's other fields.
- **`/reasoning`** shows or changes the reasoning choice for that channel conversation's active model. Run it without an argument to see the exact valid choices.
- **`/new`** starts a fresh conversation; see [Conversations](#conversations).
- **`/incognito on`** and **`/incognito off`** make the channel conversation [incognito](/docs/chat/#incognito-chats): nothing in it is read for memory while it is on.

## Conversations

Every chat with Row-Bot on a channel is also a conversation in Row-Bot, with its history, tools, approvals and goal, so you can open it in the app and carry on there.

- **Slack channels.** Each Slack thread is its own conversation. Mention @Row-Bot in a channel to start one: Row-Bot replies in a thread under your message, and that thread continues the same conversation. Mention Row-Bot again in the thread to continue. To continue with a plain reply instead, your Slack app also needs the `message.channels` event and the `channels:history` scope (`message.groups` and `groups:history` for private channels). They are optional: with them, Slack sends Row-Bot every message in the channels it is in, and Row-Bot ignores all but replies in its own threads from accounts you approved.
- **Discord servers.** Mention @Row-Bot in a channel to start a conversation. Row-Bot opens a Discord thread from your message and replies there, and replies in that thread continue the conversation without a mention. Invite the bot with the **Create Public Threads** and **Send Messages in Threads** permissions. Without them, or in a channel that has no threads, the channel keeps one conversation.
- **Direct messages, Telegram, WhatsApp and SMS.** Each direct message or chat keeps one conversation going.
- **Starting fresh.** Send `/new` to start a new conversation, on any channel (Telegram also accepts `/newthread`). In a Slack or Discord thread, the thread continues in the new conversation. Earlier conversations stay in Row-Bot. An approval the earlier conversation was waiting for no longer holds up the chat; answer it in Row-Bot.
- **Names.** A Slack thread's conversation is named from its first message and a Discord thread's from the thread's name. A name you give a conversation in Row-Bot is kept.
- **Several attachments.** Send several photos, voice notes or files in one message, or as an album, and Row-Bot answers them together in one reply. It reads each photo with your Vision model and transcribes each voice note first, with the speech model chosen for Dictation in **Settings › Voice** (Whisper or SenseVoice), which detects the language spoken. Nothing downloads for a voice note: without a speech model installed, Row-Bot replies that voice notes need one. On WhatsApp, Row-Bot waits about a second for the rest of an album.
- **Files from Row-Bot.** Ask Row-Bot to send you a file on Telegram, Discord, Slack or WhatsApp and it sends it to your own chat there, or to the chat the conversation came from, after asking (see [Sending Files](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#sending-files)).
- **A stuck conversation.** If a conversation gets stuck on a tool call that can't finish, Row-Bot starts a fresh one and asks you to resend your message.

Chats you already had keep their conversation until you send `/new`. Slack and Discord channels used to share one long conversation per channel. That conversation stays in Row-Bot, and new mentions start their own; a Discord channel without thread permissions carries on in it.

## Safety

Messages sent through a channel leave the local app. Do not enable a channel until you understand who can message it, what Row-Bot can send back, and whether workflows may deliver results there.

When work starts from a channel and a child agent asks for approval, Row-Bot sends the approval back to that parent channel conversation when the channel supports approval messages. The same approval stays visible in the parent conversation, the sidebar's attention indicator and Overview's **Needs you**, and an answer in any of them resolves it everywhere.

## Troubleshooting

- If Telegram encounters one transient network failure during initialization, Row-Bot cleans up the partial runtime and retries once. Persistent network failures remain stopped with an actionable diagnostic; invalid bot tokens are not retried.
- If Telegram starts but its command menu cannot be registered, polling remains available and the menu failure is logged as non-fatal.
- If a channel cannot start, check its fields and the public link. Automatic tunnel startup runs outside the UI event loop, so a slow tunnel helper should report status without freezing app startup.
- If a channel stopped, Monitor offers **Restart _channel_** for it.
- If inbound messages fail, verify webhook URLs and platform permissions.
- If a plain reply in a Slack thread gets no answer, mention Row-Bot in the thread, or add the optional message events described in [Conversations](#conversations).
- If Row-Bot answers a Discord mention in the channel instead of opening a thread, give the bot the **Create Public Threads** and **Send Messages in Threads** permissions, then stop and start the channel.
- If the wrong person has access, revoke them from **Paired accounts**.

## Skills

Route: /docs/skills/

Find, add, use, turn off, remove, create and troubleshoot Row-Bot skills, and how Row-Bot picks them automatically.

# Skills

Skills are instruction packs that teach Row-Bot how to approach a category of work. **Settings › Skills** is where you find skills, add them, try them, and create or edit your own (the command palette's **Add a skill** goes there). Skills you have added can also be discovered and loaded progressively when a task clearly matches their purpose.

See [Settings: Skills](/docs/settings/skills) for the page itself.

## UI Walkthrough

- **Search** finds skills in the library on this computer; **Search online catalogs** asks catalogs such as ClawHub.
- **Your skills** lists the skills you have added, built-in and your own.
- **A skill's page** shows its slash command (**Use it in chat with /_name_**), whether chats use it and which agent profiles include it, and **What's inside**: its files and scripts.
- **Add** adds the skill and turns it on. Scripts inside it never run when it is added.
- **Try it** opens a new chat with a draft that uses the skill; nothing is sent until you send it.
- **⋯ › Turn off** stops chats using it, and **⋯ › Remove…** deletes a skill you added or created.
- **⋯ › Advanced settings** opens the skill editor, where you edit and pin the skill and review proposed changes.

## Creating A Skill

1. Choose **Create a skill** in Settings › Skills.
2. Decide what task the skill should help with.
3. Write concise instructions, examples, and boundaries, including when the skill should and should not be used.
4. Save it.
5. Test it with **Try it** or a small prompt.
6. Revise if Row-Bot overuses or misunderstands it.

## Save How Row-Bot Did Something

Any reply whose work used tools has **Save as skill** (a bookmark icon) in its actions. Row-Bot drafts a skill from what it actually did in that turn, on the chat's own model, and opens it for you to review.

Row-Bot also offers this by itself, but only when a skill looks really worth it. A line under the reply names the task: **Save “Monthly expense report” as a skill?** It offers only when all of these hold:

- the work was in your own chat (never an incognito chat, one that was incognito, a channel chat, a helper's, a workflow's or Proactive Row-Bot's);
- it took at least five real steps with three different tools, and it made or changed something: research, lookups and questions never get an offer;
- every step ran (none was denied or blocked) and no skill you have already covers it;
- there is a reason to expect it again: you did something like it in another chat in the last 30 days, you showed Row-Bot how you wanted the steps done, it took a few tries to get right, or you said it comes round again ("every month", "weekly", "like last time");
- one short check on the chat's model agrees a skill would make it faster or more reliable next time, and names what changes each time.

Row-Bot offers at most three a day and one per chat. **Not now** hides that task for 30 days, and three in a row pause offers for two weeks.

The review sheet shows **Why Row-Bot offered this**, **What it will do** and the SKILL.md itself, with the chat it came from:

- **Approve** saves the skill and turns it on, so it loads by itself when a request matches. It isn't pinned. The notice that follows has **Undo**.
- **Edit** changes its name, what it does, when to use it, what changes each time, its steps and its checks. Your edit is final: no model rewrites it.
- **Reject** asks why, and Row-Bot won't offer that task again for a while.

Nothing is saved until you approve, and a draft never adds links, addresses, credentials or permission to skip approvals: Row-Bot drafts again once without them, then stops. A draft you leave waits in **Settings › Skills** under **Skill proposals**, marked **From** its chat; deleting the chat deletes the draft. Row-Bot's own offers follow the **Learn new skills** switch in Settings › Preferences (**Create skills while chatting** with Learning); **Save as skill** is always there.

## Show Row-Bot How

Some tasks are easier to show than to describe. In the Browser pane, press **Show Row-Bot how** (on a phone it's in **⋯ More browser actions**) and do the task yourself: open pages, click, type. Row-Bot keeps the **steps**, never a video: the page each one was on and the control you used, by its role and visible name.

- **While it records**, a bar says **Showing Row-Bot how** with a red dot, the number of steps and the time, and the page is outlined in red. **Done** finishes; **Undo last step**, **Discard** and **Steps so far** sit beside it. Row-Bot's own browser steps in that chat wait until you finish.
- **What you type** becomes an input the skill asks for each time. Pin a value (**Always type …**) to keep it as it is.
- **Narration** is optional: turn the microphone on and say what you're doing. It's transcribed on this computer by your local speech model (Whisper or SenseVoice), never by a cloud service, even when Talk or Realtime use one. Without a local speech model the microphone says how to install one; your steps still work.
- **Limits**: a demo stops by itself at 200 steps or 15 minutes.

**Done** asks **What is this for?** (optional, one line), then Row-Bot drafts the skill on the chat's own model and opens it in the same review sheet as **Save as skill**, with **What you showed**: the steps it was written from. **Approve** saves it, and **Try it** opens a new chat with the skill on and its request in the message box, for you to fill in and send. Every step it takes asks as usual for that chat.

**Privacy.** Nothing typed into a password, one-time code, card or other sensitive field is kept, nor anything typed on a sign-in or payment page or inside a part of the page Row-Bot can't see into: the skill hands those steps back to you, and Row-Bot never types them. Addresses are kept without their query or fragment. Page text is kept only as short control names and titles, and left out when it looks like instructions. Steps stay in memory only: they're forgotten once the skill is drafted, an hour after you finish, when you discard them, or with the chat. The audio is never written to disk; only the words are kept, beside the steps they were said around. An incognito chat keeps nothing, so the button is off there.

## What Skills Change

Skills shape Row-Bot's behavior; they do not automatically grant credentials or bypass approvals. A skill can make Row-Bot more consistent for a task, but tools still need to be enabled and approved where appropriate.

## Automatic Selection

When progressive discovery is available, Row-Bot can search enabled skills and load a relevant one for the current task. A successful automatic load appears once as **Using _skill_** and adds an active skill chip.

- Automatically selected skills are stored per parent task or child Agent, not per shared Agent Profile.
- Reopening a task restores its selected skills.
- Parent tasks and sibling children do not share automatic activation state.
- Up to five automatically selected skills are retained per task; pinned skills remain separate.
- Loading an already active skill does not show a second **Using _skill_** notice.

Automatic selection changes instructions only. It cannot add a denied tool, alter credentials, bypass approvals, expand a workspace, or change an Agent Profile. Read [Progressive Tools And Skills](/docs/guides/progressive-tools-and-skills) for the complete tool and skill flow.

## Check-ins

**Check-ins** is a built-in skill for people who want Row-Bot to consult them along the way instead of handing back finished work. With it on, Row-Bot asks two or three scoping questions before open-ended work, checks in at milestones ("Here's what I found so far. Does this cover it?"), and confirms before anything high-stakes.

- It used to be called **Proactive Agent** and was pinned in every new chat. It is no longer pinned anywhere: updating Row-Bot unpinned it once, everywhere. A chat where you turned it on yourself keeps it, and you can pin it again.
- Its two most useful habits are now part of every chat: Row-Bot mentions a memory that bears on what you're doing, in one line, and offers at most one obvious next step.
- To use it, type `/check-ins` in a chat, or pin it in **Settings › Skills** (**⋯ › Advanced settings**) to have it in every new chat.
- Check-ins asks questions and pauses for your answers, so long work stops more often. Leave it off if you'd rather Row-Bot carry on until the work is done.

Check-ins changes how Row-Bot behaves inside a chat. Row-Bot speaking first, outside a chat, is [Proactive Row-Bot](/docs/guides/proactive).

## Troubleshooting

- If a skill is not used, make your prompt match its purpose, confirm it is in **Your skills**, or call it with its slash command. The command on its own turns the skill on for the chat; inside a longer message it focuses just that turn on the skill. See [Mention an app or a skill](/docs/chat/#mention-an-app-or-a-skill).
- If a skill is too aggressive, rewrite it with clearer boundaries or remove it.
- If a skill from a catalog is unfamiliar, open **What's inside** before adding it.

## Packages (Plugins)

Route: /docs/integrations/plugins

Add, turn off, and remove packages of apps and skills in Settings Apps.

# Packages (Plugins)

A package (plugin) bundles several things, such as apps, skills and settings, under one name. Packages are managed in [Settings › Apps](/docs/settings/apps) like any other app.

## Add A Package

Find it in **Settings › Apps**, or use **Add from link or file** with a GitHub repository or a .zip file. Package rows from the Hermes catalog say **Checked when you add**: Row-Bot checks what the package contains when you add it, not while you browse. Nothing is downloaded or run until you agree on its page.

The package page's **Included** section lists what it brings. Each of those items says **Installed as part of _package_** and is managed through the package. Finish any app inside it that still needs a sign-in or a key from its own page.

## Turn Off And Remove

- **Turn off** stops the package and everything it brought. Settings and keys are kept.
- **Remove…** removes the package and everything it brought. Its saved keys and data are kept unless you choose **Also delete saved keys and data**; while they are kept, its card says **Removed** and **Delete saved data** deletes them.
- **Check for updates**, for a package from GitHub, downloads its newest version and checks it before anything changes.

Shared runtimes such as Node.js and uv stay installed.

## Safety

A package does not skip approvals or agent profile limits; its apps follow the access you choose for them. Code a package runs on this computer is not sandboxed, so add packages only from publishers you trust. Hooks and entry points written for other assistants are not run.

See [Extend Row-Bot](/docs/extending/) for how packages compare with skills, apps and Custom Tools.

## Hosted And Local Apps (MCP)

Route: /docs/integrations/mcp

How apps that are hosted or run on this computer connect, which of their actions ask first, Windows connectors, the Composio broker, and turning apps off or removing them.

# Hosted And Local Apps (MCP)

Most apps in [Settings › Apps](/docs/settings/apps) connect in one of two ways: **Hosted**, where the service runs the connection, or **Runs on this computer**, where Row-Bot starts a small program for it. Both use the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for offering tools to assistants; you never need to know that to use them.

## Connect An App

- **From a catalog**: search **Settings › Apps**, open the app and choose **Connect** or **Add**. Row-Bot shows what will happen, then sets up anything the app needs to run (Node.js or uv, and the app's own package) in its own folder, asks for any key or setting, checks the connection (and signs you in if the service asks), and asks what the app can do.
- **From a link or file**: **Add from link or file** accepts an app's https address, a GitHub repository, or a `.mcpb` bundle.
- **By its settings**: **Apps › Advanced › Add a custom connection** opens the connection editor for an app that isn't in a catalog.

Use separate connections with their own names for separate accounts, such as Work and Personal. Keys are kept in your system keychain. **Apps › Advanced** has **Use apps**, which stops every app at once, and shows the shared Node.js and uv runtimes under **On this computer**.

## Which Actions Ask First

When you choose what an app can do, Row-Bot groups its actions by effect:

- **Looks things up**: actions that only read. Read only, Ask before changes and Full access all let these run.
- **Makes changes**: routine changes such as create, add, update, edit, write, set, rename or move. They ask first unless you chose **Full access** or set the action to **Use without asking**.
- **Always asks first**: high-impact actions. An action is high-impact when the app marks it destructive, or when its name or description says it does something such as delete, send, post, publish, deploy, merge, push, commit, run, execute, pay, transfer, upload, comment, share, invite or change permissions. A routine change to something that reaches people, publishes or grants access is high-impact too, for example creating a release or a pull request, adding a collaborator or setting a password. These ask in every choice and can't be set to run without asking.

An action whose effect Row-Bot can't determine always asks. An app's own hints can only make an action stricter; the one exception is a read-only hint, and it never outweighs a name that says the action makes a change. Without that hint, an action whose name doesn't say it makes a change but whose description does always asks. Connections set up before this version keep asking before routine changes until you choose otherwise.

High-impact actions and actions whose effect Row-Bot can't determine always need approval: under **Auto** the reviewer approves one only when it clearly matches your request and otherwise asks you, and only **Hands-off**, which you choose, runs them without asking. Approval mode, agent profiles and the model's tool support still apply on top of this. Turning an action off in Row-Bot does not revoke access at the service; use the service's own account controls for that.

## Interactive Views

Some apps can show their results as an interactive view, such as a chart, a form or a board, under the step in chat. A view runs in its own sandbox and goes through the same access and approvals as any other call. See [App views](/docs/chat/#app-views); developers can read [Hosting MCP Apps Views](/docs/extending/mcp-apps).

## Windows Connectors

On Windows Insider builds with Windows' On-device Agent Registry (build 26220.7344 or later, with **Settings › System › AI components › Experimental agentic features** on), **Apps › Advanced › Catalogs** lists **Windows connectors**: connectors that Windows and your installed apps provide. Choose **Update** to list them; Row-Bot asks Windows only then. Connecting one is the usual setup, and Windows also asks you to allow it the first time Row-Bot uses it. Row-Bot never adds, removes or configures Windows connectors. On other computers and older builds the catalog isn't shown.

## Hosted Brokers (Composio)

A broker is a separate hosted service that connects many apps through one account. **Composio** is off until you turn it on in **Apps › Advanced › Catalogs** with **Use Composio**, which first explains what it means: a separate Composio account, and the requests and results for apps you use through it pass through Composio, which keeps them for up to a year by default under its own terms. Links to Composio's terms, privacy policy and data processing agreement are shown there, and nothing changes until you choose **Turn on Composio**.

While it's on, searching for an app also finds Composio, and an app's page offers a way such as **Notion via Composio** after the app's own ways to connect. Connecting signs you in to Composio (or takes a consumer key, kept in your keychain); you then connect each app in your Composio account. Composio's remote code tools start off, and its tools that act for other apps ask every time. Turning the switch off stops Row-Bot offering Composio; a Composio connection you already made stays until you turn it off or remove it on its page. Pipedream isn't available.

## Turn Off And Remove

**Turn off** stops the connection and keeps its settings and keys. **Remove…** removes the connection and its settings; its saved sign-in and keys stay in your keychain unless you choose **Also delete saved keys and data**. Shared runtimes stay installed. See [Turn off or remove](/docs/settings/apps#turn-off-or-remove).

## Developers

How setup runs on the server, the HTTP API and the tool classification are summarised in [Extend Row-Bot](/docs/extending/#how-apps-and-skills-are-set-up), with guides to catalog sources, the app catalog, bundles, sign-in and views.

## Voice And Buddy

Route: /docs/voice-and-buddy/

Use Dictate, Talk, Read aloud and Live voice, choose local or cloud speech, and set up Buddy.

# Voice And Buddy

Voice and Buddy make Row-Bot feel less like a text box and more like a desktop companion. Voice handles speech input and optional spoken output. Buddy is a living character that reacts to what Row-Bot is doing and, in the native Windows and macOS apps, can be dragged from the sidebar onto the desktop as a pet that sits on your windows.

## Voice Modes

- **Dictate** turns speech into composer text so you can review it before sending.
- **Talk** is a spoken conversation with Row-Bot Voice: hands-free, with the chat's own model, tools, memory and approvals.
- **Read aloud**, a button on each reply, speaks that reply in the voice chosen in Settings › Voice: Kokoro on the computer running Row-Bot, or a cloud voice you chose. Talk's spoken answers use the same voice.
- **Local voice** uses Whisper by default, or the optional SenseVoice Small engine after you install it explicitly. For Talk, a **faster speech model** picked for your computer (Moonshine Base on a processor or a Mac, Nemotron Speech Streaming on an NVIDIA graphics card the speech runtime can use) shows your words as you speak and answers sooner; download it under Settings › Voice › Talk.
- **Live voice** (optional) talks through a cloud speech-to-speech model: OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live or Grok Voice, with your own key for that provider. It knows the chat's recent messages, the agent profile's name and a few relevant memories, answers small talk itself and hands real work to Row-Bot, which uses the chat's own model, tools and approvals. While Row-Bot works it tells you what it is doing, and it says Row-Bot's answer when it is ready. Its own replies are saved in the chat, marked as Live voice lines.

## Start Talking

In a chat, the **Talk** button (beside the microphone that dictates) opens its menu: **Talk with Row-Bot** starts Row-Bot Voice, and the **Live voice** rows start a cloud provider (see [Live Voice](#live-voice)). On a phone with no Live voice key saved, one tap starts Row-Bot Voice. Talk waits while a reply is still running. Home's Ask box starts voice in a new chat too (see [Home And Phones](#home-and-phones)).

Row-Bot hears when you start and stop speaking. It answers when you pause; **When you pause** in Settings › Voice sets how soon. Talk over Row-Bot and its voice drops at once; keep talking and it stops, and the rest of that answer stays on screen. A short "mhm" or "okay" doesn't stop it. After five minutes with nothing said, voice pauses; tap it to resume.

## The Voice Bar

Voice runs in a bar above the composer. Its round button shows the state (**Listening**, **Thinking**, **Speaking**, **Waiting for you**, **Muted** or **Paused**): tap it to stop Row-Bot speaking, to unmute, or to resume. The bar's buttons, each with its name as a tooltip:

- **Hold to talk**, with push to talk on (see [Push To Talk](#push-to-talk)).
- **Share camera or screen** (see [Show Row-Bot Your Camera Or Screen](#show-row-bot-your-camera-or-screen)).
- **Microphone and speaker** (the headphones button) picks the devices (see [Microphone And Speakers](#microphone-and-speakers)).
- **Show captions** or **Hide captions**: your words and Row-Bot's, as they are said. **Live captions** in Settings › Voice sets the default.
- **Mute** or **Unmute**.
- **Type instead** mutes and shows the composer; press it again to go back to talking.
- **Show details**: how quickly Row-Bot replied and the language it last heard.
- **Full screen**, on a phone.
- **End voice**.

The bar also says which resources spoken requests can change, what to do when an action needs your OK, and when a key, a device or a language is missing.

## Live Voice

Open the **Talk** menu in a chat and choose a Live voice provider. Each one shows its approximate price a minute (from the provider's published prices, with the date checked); the provider bills your key, not Row-Bot. A provider without a saved key says so and links to Providers. Before you use a provider the first time in a browser, a panel says plainly that your voice, the chat's recent messages, the agent profile's name and a few related memories go to that provider while you talk (in an incognito chat, no memories), and you choose **Start** with the provider's name to go on. Live voice then runs in the same voice bar as Row-Bot Voice, with its captions and controls. It is always hands-free: push to talk is for Row-Bot Voice.

Your provider key never leaves the computer running Row-Bot. For Gemini Live and Grok Voice, the page connects only to Row-Bot, which relays your voice and the provider's speech. For OpenAI Realtime, Row-Bot sets up the call with a short-lived credential it keeps, and the call's audio then goes directly between your browser and OpenAI. Row-Bot Voice, on your own computer, stays the default.

## Show Row-Bot Your Camera Or Screen

While you talk, the video button in the voice bar shares your camera or, in a desktop browser or the Windows app, a screen or window. On a phone it shares the camera, and **Switch camera** flips between front and back. Nothing is captured until you choose to share. While sharing, the bar always says **Camera on** or **Sharing your screen** with a small live preview (larger in the phone's full-screen view), and one tap on the button stops it. Ending voice, or a long quiet pause, stops sharing too. Sharing goes on while you are muted.

With Row-Bot Voice, nothing is streamed: when you finish saying something, Row-Bot takes one still of what you are showing and sends it with what you said, as an image in your message. You see exactly what was sent, and it is kept like any image you attach (in an incognito chat too, with the chat's other files). If the chat's model can't see images, the bar says so and links to the Vision model setting; nothing is sent. Something you say while Row-Bot is still working steers it with your words only.

Gemini Live sees what you share as well: it is shown a still about every two seconds while you share, so it can talk about it, and its disclosure says so. OpenAI Realtime and Grok Voice don't take pictures in a live session, so they offer no sharing.

## Wake Word

Turn on **Hey Row-Bot** in Settings › Voice, under **Wake word**, to start talking without a tap. It is there only on the computer running Row-Bot (in the Row-Bot app, or a browser on that computer), never on a phone or another device. While a Row-Bot window is open, the window listens for "Hey Row-Bot" and the computer running Row-Bot recognises it with a small model that ships with Row-Bot. Nothing is recorded, saved or sent anywhere. When it hears the phrase, Row-Bot Voice starts in the open chat, or in a new chat if none is open.

While it listens, the navigation shows **Listening for "Hey Row-Bot"**. Click it to stop listening in that window, and click again to start again. While voice is on, the wake word waits and its microphone is closed. Closing the window stops it. If your computer stops the microphone while the window is hidden, the mark says so and listening resumes when the window is back. "Hey robot" sounds the same, so Row-Bot wakes to that too.

## Choosing A Mode

Use Dictate when accuracy and review matter. Use Talk when you want a conversation. Use local voice when privacy and offline-style behavior matter. Whisper remains the default local transcription engine; a faster speech model makes Talk quicker. SenseVoice is an optional alternative on Windows, Linux, and Apple Silicon macOS; Intel macOS continues to use Whisper. A cloud speech service (**Listen with**) or a cloud voice (**Speak with**) in Settings › Voice keeps Row-Bot Voice but uses that company, with your key. Use Live voice for the most natural conversation when you accept that audio goes to the provider you choose, at its price.

## Languages

Row-Bot hears which language you speak (**Language** in Settings › Voice, **Detect automatically** by default), and you can choose one instead. Whisper understands every language in the list; the faster speech models understand English only, and Settings says so if you speak another. Kokoro answers in English, Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian and Brazilian Portuguese. It can't speak other languages, such as Japanese or Chinese, yet: those answers stay on screen and the voice bar says so. A cloud voice speaks the languages its company lists. See [Settings: Voice](/docs/settings/voice).

## Voice Notes In Chat Apps

On Telegram and WhatsApp, a voice note you send is transcribed on the computer running Row-Bot, and Row-Bot answers with its text and then a voice note, in the voice chosen in Settings › Voice. Turn this off with the channel's **Reply to voice notes with a voice note**. See [Channels](/docs/integrations/channels).

## While Row-Bot Works

When you talk with Row-Bot Voice and it uses a tool, it says a short line such as "Checking your calendar…" so you know it is working, and "Still working on it…" if nothing has been said for a couple of seconds. These lines are spoken only: they are not saved in the chat and the model never sees them. They never play over you or in the middle of an answer.

You can keep talking while it works. Ask "how's it going?" and it tells you what it is doing without stopping. Anything else you say goes to the work in progress, and Row-Bot says "Got it, I'll do that next." When helpers finish after the turn has ended, their answer is spoken at the next pause, as long as voice is still on. Pictures and videos appear in the chat as they are made; in the phone's full-screen voice view, the newest one shows under the captions and opens with one tap.

When something needs your OK, Row-Bot says what it is and the approval card appears. For an action that can be undone, such as moving a file or adding a calendar event with no guests, you can say "yes" or "no" once it has finished asking ("Say yes or no, or tap the card"). Anything that deletes, sends, posts, pays, publishes, runs a command or uses an app's tool needs a tap on the card, and Row-Bot says "This one needs a tap on the screen." A "yes" said over Row-Bot's own voice, a mixed answer such as "yes, but…", or silence never approves anything.

## Optional SenseVoice Setup

Open Settings -> Voice, find **SenseVoice** under **Voice models**, and choose **Install SenseVoice Small**. Then choose it under **Speech engine** (**Talk listens with** or **Dictation listens with**). Installation is an explicit approximately 940 MB download from ModelScope. Row-Bot verifies the contained snapshot before saving it under the active data directory, and normal transcription then uses that local snapshot with update checks disabled. Startup, readiness checks, and ordinary transcription never download or repair the model automatically.

## Microphone And Speakers

Row-Bot records and plays voice in your browser. Choose the microphone (and, in Chrome, Edge and the Windows app, the speaker) under **Settings › Voice › Microphone and speaker**, or from the headphones button in the voice bar while you talk. Devices have the names your operating system gives them, a Bluetooth headset included; the browser shows the names once Row-Bot may use the microphone. The choice is kept in that browser only. Safari, iPhone and Firefox play through the system's own output, so they offer no speaker choice.

If the microphone you chose is disconnected while you talk, Row-Bot keeps listening with the default one at once and the bar says so; when it is connected again, Row-Bot goes back to it. The same goes for the speaker.

## Push To Talk

Hands-free is the default: Row-Bot hears when you start and stop. Turn on **Push to talk** under Settings › Voice › Talk to have it listen only while you hold **Hold to talk** in the voice bar, or hold **Space** while you aren't typing in Row-Bot's window. In the Windows app you can also choose a key to hold anywhere, even while another app is in front (**Hold a key to talk**: Ctrl + Alt + Space, Ctrl + Shift + Space or F13). It is off until you choose one, works only while voice is open with push to talk, and Row-Bot listens for that one key only; while it is on, other apps don't get that key. On a Mac this isn't offered yet.

## Home And Phones

Talk and Dictate start from Home's Ask box on a computer too: with nothing typed, its microphone dictates and its Talk button talks in a new chat.

On a phone, Row-Bot keeps the screen on while you talk. A phone stops listening when the screen locks or turns off, or when you switch to another app: on iPhone that includes a Row-Bot added to the Home Screen, and on Android the screen turning off. The voice bar says so once. Where the phone or browser shows media controls (the lock screen, a headset's button), they show **Row-Bot · Listening**; play and pause unmute and mute, and hanging up ends voice.

## Buddy Controls

- **Show Buddy** controls companion visibility.
- **Drag to tear off** moves Buddy itself from its sidebar dock onto the desktop, where it lands on a window's top edge or above the taskbar or Dock. Releasing over the dock cancels the drag.
- Click the desktop Buddy to open its speech bubble. The bubble follows the selected conversation, whether it is a chat, a design or a code folder, and shares its saved draft, current response, tools, and approval mode.
- Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line. **Stop** stops the selected thread's active response.
- **Simple approvals** can be approved or denied in Buddy. **Complex approvals** open the full thread for review.
- **Open full thread**, **Dock Buddy**, and **Hide Buddy** are in the bubble and in Buddy's right-click menu.
- Tear-off is session-scoped; restarting Row-Bot returns placement to the normal sidebar dock. Browser/server mode does not create a desktop pet.
- **Personality** changes the tone of Buddy cues, and **Bubbles** changes how status appears.
- **Look** chooses a bundled or custom appearance; **New look…** makes one with your image model.
- **Motion** chooses how lively Buddy is: **Calm**, **Normal** or **Lively**.

See [Settings: Buddy](/docs/settings/buddy) for the complete drag, messaging, approval, tray-recovery, and troubleshooting walkthrough.

## Talk To Buddy

Buddy's bubble accepts typed messages for the thread named at its top. It does not contain a separate microphone control: Talk and Dictate remain in the full Row-Bot thread, where device state, transcription, and provider disclosure are visible. Use **Open full thread**, start Talk or Dictate there, and Buddy will continue reflecting that selected conversation.

While you talk, Buddy shows that it is listening and its mouth moves with Row-Bot's voice, with Row-Bot Voice, Live voice and Read aloud alike, in the sidebar and as the desktop pet. Undocking Buddy does not change which voice provider is used, create a new voice session, or bypass tool approvals.

## Privacy And Safety

What you say becomes chat text, and goes to the chat's model like anything you type. Beyond that, each part of voice stays on the computer running Row-Bot unless you choose a company for it:

- **Row-Bot Voice** (the default): your browser sends your voice only to Row-Bot, over its own signed-in connection. Whisper, SenseVoice or a faster speech model writes it down there, and Kokoro speaks there. Nothing goes to a speech service.
- **A cloud speech service** under **Listen with** (Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI or Google): the stretches where you speak go to that company, one at a time, while you talk. Dictation and chat-app voice notes stay local.
- **A cloud voice** under **Speak with** (ElevenLabs, Cartesia or Google): the text of each sentence Row-Bot says goes to that company, for Talk, Read aloud and chat-app voice notes. **Describe a voice** sends only your description, never a recording.
- **Live voice** (OpenAI, Google or xAI): your voice, the chat's recent messages, the agent profile's name and a few related memories (none in an incognito chat) go to that provider while you talk, and so do Row-Bot's answers and short progress lines, which it says for Row-Bot; Gemini Live is also shown what you share on camera or screen.
- **Camera or screen**: captured only after you start sharing. With Row-Bot Voice, one still per thing you say leaves the page, saved in your message like an attached image, and goes where your images go (the chat's model or its Vision model).
- **Wake word** (if you turn it on): the Row-Bot window on the computer running Row-Bot listens for "Hey Row-Bot", and that computer recognises it. Nothing it hears is kept or sent anywhere.
- **Downloads**: speech models download only when you press **Download** or **Install**: Whisper from Hugging Face, Kokoro and the faster speech models from GitHub, SenseVoice from ModelScope. Installing SenseVoice sends no audio, prompts or usage data; inference stays local after installation.
- **Devices and controls**: the microphone and speaker you choose are kept in your browser and never sent to Row-Bot. The system's media controls show only **Row-Bot · Listening** (or what voice is doing).

Every cloud key is yours; the company bills it, not Row-Bot. Buddy preferences and looks are local and Buddy animates on your computer; making a new look calls your configured image model. The desktop Buddy reads only the position and size of the window you are using (never its title or contents) to sit on it.

## Troubleshooting

- If Dictate records nothing, check that the browser may use the microphone, and which microphone is chosen in Settings › Voice › Microphone and speaker.
- If the wake word starts voice when you didn't say it (a TV, music, or someone saying "hey robot"), end voice and click **Listening for "Hey Row-Bot"** to stop listening in that window, or turn **Hey Row-Bot** off in Settings › Voice. If it doesn't hear you, speak toward the microphone and check which microphone is chosen.
- If a Bluetooth headset sounds muffled while you talk, that is the headset switching to its call mode (a lower sound quality) to use its microphone; choose the computer's own microphone to keep the headset's full sound.
- If Read aloud says it needs the Kokoro voice, install Kokoro under **Read aloud** in Settings › Voice.
- If Talk answers before you have finished, set **When you pause** to **Give me time to think** in Settings › Voice, or turn on **Push to talk**.
- If Talk doesn't hear you on a phone, check that the screen is on and Row-Bot is the app in front: phones stop listening otherwise.
- If SenseVoice reports missing packages, install the `voice` extra for a source checkout or repair the packaged app. If its snapshot is missing or incomplete, reinstall it from Voice settings.
- If SenseVoice is unavailable on Intel macOS, select local Whisper instead.
- If a Live voice provider is unavailable, add that provider's API key in Providers.
- If Buddy does not appear, enable **Show Buddy** or use the tray's **Show Buddy** action when it is torn off.
- If Buddy will not undock, use the native Windows or macOS app and start the drag on Buddy itself. Remote browsers and browser/server mode keep it docked.

## Catalog Source Adapters

Route: /docs/extending/source-adapters

For developers: the source adapter interface in src/row_bot/integrations/sources.py, how a new catalog source is added as one adapter plus data, and the passive-read rules every source follows.

# Catalog Source Adapters

This page is for developers adding a catalog to **Settings › Apps** or **Settings › Skills**. Every catalog, from the shipped MCP Registry mirror to ClawHub, is one adapter in `src/row_bot/integrations/sources.py`. The server decides what each adapter may do and serves the list; the client never hard-codes sources.

## The Adapter Interface

An adapter subclasses `Source`:

| Member | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable id, `[a-z0-9_]{1,40}`, such as `official` or `clawhub`. |
| `kind` | What it lists: `skill`, `mcp`, `plugin` or `builtin`. Served as `kinds`. |
| `label`, `message` | The name and one plain sentence shown under **Apps › Advanced › Catalogs**. |
| `access` | `local` (shipped data), `snapshot` (a shipped copy that updates), `public` (a live catalog) or `unavailable`. |
| `eligibility` | `eligible`, `explicit_only`, `auth_required`, `contract_unresolved` or `unsupported`. Decided on the server; a source that isn't eligible or `explicit_only` only reports its status. |
| `network` | `none` (never contacts anything) or `explicit` (contacts its catalog only for an explicit online search or an update). |
| `search(Search) -> Found` | Returns rows for `search.query`. Must honour `search.refresh` (true only for **Search online catalogs**), `search.cancelled` and `search.validate`. |
| `lookup(reference)` | Resolves one entry from local data only, for its page and its install plan. |
| `update(cancelled)` | Only for `network = "explicit"`: refreshes the source's local copy and returns a small summary, or raises. A failed update keeps what the source had. |
| `listed()` | False hides the source on this computer, as Windows connectors do where Windows doesn't have them. |
| `view()`, `status(**fields)` | The served description and a per-search status (`cached`, `stale`, `pending`, `empty`, `unavailable`…). Rarely overridden. |

`Search` carries `owner_id`, `query`, `refresh`, `cancelled`, `validate` and `everything` (the **Show all results** request). Build rows with `_available(...)`, which fills the letter-avatar icon and plain-text description, and add them with `found.add(row, reference)`. The `reference` is what the install plan reads later, so it must be one `plans.compute` understands. Filter with `matches(query, *texts)`, which needs every query word.

## Adding A Source

1. Write one `Source` subclass and add an instance to `SOURCES` at the end of `sources.py`. Its position is its ranking precedence among equal rows.
2. Put its data beside it: shipped package data under `src/row_bot/integrations/`, or a cache that only `update` writes.
3. To let its entries open by id (their page and their plan), add a branch to `catalog_entry()`, which resolves ids from local data only.
4. If it has an `update`, `catalogs.updatable()` picks it up: it appears with **Update** in **Apps › Advanced › Catalogs** and in the optional schedule.
5. Record the public contract you checked (terms, authentication, rate limits) in `docs/INTEGRATION_SOURCES.md`.
6. Add deterministic tests with a faked catalog under `tests/subsystem/integrations/`.

`GET /api/v1/integrations/sources` serves every listed source with its catalog state; `POST /api/v1/integrations/sources/{id}/update` starts an update in the background.

## Passive Reads

- **Searching, browsing and opening a page are passive.** They read shipped data, the local index and saved results, and nothing else. They launch no program, install nothing and send nothing.
- **Only two things contact a catalog:** an explicit **Search online catalogs** (`POST /api/v1/integrations/items/search` with `refresh`), and an update, chosen by the person or by the schedule they turned on. Each search runs a source under an 8-second deadline.
- **Updates fetch through `integrations/safe.py`**: https only, reviewed hosts or public addresses, per-hop redirect checks, size and time caps. Registry icons are fetched only during an update and re-encoded locally; rendering never fetches.
- **A catalog listing grants nothing.** Eligibility is decided on the server, and nothing runs before the person agrees to an install plan.

The global network guard in `tests/conftest.py` fails any deterministic test that connects off the computer. `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_apps_and_sources.py`, `test_catalog_updates.py` and `tests/subsystem/client_protocol/test_integration_discovery.py` check that passive reads never fetch, that unavailable sources never run, and which sources can update.

## Ranking

Ranking lives in `sources.py`, and the local Registry index (`integrations/index.py`) applies the same key in SQL. `order()` puts featured and vendor-verified entries first, then an exact name, a strong text match, featured order, a complete setup, freshness (90 days, a year), the source's popularity and its precedence. `rank()` merges rows that share a source-neutral identity, keeping every source as an attribution, and shows one card per app; `way_order()` orders an app's ways to connect, reviewed and built-in ways first.

## Contribute To The App Catalog

Route: /docs/extending/app-catalog

For developers: the apps.json record format, the Official and Reviewed rules, how search ranks results, bundled icons and their licences, the featured skills and broker lists, and how to check catalog coverage.

# Contribute To The App Catalog

This page is for developers adding or correcting an app, a featured skill or a logo. The app catalog is package data in `src/row_bot/integrations/`; it is validated when Row-Bot loads it, so a bad record fails loudly instead of showing wrong information.

## App Records (`apps.json`)

`apps.json` has `"schema_version": 2` and one record per line under `apps`. Each record is one service people recognise, and catalog entries attach to it only through the references it lists. A record with an unknown field is refused.

| Field | Meaning and rules |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Lowercase `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}`, unique. Also the page address, `/settings/apps/<id>`. |
| `name`, `publisher`, `summary` | The display name, who makes the service, and one plain sentence about what it does. |
| `category` | One of `productivity`, `developer`, `data`, `design`, `communication`, `finance` or `local_tools`. |
| `synonyms`, `jobs` | Words and tasks people search for, such as "wiki" or "send an email". Search matches them. |
| `example_prompts` | Things to ask, shown on the app's page. At least two for an app that has a connection of its own. |
| `refs` | The reviewed references that attach catalog entries: `curated:`, `registry:` (an exact server or a namespace), `endpoint:` (a host), `npm:`, `pypi:`, `oci:`, `repo:`, `hermes:`, `bundled:`, and Row-Bot's own `account:`, `channel:` and `tool:` ways. A reference may belong to one app only. |
| `vendor` | `domains` and `github_orgs` the vendor controls; the verified badge is granted from these. |
| `variants` | The app's ways to connect in its preferred order: `hosted_mcp`, `local_mcp`, `package`, `account`, `channel`, `api_key_tool`, `broker`. |
| `auth` | `oauth`, `api_key`, `none`, `account`, `mixed` or empty. |
| `docs_url`, `key_url` | https links: the vendor's documentation and where to get a key. |
| `icon` | `si:<slug>` for a bundled mark, or empty for a letter avatar. |
| `featured_rank` | Optional. Featured apps are ranked 1 to N with no gaps or repeats. |
| `local_app`, `local_check` | For an app that works with a program on this computer: its name, and `{"port": 9876}` (a loopback port from 1024 to 65535) or `{"process": "blender"}`. The check looks only at this computer. |
| `facts` | `checked` (the date you checked) and `sources`: the vendor pages that support the record. |

Unmatched catalog entries stay browsable as **Community**. Never attach an entry by its name alone.

## Labels: Official, Reviewed, Built In, Community

Every result carries one label, decided on the server by rule.

**Official** (**by _Vendor_**) is granted by rule, never by a name or a description:

- a Registry record is the vendor's when its namespace is a vendor domain reversed (`com.notion` for `notion.com`) or `io.github.<vendor org>`. The Registry checks namespace ownership, so Registry records are judged by namespace alone;
- a reviewed recipe or your own connection is the vendor's when its endpoint is under a vendor domain, or is an `endpoint:` the vendor's documentation names exactly.

Shared hosting domains, where anyone can have a subdomain (`github.io`, `vercel.app`, `netlify.app`, `pages.dev`, `amazonaws.com`, `supabase.co` and others in `apps.SHARED_HOSTING`), are never vendor domains: the catalog refuses to load with one.

**Reviewed** is everything Row-Bot reviewed: the setup recipes in `src/row_bot/mcp_client/recommended_servers.json` (the **Vendor recommendations** catalog), the featured skills, Row-Bot's examples, and any way with `tested_with_row_bot`. Set a recipe's `tested_with_row_bot` only after its live check passes. To give a popular app whose vendor publishes nothing a reviewed way (as Reddit has), add a recipe that pins one version, an `apps.json` record whose `refs` name it (`curated:<id>`, and the Registry record and package), and notes that say plainly what it can and can't do.

**Built in** is Row-Bot's own accounts, channels and key tools, and packages bundled with it. **Community** is everything else.

## How Search Ranks

Search is local and deterministic; the key lives in `integrations/sources.py` (`order`) and is mirrored in the Registry index's SQL (`integrations/index.py`), so the index keeps the right top 200:

1. A name match (the query is a name, or every query word starts a word of the name, the app's name, synonyms or jobs) before a match found only in a description.
2. A community result never outranks an official, reviewed or built-in one on its name alone.
3. An exact name before a partial one, then the label (official and built in, then reviewed), then the app's `featured_rank`.
4. Quality: `3·log10(1 + stars)`, plus activity (2 when pushed within 90 days, 1 within a year, −2 when archived), plus 1 each for a description of 12 or more words, a licence, an icon and a known sign-in, less 3 for a fork whose parent is listed and 2 for a first version under 30 days old that nobody has starred.
5. Setup: hosted first, then a key, then runs on this computer, then no supported recipe; then stable ties.

The first result is the **Best match** when it is a name match and official, reviewed or built in, or has a quality of 6 or more. Every weight is a named constant. A change that moves a result is a reviewed change: the golden queries in `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_search_ranking.py` (reddit, notion, github, slack, postgres, calendar, filesystem) say what each must show first.

Stars, last push, archived flags, fork parents and licences come from `src/row_bot/mcp_client/registry_signals.json.xz`, written at release preparation (see [the release process](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/docs/RELEASING.md)). Search only reads that file; it never asks GitHub or the Registry.

## Icons (`icons.json`)

Logos are Simple Icons marks, bundled only for the apps that name them. Each mark in `icons.json` records its `title`, `hex` colour, SVG `path`, `license` (CC0-1.0 for most marks; others record their own), `source` and, where the brand has them, `guidelines`. Rebuild the file from an extracted `simple-icons` package after changing `icon` fields:

```powershell
uv run python scripts/build_app_icons.py path/to/simple-icons/package
```

An app without a mark gets a letter avatar drawn locally. Registry icons are fetched only during a catalog update, as raster images from the publisher's own domain, re-encoded locally; remote SVG is never accepted, and drawing a card never fetches anything.

## Featured Skills (`skills.json`)

`skills.json` lists references, not copies: each skill is read from its repository at the pinned commit when someone adds it. A record has `id`, `name`, `publisher`, `summary`, `category`, `synonyms`, `jobs`, `repo` (`github.com/<owner>/<repo>`), `path`, `commit` (the full 40-character hash), `license`, `license_url`, `featured_rank`, `checked` and, optionally, `app` (an `apps.json` id). Check the licence at that commit. The library takes permissive and weak-copyleft open-source licences (MIT, Apache-2.0, MPL-2.0 so far); proprietary, unlicensed and share-alike skills stay out.

## Broker Names (`broker_apps.json`)

Composio's own catalog can't be listed without an account, so `broker_apps.json` is Row-Bot's own list of well-known app names, each 1 to 80 characters. While Composio is turned on, a search naming one of them shows Composio, and that app's page offers "_App_ via Composio". It is a list of names to search by, not a claim that Composio supports each one.

## Check Coverage

`scripts/integration_coverage.py` computes an install plan for every local catalog entry (the reviewed recipes, the whole shipped Registry mirror, featured skills and examples) in a throwaway data folder. It fetches nothing and reads no user data.

```powershell
uv run python scripts/integration_coverage.py --output .tmp/integration-coverage
```

It writes `coverage.json` (each entry with "complete" or the exact blocker) and `coverage.md` (counts per source, every blocker, and featured apps without a complete plan). `--hermes` adds a saved Hermes catalog. Run it before and after a catalog change and explain any featured app that stops connecting.

## Tests

`tests/subsystem/integrations/test_app_catalog.py`, `test_icons.py`, `test_skill_catalog.py`, `test_brokers.py` and `test_apps_and_sources.py` check the featured ranks, categories, prompts, sources, icon licences, label rules and attachment; `test_search_ranking.py` and `test_catalog_signals.py` check ranking, merging and the shipped signals. Run them with `uv run python -m pytest tests/subsystem/integrations`.

## MCP Bundles (.mcpb)

Route: /docs/extending/mcp-bundles

For developers: how Row-Bot imports .mcpb bundles, which manifest fields it reads, how user_config becomes setup inputs, platform and runtime checks, signatures, and Registry bundles downloaded only after consent and a checksum match.

# MCP Bundles (.mcpb)

This page is for developers who publish an MCP server as an `.mcpb` bundle (formerly `.dxt`) and want it to work in Row-Bot. People add a bundle with **Settings › Apps › Add from link or file**, or connect a Registry record that points to one. The reader is `src/row_bot/mcp_client/bundles.py`; installing and launching are in `mcp_client/packages.py`.

## What Row-Bot Checks When A Bundle Is Chosen

A picked file is staged in Row-Bot's data folder for up to a day and read without being unpacked or run:

- **Size**: at most 128 MiB as a file, 512 MiB unpacked, 20,000 files, and a manifest of at most 1 MiB.
- **Manifest**: `manifest_version` (or the older `dxt_version`) `0.1` to `0.4`, with `name`, `version`, `description`, `author.name` and `server`. Known optional fields are type-checked; an unknown field refuses the bundle, because what Row-Bot can't read it doesn't accept.
- **Server**: `server.type` is `node`, `python` or `binary`; `uv` bundles, which install packages when they start, are read but not run. `server.entry_point` must be inside the archive, and `server.mcp_config` supplies `command`, `args`, `env` and `platform_overrides`. The command must be `node`, `python`, `python3` or a program inside the bundle.
- **Platform**: `compatibility.platforms` (all three when absent) must include this computer's (`win32`, `darwin` or `linux`), or the bundle is refused. `compatibility.runtimes` must be well formed but isn't checked against this computer.
- **Signature**: see below.

## Settings The Bundle Asks For

Each `user_config` entry becomes a field in the setup's **Add your settings** step:

| `user_config` | Setup input |
| --- | --- |
| `title`, `description` (both required) | The field's label and help. |
| `type`: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `directory`, `file` | Text, number, yes or no, or a path. |
| `sensitive: true` | A secret, kept in the system keychain and never shown again. |
| `required` | Whether it must be filled. |
| `default` | The starting value; `${HOME}`, `${DESKTOP}`, `${DOCUMENTS}` and `${DOWNLOADS}` become this computer's folders. |

`multiple: true` isn't supported. In `mcp_config`, `${__dirname}` is the unpacked bundle and `${user_config.key}` is the person's value, which may fill an argument or an environment variable but never the `command`: a person's value never chooses what runs. Environment variables that change what runs, such as `PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS` or `LD_PRELOAD`, are refused, except `NODE_PATH` or `PYTHONPATH` inside the bundle.

## Signatures

A signed bundle is the zip followed by an `MCPB_SIG_V1` block holding a detached CMS (PKCS #7) signature over the zip, ending with `MCPB_SIG_END`. Row-Bot accepts SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 with RSA or ECDSA keys, and checks that the signature matches the bundle's bytes.

- **Signed and matching**: the review shows the name the certificate gives itself and its fingerprint, and says that nobody checked that name. Row-Bot doesn't decide whether the certificate is trusted.
- **Unsigned**: the review says Row-Bot can't tell who made it.
- **Damaged or not matching**: the bundle is refused. A tampered bundle never passes as an unsigned one.

## Install And Launch

After the person agrees, the bundle is extracted into a new private folder: only regular files and folders, no links, encrypted entries or path escapes, with the written bytes counted against the limits. Its lock is the file's SHA-256, and its unpacked tree digest is recorded and checked again before every launch; a changed file or folder stops it. `node` bundles run with Row-Bot's managed Node.js (or Node.js on the path), `python` bundles with Row-Bot's own uv-managed Python, and `binary` bundles from inside their folder. Nothing in a bundle runs before consent.

## Bundles From The Registry

A Registry record of type `mcpb` gets a recipe only when it gives an https download address and a `fileSha256`; one without a checksum is listed with "Download this bundle from its publisher, then add it from a file". Its consent sheet names the file and its host, "checked against its Registry checksum". Only after the person agrees does Row-Bot re-check the record against the live Registry, download the file through its safe fetcher (https, public addresses, at most 128 MiB), and compare its SHA-256. A bundle that doesn't match is never used or saved: "The bundle didn't match the checksum its Registry record gives, so Row-Bot didn't use it."

## Testing

Deterministic tests build bundles in a temporary folder: `tests/subsystem/mcp/test_bundles.py` covers reading, signatures, tampering and contained extraction, and `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_runtimes.py` covers Registry bundles and checksums.

## Sign-In And Client Metadata

Route: /docs/extending/sign-in-and-client-metadata

For developers: how Row-Bot signs in to a hosted app, using its published OAuth client metadata document (CIMD), dynamic client registration or the person's own OAuth app, and how a sign-in finishes on another device.

# Sign-In And Client Metadata

This page is for developers running an MCP server behind OAuth who want Row-Bot to sign in to it, and for anyone reviewing how Row-Bot does it. The code is in `src/row_bot/mcp_client/auth.py`, `application/client_mcp_auth.py` and the `sign_in` step of `integrations/plans.py`.

## Row-Bot's Client Metadata Document

Row-Bot has no client secret and no hosted service. Its OAuth client ID is the address of a static Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), `https://row-bot.ai/oauth/client-metadata.json`, published from `docs-site/static/oauth/client-metadata.json`:

```json
{
  "client_id": "https://row-bot.ai/oauth/client-metadata.json",
  "client_name": "Row-Bot",
  "client_uri": "https://row-bot.ai",
  "logo_uri": "https://row-bot.ai/img/brand/row_bot_glyph_256.png",
  "application_type": "native",
  "redirect_uris": [
    "http://127.0.0.1/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback",
    "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback"
  ],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "response_types": ["code"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
}
```

It names only loopback redirects, so a sign-in made with it returns to the computer that started it, or, from another device, ends on an address the person pastes back (see [The Redirect](#the-redirect)). It holds no secret or key.

## How Row-Bot Finds Out A Sign-In Is Needed

During an agreed setup, the `test` step sends one unauthenticated `initialize` request. A 401 or 403 makes Row-Bot read the server's protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) and then its authorization server's metadata (RFC 8414), and turns the plan's `sign_in` step on. So a hosted app whose catalog listing says nothing about sign-in can still sign in. These reads are limited to public https addresses and 64 KiB, and happen only inside a setup the person agreed to.

## Which Client Row-Bot Uses

1. **The person's own OAuth app**, when they gave one for this connection before, or when a reviewed recipe says the service needs one (GitHub's OAuth-app way, for example).
2. **CIMD**, when the authorization server's metadata says `client_id_metadata_document_supported` and the sign-in uses a loopback address the document lists. CIMD is preferred when the server supports both, except for a device code (below), which needs a registered client.
3. **Dynamic client registration**, when the server has a `registration_endpoint`. Row-Bot registers as a public client named Row-Bot with only its callback address.
4. **Otherwise the setup pauses** at **Add your OAuth app** for a client ID and an optional client secret. The help gives the callback address to register. With a secret, Row-Bot authenticates with `client_secret_post`.

The authorization request uses PKCE with S256. A reviewed recipe may set `oauth_scope` to ask for less than everything the server lists. During sign-in Row-Bot checks that the issuer is the expected one, refuses HTTP redirects, contacts public https addresses only, and sends the access token only to the app's own server.

## The Redirect

How the answer comes back depends on where the sign-in starts (`delivery` on the plan's `sign_in` step):

- **This computer** (`this_computer`): the Row-Bot desktop app on the computer Row-Bot runs on. The callback is `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback` on the port Row-Bot is using (8080 by default), and the browser opens on the same computer. The client metadata lists the address both without a port and with 8080; an authorization server that follows RFC 8252 §7.3 accepts any port on a loopback redirect.
- **Another device, with Row-Bot's public address** (`public`): when Row-Bot has exactly one approved public https origin and the server has a `registration_endpoint`, Row-Bot registers a client for that sign-in with the public callback, `https://<origin>/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback`, and the browser returns there by itself. CIMD and the person's own app don't list that address, so they use the next way.
- **Another device, pasting the address back** (`paste`): the redirect is `http://127.0.0.1/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback`, which doesn't load on that device. The person pastes the address the browser ended on, and the client sends it to `POST /api/v1/integrations/plans/{plan_id}/sign-in` with the session that started the setup. Row-Bot never fetches it and reads only `state` and `code` or `error`. It must be exactly the sign-in's own callback (scheme, host, port and path), carry each of those once, and name no part of the token exchange (`redirect_uri`, `code_verifier`, `client_id`…). It is then checked exactly as the callback route checks one: this owner's own waiting sign-in, its one-time state (the PKCE verifier never leaves Row-Bot), once, within five minutes, while the connection is unchanged. Refusals are `mcp_auth_address_invalid`, `mcp_auth_address_other`, `mcp_auth_address_used` and `mcp_auth_address_expired`.
- **Another device, with a code** (`device`): when the authorization server publishes a `device_authorization_endpoint` and lists `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` (RFC 8628), and Row-Bot has a client that can use it (one it registers with that grant, or the person's own app), Row-Bot shows the code and the service's page, then asks the token endpoint at the service's interval (five seconds more after `slow_down`) until the person allows or denies it or the code expires. If the service gives no code, for example a GitHub OAuth app with device flow switched off, the sign-in carries on as a pasted address.

The callback route, which needs no session, accepts only the state of a sign-in waiting for this computer's browser or the public address, never a pasted or device sign-in's.

For your own OAuth app, register `http://127.0.0.1/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback` (with a port if your service requires one). The same address works from this computer and, pasted back, from another device.

## Tokens

Tokens, the client registration and the person's own client secret are saved together for that one connection in Row-Bot's secret store (the system keychain, or Row-Bot's encrypted store where there is none), never in settings files, logs or API responses. They are bound to the connection's name, address and launch; if those change, the person signs in again. When a refresh fails or a token stops working, the app shows **Sign in needed**, and its main action is **Sign in again**.

## Testing

`tests/subsystem/integrations/test_sign_in.py` covers discovery, CIMD before dynamic registration, the person's own app, scopes, the expired-sign-in state and the published document. `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_sign_in_elsewhere.py` covers signing in from another device: the public address, pasted addresses and every refusal, and device codes. The live GitHub check, `tests/e2e/test_github_live.py`, is opt-in; see [Extend Row-Bot](/docs/extending/#how-apps-and-skills-are-set-up).

## Hosting MCP Apps Views

Route: /docs/extending/mcp-apps

For developers: how Row-Bot shows an app's ui:// view in chat, with the sandboxed frame, its Content-Security-Policy, declared domains, the bridge messages it answers, limits, and calls that go through approvals.

# Hosting MCP Apps Views

This page is for developers building an MCP server with interactive views (MCP Apps, spec version `2026-01-26`) or working on Row-Bot itself. For using views, read [Apps in a chat](/docs/chat/#app-views). The server side is `src/row_bot/integrations/views.py`; the frame and bridge are `frontend/src/features/apps/AppViewFrame.tsx` and `view-bridge.ts`.

## Negotiation

While **Show app views in chat** is on, Row-Bot's `initialize` request carries the `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui` extension with `mimeTypes: ["text/html;profile=mcp-app"]`. The choice is made when a connection opens; changing the switch doesn't renegotiate an open session.

## Declaring A View

- A tool names its view in `_meta.ui.resourceUri` (the older `_meta["ui/resourceUri"]` is read too): a `ui://` URI of at most 512 printable characters.
- `_meta.ui.visibility` defaults to `["model", "app"]`. A tool without `"model"` is never offered to the agent; a view can call only tools that include `"app"`.
- Row-Bot reads the view with `resources/read` on the app's own connection. It uses the first content item whose `mimeType` is exactly `text/html;profile=mcp-app` and whose `uri` is the one requested, as `text` or base64 `blob`, up to 1 MiB, within 30 seconds.
- The content item's `_meta.ui` (not the tool's) supplies `csp` and `prefersBorder`.
- A view appears under a tool step that succeeded, for a tool the person accepted, while both view switches are on and the app is on in that chat. It is read again each time its card comes near the screen; nothing is cached.

## The Frame

`POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/views` with `{"call_id": …}` renders a step's view and returns `frame_url`, `/app-views/{render_id}`, where the render id is 128 random bits. The frame's HTML must be fetched within 120 seconds and is served once; a second request gets 404.

The iframe has `sandbox="allow-scripts"` and nothing else, so the view runs in an opaque origin with no access to Row-Bot's page, cookies, storage or API. A second navigation inside the frame closes the view. The response carries `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, a `Permissions-Policy` that denies camera, microphone, geolocation, clipboard, USB, serial, payment and display capture, and this policy, where R is the accepted `resourceDomains`:

```text
default-src 'none'; script-src 'unsafe-inline' R; style-src 'unsafe-inline' R;
img-src data: R; media-src data: R; font-src R; connect-src <connectDomains>;
frame-src <frameDomains>; object-src 'none'; base-uri <baseUriDomains>;
form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; sandbox allow-scripts
```

An empty list becomes `'none'`. No load directive allows `'self'`, which would be Row-Bot's own origin.

## Declared Domains

`_meta.ui.csp` may list `resourceDomains`, `connectDomains`, `frameDomains` and `baseUriDomains`. Each value must be an https origin such as `https://cdn.example.com` or `https://*.example.com`, with no port, path or query. Row-Bot silently drops:

- IP addresses, single-label names and `localhost`;
- private-network names such as `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, `.home`, `.corp`, `.test` and `.example`;
- wildcard-DNS services such as `nip.io`, `sslip.io` and `localtest.me`;
- public suffixes, checked against the bundled Public Suffix List, so `https://*.com` and `https://github.io` are refused.

It keeps at most 16 values per kind. The view's card lists the accepted domains: "This view also loads from …".

## The Bridge

The bridge speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over `postMessage`. It accepts messages only from its own frame's window, with origin `null`, up to 1 MiB.

| From the view | Row-Bot's answer |
| --- | --- |
| `ui/initialize` | Host info, capabilities (`serverTools`, `openLinks`, `logging`) and host context: the tool, `theme` (`light` or `dark`), `displayMode: "inline"`, `containerDimensions.maxHeight: 720`, locale, time zone and platform. |
| `ui/notifications/initialized` | Sends `ui/notifications/tool-input`, then `ui/notifications/tool-result`, or `ui/notifications/tool-cancelled` when the chat kept no result. |
| `ui/notifications/size-changed` | Resizes the frame, between 48 and 720 pixels. |
| `tools/call` | Calls one of the app's tools, as described below. Refused before `initialized`. |
| `ui/open-link` | Opens an http or https link in the person's browser, only right after a click in the view, at most 3 a minute. |
| `ui/request-display-mode` | Always `inline`. |
| `ping` | `{}` |
