| Anything else, such as `ui/message`, `ui/update-model-context` or `resources/read` | `-32601 Method not found`. |

Row-Bot sends `ui/notifications/host-context-changed` when the theme changes and `ui/resource-teardown` before it removes a view. A view that hasn't sent `initialized` within 10 seconds is closed. Other notifications, including logging, are ignored.

The result a view receives is rebuilt from the chat's text form of the tool result: its text, `isError`, and `structuredContent` when there was one. Images and other non-text content don't reach the view.

## Calls From A View

A view's `tools/call` becomes `POST /api/v1/views/{render_id}/tools/call`. Before it runs, Row-Bot checks that:

- the tool belongs to the view's own app, includes `"app"` in its visibility, and is turned on for that app;
- both view switches are on, and the app is on in that chat and allowed by the chat's agent profile;
- the chat's approval mode allows it, through the same rule as the agent's calls. Destructive, high-impact and unknown-effect tools ask in every mode and are refused under **Block**. A routine change the app's access asks about asks under **Ask** and **Auto** (a view's call has no request of yours for the reviewer to compare with), runs under **Hands-off** and is refused under **Block**. Reads run.

When a call asks, the standard approval card appears inside the view's card, as well as wherever approvals appear. The call waits up to 5 minutes without holding a server thread, and no answer counts as a denial. Access is checked again just before the call runs, and the result goes back to the view only, not into the transcript.

Limits: 20 calls a minute per view, 64 KiB of arguments, one waiting call per view and three across all views, four app round trips at once, 60 seconds per call, and a 1 MiB result.

## Switches

- **Apps › Advanced › Apps in chats › Show app views in chat**: every app. On by default.
- **Show views in chat** on an app's page: that app only. On by default when what the person agreed to included a view, and off for apps accepted before views existed.

Settings are read and written through `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/integrations/views` and `PUT /api/v1/integrations/views/apps`.

## Testing A View

The deterministic fixture `tests/fixtures/mcp_apps/counter_server.py` is a small server with a view; `tests/subsystem/mcp/test_app_views.py` and `frontend/src/features/apps/view-bridge.test.ts` cover the server and the bridge. Test your own view the same way: no live service is needed.

## Operations, Data, And Recovery

Route: /docs/operations/

Back up, restore, update, repair, and uninstall Row-Bot without losing track of local data and credentials.

# Operations, Data, And Recovery

Row-Bot is local-first, so operational safety starts with knowing which data directory and workspace are active. Conversations, settings, memory, Knowledge, workflows, documents, designs, code folder records, skills, plugins, logs, channel state, and MCP configuration can live under that directory. Operating-system key stores may hold credentials separately.

## Remote Access And Server Operations

Use [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access) for the complete guide to one-time invitations, desktop and compact owner sessions, Tailscale Serve, LAN, SSH forwarding, Docker, HTTPS reverse proxies, browser-local voice, access recovery, and proxy error diagnostics.

Use [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker) for pull-first Compose startup, release and digest pins, persistent volumes, offline backup and restore, explicit upgrade and rollback, host Caddy or Tailscale, secret-file mounts, and container-specific Developer boundaries.

Use [Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting) to run the image as one container, the way a hosting service does: its settings, the secret-store key, sizes and updates.

Use [Headless Runs](/docs/operations/headless-run) to give Row-Bot one task from a script, CI job or benchmark harness with `row-bot run`: no window or server, a throwaway data folder, an ATIF trajectory and an exit code.

Remote access remains off by default in ordinary desktop launches. Server operators should back up access state with the rest of the active data directory, keep one worker, publish one canonical origin, terminate remote traffic with HTTPS, and trust only the exact reverse proxy that connects to Row-Bot.

## Back Up

**Settings › Data › Back up and restore** makes a copy of your Row-Bot on this computer, without passwords or sign-ins. Choose **Back up now**; the command palette finds it as "back up". Files a reply was still uploading are left out, and a file that can't be read is named in the result ("Left out a file that couldn't be read: …") instead of stopping the backup.

The backup is saved in the workspace's Backups folder. In the desktop app on the computer Row-Bot runs on, **Show in folder** opens it there. On any other device, such as a phone, another computer's browser, or a server or Docker install, **Download** saves the last backup on that device.

To copy everything by hand instead:

1. Stop running workflows, channels, servers, and active replies.
2. Close Row-Bot so databases are not changing during the copy.
3. Copy the whole active data directory to protected storage.
4. Back up code folders, exported design files, and wiki vaults separately when they live elsewhere.
5. Record the Row-Bot version used with the backup.

## Restore

**Restore from backup** on the same page restores a backup made there. In the desktop app you pick the file; on any other device you choose it in the browser, and it's sent to Row-Bot first (**Stop** cancels the transfer). Row-Bot checks the file, refuses one that isn't a Row-Bot backup, comes from a newer Row-Bot, or is damaged, and lists what to set up again afterwards, such as passwords and sign-ins. Nothing changes until you choose **Restore on restart**: the restore applies the next time Row-Bot starts, with your current profile kept aside in a `before-restore-<time>` folder. A sent file you don't restore is deleted.

To restore a hand-made copy, restore related databases and files as one set while Row-Bot is closed. Point a test launch at the restored directory first, then check conversations, providers, workflows, Knowledge, documents, designs, code folders, plugins, MCP, and channels. Reconnect secrets that were stored in an OS keychain and were not included in the backup.

## Import From Another Assistant

**Settings › Data › Import from another assistant** scans Hermes Agent (the folder `HERMES_HOME` names, `~/.hermes`, or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` on Windows) or OpenClaw data on this computer and lists what it found and where each item goes. Nothing is written until you confirm. What you already have is never replaced unless you turn on **Replace what you already have**, and then a backup is kept first. First launch offers it when it finds one of them.

- **Memories** (Hermes's `memories/MEMORY.md` and `USER.md`; OpenClaw's `MEMORY.md`, `USER.md` and daily notes) open in **Import memories** for you to check. Nothing is saved to memory until you import them there.
- **Past chats** (Hermes's `state.db`) are offered unticked. Ticked, they wait in **Import memories** too, where Row-Bot can look in what you wrote for memories if you turn that on.
- **Persona** (`SOUL.md`) becomes the personality in **Settings › Preferences**, shortened to fit.
- **Agent instructions** (`AGENTS.md`) become a skill, *Instructions from Hermes* (or OpenClaw), which nothing uses until you choose it.
- **Skills** are copied to **Settings › Skills**.
- **MCP servers** are added to **Settings › Apps**, turned off. Their setting values, such as keys in `env` or headers, aren't copied: fill them in, check the server, then turn it on. A server with the same name as one of yours is left alone.
- **Main model** is set when its provider is one Row-Bot has, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Google, xAI or Ollama. Others, such as Nous Portal models, are listed as not brought over.
- **Model servers** (Hermes's custom providers) become **Custom endpoints**, unless you have one with the same name.
- **API keys and tokens** come over only if you tick **Include API keys and tokens**, into the system keychain.

Memories, past chats and MCP servers come over only into the data folder this Row-Bot uses, so leave **Target folder** empty for them. Cron jobs aren't converted: make a workflow for each one. Hermes's sessions, logs, cron jobs and plugins can be copied into the import's report for you to look at, not imported. OpenClaw's channels and its approval, tool, hook and cron settings are listed for you to set up by hand. Moving from Hermes? [Coming From Hermes?](/docs/getting-started/coming-from-hermes) walks through it, with what doesn't come over and how Hermes's ideas map to Row-Bot's.

The same page's danger zone holds irreversible clean-up, such as removing tracker data.

## Sandboxes

**Settings › Data › Sandboxes** makes a second Row-Bot on made-up data, for trying a workflow or skill before it touches real accounts, filming a demo, or showing Row-Bot to someone without your data. Name it, choose what it starts with (a small shop with its own web app and a customer inbox, a charity's documents, household paperwork, sample code, or nothing), and choose **New sandbox**. Ask Row-Bot in a chat and it can make, start and open one too; starting one asks first, by the approval level. It reuses a signed-in sandbox with the same data rather than making another, unless you ask for a new one.

- **Start** runs it on this computer only, with its own chats, settings, memory, workspace and sign-ins. A hosted model needs its own sign-in there, once; local models work at once, and a sandbox Row-Bot makes from a chat on a model on this computer starts with that model chosen. Chats in a sandbox Row-Bot made start at the approval level of the chat that made it (Hands-off becomes Auto), so a demo isn't left waiting on an approval in a window you can't see; change it there like any chat's.
- **Open** signs your browser in to it with a one-time link. Row-Bot's own browser can open it the same way, to film a demo. There, Row-Bot sends without asking (to the sandbox's chat, or a made-up customer), as it reaches no one; paying, deleting, account changes and uploads in a sandbox still ask.
- **Its mark**: every window of a sandbox says **Sandbox · made-up data** in the sidebar.
- **What it can't do**: see your own Row-Bot, its data folder or your keys and tokens; update Row-Bot; count installs; or start sandboxes of its own.
- **Reset** takes it back to what it started with, keeping its model sign-in, **Stop** ends it, and **Delete** removes it. Every sandbox stops when Row-Bot quits. At most five.

## Update, Repair, And Uninstall

Row-Bot downloads updates in the background and installs them when it restarts; **Settings › Updates** shows the version you have, the update **Channel**, what is downloading or ready, and **Restart now**. **Repair** there goes back to the version you had before. [Updates](/docs/operations/updates) explains each step, how to turn background downloads off, and what updates contact.

Back up before a major update: Repair goes back to earlier application files but is not a data backup. Uninstalling the application and deleting the data folder are separate decisions; [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation#uninstall) lists both locations for each system.

## Logs And Support

Use Monitor and the local log folder to diagnose startup, provider, workflow, channel, and background failures. Before sharing diagnostics, remove names, paths, account identifiers, document content, prompts, message content, tokens, and screenshots that expose private data.

## Updates

Route: /docs/operations/updates

How Row-Bot downloads updates in the background, restarts into them, goes back with Repair, and what it contacts.

# Updates

Row-Bot keeps itself up to date. It looks for a new release about once a day, downloads only what changed in the background, and prepares it next to the version you are using. Nothing changes until Row-Bot restarts: choose **Restart to update**, or simply quit Row-Bot and the update is installed then.

Everything on this page is in **Settings › Updates**.

## What Happens In The Background

1. **Check.** About once a day, Row-Bot asks GitHub whether a newer release is out on your **Channel**: **Stable**, or **Beta** to get new features first. **Check now** checks straight away.
2. **Download.** Only what changed is downloaded: Row-Bot's own code (about 8 MB), its images and sounds only when they changed, and only the libraries whose versions changed. Every file is checked before it is used.
3. **Prepare.** Row-Bot builds the new version in its own folder next to the one you are using and tests that it starts. The version you are using is never changed. This takes a minute or two on Windows and less on macOS and Linux, and Row-Bot keeps working meanwhile.
4. **Ready.** The sidebar shows **Restart to update**, the tray menu (the menu bar on macOS) shows **Restart to Update**, and Settings › Updates shows the new version with **What's new** and **Restart now**.

If preparing fails, nothing changes: Settings › Updates says what happened and offers **Try again**.

## Turn Background Updates Off

Background checks and downloads are on by default. Two switches in Settings › Updates change that:

- **Check for updates automatically**: turned off, Row-Bot checks only when you choose **Check now**.
- **Download updates automatically**: turned off, a new release is only offered; choose **Download** to prepare it.

The first launch of an installed Row-Bot mentions this once, with a link to Settings › Updates.

## Restart To Update

Choose **Restart to update** in the sidebar, **Restart now** in Settings › Updates, or **Restart to Update** in the tray. Row-Bot closes, switches to the new version and opens again, usually within seconds.

You don't have to restart now. If you leave it, the update is installed the next time you quit Row-Bot, and the new version opens the next time you start it.

When Row-Bot is busy (a reply is being written, a workflow is running, a channel message is being delivered or a document is being processed), **Restart now** asks first:

- **Restart when idle**: Row-Bot restarts by itself as soon as nothing is running.
- **When I quit**: the update is installed the next time you quit Row-Bot.
- **Restart anyway**: stops the work and restarts now.

The tray item on Windows (and on Linux, when Row-Bot runs with a tray icon) waits too: while Row-Bot is busy, it says Row-Bot will restart when its current work finishes. On macOS the menu bar item restarts straight away; use Settings › Updates to wait for running work.

Goals that were working carry on by themselves after a restart Row-Bot makes to install an update. After a quit, they come back paused as usual (see [Profiles, Goals, And Agents](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/)).

Any device signed in to your Row-Bot, such as your phone, can see the update status and choose **Restart now**; the same check for running work applies.

## If An Update Doesn't Start

If the new version fails to start twice, Row-Bot goes back to the version you had by itself. Settings › Updates then says **Version X didn't start**. Row-Bot doesn't download that version again by itself: choose **Download again** only if you want to retry it. A newer release is offered as usual.

## Go Back To The Previous Version

If a new version misbehaves, **Repair** in Settings › Updates offers **Go back to X.Y.Z**, the version you had before. Choose **Go back and restart**; your data stays as it is.

The version you left stays installed, and Row-Bot doesn't switch back to it by itself. When Settings › Updates offers it again, it says you went back from it; choose **Download** and it is ready at once, without downloading anything. Repair is for a version that misbehaves; it is not a backup (see [Back Up](/docs/operations/#back-up)).

## When You Need The Full Installer

Most updates download in the background. A few can't, and Settings › Updates shows **Version X needs the full installer** with **Download the full installer**, which downloads the installer for your system from GitHub. This happens when:

- the release moves Row-Bot to a newer version of Python,
- a library that changed has no ready-made package for your system, or
- your version is too old to update in place.

Run the installer as you did the first time. Your data and settings stay.

## What Updates Contact

- **GitHub**: `api.github.com` to check for releases, and GitHub's release file hosts (`github.com`, `objects.githubusercontent.com`, `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`) to download them.
- **Library downloads**, only when a release changes libraries: the Python Package Index's file host `files.pythonhosted.org`, and `download.pytorch.org` (which hands over to `download-r2.pytorch.org`) for PyTorch.

Downloads use HTTPS to these hosts only. Every file is checked against a SHA-256 checksum before it is used: Row-Bot's own files against the list published with each release, and every library against the exact checksum recorded for that release. Libraries are only ever installed from ready-made packages, never built on your computer. Update checks and downloads carry no account, usage or personal data. Row-Bot's only telemetry, install stats, is separate: on by default, described in [Install Stats](/docs/privacy-safety#install-stats), and off in one click in Settings › System › Privacy or with `ROW_BOT_INSTALL_COUNT=0`.

## Where Versions Live

| System | Versions |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | `%LocalAppData%\Programs\Row-Bot\versions` |
| macOS | `Row-Bot.app` itself, plus `~/Library/Application Support/Row-Bot/versions` for updates |
| Linux | `~/.local/share/row-bot/releases` |

Row-Bot keeps the version you use and the one before it, for Repair, and removes older ones in the background. Your data never lives in these folders; see [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation#where-row-bot-keeps-things).

## Linux Servers And systemd

`row-bot serve` installs updates the same way. When it restarts to update, it keeps its arguments, so `row-bot serve --port 8080` comes back on port 8080. Run by systemd, Row-Bot leaves the restart to the service: it exits with code 75, so use `Restart=always`, or add `RestartForceExitStatus=75` to your own restart policy. `systemctl stop` installs a ready update, and the next start runs it. See [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation#run-as-a-server).

## Docker And Hosts That Update Row-Bot

Row-Bot in Docker never updates itself: the official image sets `ROW_BOT_UPDATES=external`. Row-Bot then runs no checks, downloads or preparation, and the agent has no update tool. Settings › Updates says the host installs updates; for Docker, pull a newer image and start the container again (see [Explicit Upgrade And Rollback](/docs/operations/docker#explicit-upgrade-and-rollback)).

A program on the host that updates Row-Bot can show its state in Settings › Updates and take requests from it. Both sides share one folder: `ROW_BOT_UPDATES_DIR`, or `host-updates` in the data folder by default.

The host writes `status.json`:

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "state": "idle",
  "current_version": "5.2.1",
  "available_version": "5.2.2",
  "message": "One sentence for people",
  "notes_url": "https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/releases/tag/v5.2.2",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-11T12:00:00Z",
  "handled_request": "id of the last request it acted on"
}
```

- `state` is one of `idle`, `checking`, `downloading`, `ready`, `applying`, `failed` or `paused`.
- `available_version`, `message`, `notes_url` and `handled_request` are optional (`available_version` may be `null`). `notes_url` must start with `https://`.
- The file must be at most 16 KB. A missing or unreadable file counts as no status, and Settings › Updates then says to pull a newer image.

When someone chooses **Update now**, **Skip**, **Pause updates**, **Resume updates** or **Check now**, Row-Bot writes `request.json`:

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "a UUID",
  "action": "update_now",
  "version": "5.2.2",
  "requested_at": "2026-10-11T12:00:00Z"
}
```

- `action` is one of `check`, `update_now`, `skip`, `pause` or `resume`; `version` may be `null`.
- Row-Bot replaces the file atomically, and a newer request replaces one the host hasn't handled yet. The host reads it, deletes it, acts on it, and names its `id` in `handled_request`.

Row-Bot never runs anything on the host's behalf; this folder is the whole interface.

## Source Checkouts

A Row-Bot started from a source checkout never updates itself; Settings › Updates says so. Update it with `git pull` and `uv sync --locked --all-extras --group test`, then rebuild the client (see [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation#run-from-source)).

## Remote Access And Server Mode

Route: /docs/operations/remote-access

Use Row-Bot as one owner from trusted devices through Tailscale, LAN, SSH, Docker, or an HTTPS reverse proxy.

# Remote Access And Server Mode

Row-Bot Remote Access lets one owner use the same instance from several trusted browsers. It is a **single-owner, multi-device** system, not a multi-user service or a hostile tenant-isolation boundary.

Reachability, authentication, and presentation are separate:

- A network route lets a browser reach Row-Bot's neutral connection page.
- A one-time invitation authorizes one browser to create a revocable session.
- Every authenticated interactive browser represents the same owner.
- Desktop or compact presentation changes layout only, never authority.

Normal desktop launches remain local-first. They listen on loopback, where the desktop app needs no sign-in, unless you explicitly enable another route. Authenticated server mode is stricter: every browser must connect with a valid session, including a browser on the server itself.

## Configure Remote Access In The App

Open **Settings › Devices & remote access** from any signed-in owner session, including on a phone. The command palette finds it as "phone" or "connect device".

1. Choose **Connect a phone or computer**.
2. Choose **How will it reach this computer?**: **Tailscale** (private and encrypted HTTPS, recommended), **Same Wi-Fi** (a direct address on your network, over HTTP), **Internet** (from anywhere, through your public link), or **Another address** (a DNS alias, hostname or other browser-facing address you set up yourself, entered as its exact HTTP or HTTPS origin).
3. Choose how long it should **Stay signed in**: **30 days** or **12 hours**.
4. **Scan the code** on the other device, or open the shown address there. Codes work only once; **Show a new code** replaces an expired one.
5. Review the confirmation page on that device, then press **Connect**. The page on the computer then says **Connected**, and **Connect another** starts again.
6. **Your devices** lists every signed-in phone and computer and signs one out.

Row-Bot saves a new address, applies its exact Host/origin admission rule immediately, and creates the origin-bound code without a restart. **Same Wi-Fi** first asks to let devices on your network reach Row-Bot, which restarts it to listen on your network. Under **Advanced**, **Network** shows where Row-Bot listens (**This computer only**, or **This computer and my network**) and its **Allowed addresses**, and **Public link** sets up the ngrok tunnel, which opens only when you start it.

The choice of routes refreshes from current state when the code is created. Row-Bot refuses a stale or no-longer-reachable selection instead of issuing a misleading link.

Saved trusted addresses remain in `access_routes.json` across restarts and appear among the ways to reach this computer. Remove one from **Allowed addresses** when it is no longer needed; new HTTP and WebSocket requests through that exact address are rejected immediately. Removing the address can interrupt current access through it.

Enter one exact `http://` or `https://` origin with an optional port, such as `http://row-bot.lan:8080` or `https://row-bot.example.com`. Credentials, paths, queries, fragments, wildcards, malformed ports, and non-HTTP(S) schemes are rejected. A non-default port trusts only that exact authority, not another port.

Trusting an address changes only Row-Bot admission and invitation routing. Row-Bot performs no DNS lookup or reachability probe and does not create DNS records, provision TLS, configure a proxy, open a firewall, or change the listen address. HTTP traffic is unencrypted. HTTPS still requires external DNS and TLS setup; a TLS-terminating reverse proxy must also use the existing exact trusted-proxy configuration.

Origins supplied through `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_ORIGINS` are listed as **Managed externally** and cannot be edited in the UI. When `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is set, deployment configuration owns Host admission, so trusted-address add/remove controls are read-only and do not override it.

## Invitations, Sessions, And Layouts

| Item | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Invitation | A secret link that expires after 10 minutes and can be consumed once. Opening or previewing it does not connect the device; the recipient must press **Connect**. |
| Session | A separate HttpOnly browser credential created after acceptance. Raw session secrets are never placed in the URL. |
| Trusted device | A session lasting up to 30 days. An active owner UI checks at startup and every 12 hours, renewing the session to 30 days when it enters the final seven days. |
| Temporary access | A session lasting up to 12 hours. |
| Desktop layout | The full owner product in its wide-screen presentation. |
| Compact layout | The same owner authority in a phone-safe presentation, including every Settings page. Design and Developer panels open as full-screen sheets. |

Row-Bot stores only hashed invitation and session secrets in the versioned access database. Sessions survive normal restarts and can be revoked individually. Revoking a device revokes its sessions.

An inactive trusted browser can still expire after 30 days; recover by creating a new one-time invitation from a trusted local terminal, SSH session, or container exec. Temporary 12-hour sessions and migrated legacy sessions retain their fixed expiry and do not renew.

Row-Bot has no guest or multi-user sharing boundary. Device names, user agents, routes, and layout choices are session metadata, not entitlements. Existing action approval gates continue to govern sensitive tools and operations.

Treat an unused invitation like a password. Do not paste it into chat, logs, issue reports, screenshots, shell history you plan to share, or a public URL.

## Choose A Connection Route

| Route | Best fit | Important boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local desktop | Browser and Row-Bot are on the same computer. | Default desktop mode stays on loopback and does not expose a remote listener. |
| Tailscale Serve | Recommended private HTTPS access across your tailnet. | Tailnet membership does not replace a Row-Bot invitation or session. |
| Direct LAN | A private, trusted local network. | Remote LAN HTTP is unencrypted and does not provide a secure browser context for microphone capture. |
| Trusted hostname or address | An existing exact DNS alias, hostname, or browser-facing IP and port. | Row-Bot trusts only the saved origin; it does not provide DNS, TLS, proxy, firewall, or reachability setup. |
| SSH tunnel | An operator can SSH to a remote host and wants no published Row-Bot port. | Keep Row-Bot on loopback and create the invitation for the workstation-facing forwarded origin. |
| Docker | A headless, isolated, reproducible instance. | The supplied Compose file publishes to host loopback by default and persists `/data`. |
| HTTPS reverse proxy | An operator owns DNS, TLS, proxy configuration, backups, and ingress policy. | Trust only the exact proxy address or CIDR that connects to Row-Bot. |

An active route means the connection page is reachable. It does not mean the browser is trusted.

## Tailscale Serve

Tailscale Serve is the recommended desktop route because it provides a private HTTPS origin without changing Row-Bot's default bind address.

Row-Bot does not install Tailscale, sign you in, enable Funnel, reset the complete Serve configuration, change firewall rules, or overwrite an unrelated route. Status checks and planning are read-only. Enabling a route requires you to review the exact private Serve change, accept the third-party disclosure, and confirm it in the UI.

Row-Bot refuses to mutate when Funnel is active, a conflicting route exists, ownership cannot be verified, or the Tailscale CLI outcome is ambiguous. It records ownership only after it verifies the exact route it created, and it removes only that unchanged owned route.

After a verified enable or disable, Row-Bot asks its launcher to restart the app. That restart activates the matching proxy policy:

- only loopback connections from the local Tailscale proxy are trusted;
- only the verified owned `.ts.net` host and HTTPS origin are added;
- the owned route must still target this exact Row-Bot app port.

If the launcher is unavailable, the UI tells you to restart Row-Bot manually. A manually managed Tailscale or reverse-proxy route is not treated as Row-Bot-owned; configure its public URL, allowed host, and exact proxy trust explicitly.

After Tailscale reports **Active Owned**, create the invitation for its verified private origin. The recipient still needs the one-time invitation and resulting Row-Bot session.

## Direct LAN

Use **Allow local-network connections** only on a network you trust. The launcher restarts Row-Bot after the durable listen setting changes.

Anyone who can reach the port can see the neutral connection page, but cannot use the application without a valid session. Over LAN HTTP a signed-in browser can send messages and make changes as it can on this computer; only the microphone needs `localhost` or HTTPS. LAN HTTP is unencrypted. Prefer Tailscale or an operator-managed HTTPS origin on shared, guest, workplace, or otherwise untrusted networks. Row-Bot does not change the host firewall.

## SSH Tunnel

Start Row-Bot on loopback:

```bash
row-bot serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Forward a workstation port:

```bash
ssh -N -L 18080:127.0.0.1:8080 user@row-bot-host
```

Create the invitation for the origin the browser will actually use:

```bash
row-bot access invite \
  --layout desktop \
  --origin http://127.0.0.1:18080
```

## Advanced / Managed Deployments

Environment variables and CLI flags remain useful when deployment tooling must own policy. `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_ORIGINS` entries are visible but read-only in Settings. Setting `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` makes Host admission externally managed and disables trusted-address mutation in the UI; durable UI addresses never override that explicit policy.

### Authenticated Server Mode

`row-bot serve` starts one authenticated headless instance. It defaults to loopback, one worker, no tray, no splash, no opened browser, and no automatic Ollama startup.

For a host-installed HTTPS reverse proxy:

```bash
row-bot serve \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8080 \
  --public-url https://row-bot.example.com \
  --allowed-host row-bot.example.com \
  --trusted-proxy 127.0.0.1/32
```

The equivalent core environment settings are:

```text
ROW_BOT_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=server
ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL=https://row-bot.example.com
ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=row-bot.example.com
ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=127.0.0.1/32
ROW_BOT_WORKERS=1
# Optional: turn install stats off on this server (see Privacy And Safety).
ROW_BOT_INSTALL_COUNT=0
```

Use the address that actually connects from the proxy to Row-Bot. Do not trust every private address, a whole Docker bridge range, or caller-supplied forwarding headers. Do not buffer the event stream (`/api/v1/events`, `text/event-stream`) and terminate remote traffic with HTTPS. The reviewed [Caddy example](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/deploy/reverse-proxy/Caddyfile.example) and [systemd service](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/deploy/systemd/row-bot.service.example) are starting points, not substitutes for operator-owned firewall, rate-limit, logging, backup, and recovery policy.

The deprecated `row-bot --server --no-open` form remains compatible, but new scripts and services should use `row-bot serve`.

### Cloudflare Tunnel

A Cloudflare Tunnel is an HTTPS reverse proxy: Cloudflare serves your hostname and `cloudflared` passes each request on to Row-Bot. Row-Bot does not install `cloudflared` or set up the tunnel, DNS, or Cloudflare Access.

1. Point the tunnel at Row-Bot's loopback address, such as `http://127.0.0.1:8080`, rather than `localhost`, so requests come from one known address. Do not set the tunnel's HTTP Host Header to another name; Row-Bot checks the public hostname.
2. Trust only the address `cloudflared` connects from. When it runs on the same computer, set `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=127.0.0.1/32` before Row-Bot starts, or pass `--trusted-proxy 127.0.0.1/32` to `row-bot serve`.
3. Add the public origin, such as `https://row-bot.example.com`, as **Another address** in the app (or with `--public-url` and `--allowed-host`), and create the invitation for it.

Cloudflare sends `CF-Connecting-IP` beside `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Row-Bot accepts it and takes the client address from `X-Forwarded-For`. Leave Cloudflare's **Remove visitor IP headers** managed transform off, because Row-Bot needs `X-Forwarded-For`, and leave **Add "True-Client-IP" header** off, because Row-Bot refuses that header.

## Docker

The supplied Docker image contains the complete supported server feature set: all canonical Python extras, matching headless Playwright Chromium, native media libraries, `uv`/`uvx`, and pinned Node.js with `node`/`npm`/`npx`. It does not contain invitations, sessions, credentials, downloaded voice models, arbitrary MCP servers, or Tailscale.

Compose publishes `127.0.0.1:8080` by default and persists private state and explicit model/runtime downloads under `/data`. Every browser must claim an invitation, including a browser on the Docker host. Docker bridge and gateway addresses never grant owner identity.

Follow [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker) for the pull-first public runbook, and use the repository's [Docker operator notes](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/deploy/docker/README.md) when building from source. The public guide covers:

- invitation bootstrap with `docker compose exec`;
- intentional LAN or HTTPS publication;
- multiple isolated instances;
- health and readiness checks;
- read-only secret files;
- backups, upgrades, restore, and rollback;
- trusted-session renewal and inactive-session recovery;
- browser, MCP runtime, local-model cache, and headless feature boundaries.

Never mount the host Docker socket merely to satisfy a tool or MCP server.

## Voice From A Remote Browser

Local browser voice uses the requesting browser's microphone and speaker. Talk streams that browser's audio to Row-Bot over a WebSocket on Row-Bot's own signed-in address, and Row-Bot streams its voice back the same way; Dictate sends each recording to Row-Bot when you finish. Row-Bot transcribes with the selected local engine (Whisper by default, a downloaded faster speech model for Talk, or SenseVoice after its explicit installation) and speaks with Kokoro, unless you chose a cloud speech service or voice in Settings › Voice. A headless server or container does not need access to the host microphone or speakers.

Browsers permit microphone capture on `localhost` or in a secure HTTPS context. Plain HTTP on a remote LAN address is insufficient. Use Tailscale HTTPS or a correctly configured HTTPS reverse proxy for remote dictation or talk. Tailscale Serve, the public link and the Caddy example carry the WebSocket; another reverse proxy must pass WebSocket connections through for Talk and Live voice to work.

Whisper, SenseVoice, Kokoro and faster speech model installation remains an explicit owner action and can use several gigabytes of persistent cache. SenseVoice alone is an approximately 940 MB ModelScope download and is unavailable on Intel macOS. Live voice and cloud speech services are separate provider features with your own keys; local browser voice never switches to them by itself.

## Offline Access Management And Recovery

Use a trusted local terminal, SSH session, or `docker compose exec`:

```bash
row-bot access invite --layout desktop --origin https://row-bot.example.com
row-bot access invite --layout compact --temporary --origin https://row-bot.example.com
row-bot access list
row-bot access revoke DEVICE_ID
row-bot access revoke SESSION_ID --session
row-bot access revoke-all --yes
row-bot access doctor
```

`list` and `doctor` never print reusable session secrets. Invitation commands are the only commands that print a raw one-time link.

If every owner session is lost, create a new owner invitation from a trusted terminal. Back up the complete active `ROW_BOT_DATA_DIR` while Row-Bot is stopped. It contains conversations, configuration, instance identity, invitations, devices, sessions, and other private state; operating-system keyring credentials may require a separate recovery plan.

## Troubleshooting

- **`untrusted_forwarding_headers`**: a proxy supplied forwarding headers from an address Row-Bot does not trust. For a Row-Bot-owned Tailscale route, restart once if the UI reports that restart is required. For an operator proxy, set only its exact connecting address in `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`. Do not fix this by trusting a broad network.
- **`unsupported_forwarding_headers`**: a trusted proxy sent a client-address header Row-Bot does not use, such as `X-Real-IP`, `True-Client-IP`, or `X-Forwarded-Server`. Have the proxy send `Forwarded`, or `X-Forwarded-For` with `X-Forwarded-Proto` (and `X-Forwarded-Host` if it changes the host), and remove the others. Cloudflare's `CF-Connecting-IP` is accepted beside `X-Forwarded-For`; see [Cloudflare Tunnel](#cloudflare-tunnel). Do not fix this by trusting a broad network.
- **`missing_x_forwarded_for`**: a trusted proxy sent `X-Forwarded-Proto` or `X-Forwarded-Host` without `X-Forwarded-For`, for example with Cloudflare's **Remove visitor IP headers** on. Have the proxy send `X-Forwarded-For`.
- **`unexpected_host`**: on a desktop launch, open **Settings › Devices & remote access**, add the exact browser-facing origin (as **Another address** when connecting a device, or under **Advanced › Network › Allowed addresses**), and retry without restarting. In a managed deployment, the host may instead be missing from `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, or the proxy may have forwarded a different host.
- **Origin or invitation mismatch**: create the invitation for the exact browser-facing scheme, host, and port. Do not reuse an invitation after changing routes.
- **Tailscale conflict or unowned route**: inspect the existing Serve configuration. Row-Bot will not reset or overwrite it.
- **Phone reaches the page but cannot use Row-Bot**: reachability is working; create or reclaim the correct invitation and confirm the device was not revoked.
- **Remote microphone unavailable**: use HTTPS, grant microphone permission in that browser, and install the local voice model explicitly.
- **Server starts but is not ready**: check `/healthz`, `/readyz`, local logs, and `row-bot access doctor`.

For command lookup, see the generated [CLI reference](/docs/reference/generated/cli) and [environment reference](/docs/reference/generated/environment-and-config).

## Docker And VPS Operations

Route: /docs/operations/docker

Run one persistent Row-Bot server with Docker Compose, private host access, or an operator-managed HTTPS edge.

# Docker And VPS Operations

The official container runs one **single-owner, multi-device** Row-Bot instance. It is not a multi-user service or a hostile tenant-isolation boundary. Every browser, including one on the Docker host, must claim a one-time invitation before it receives a revocable owner session.

The default Compose topology publishes only `127.0.0.1:8080`, runs the application as UID/GID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, and keeps private state in separate named data and encryption-key volumes. It does not mount the Docker socket, host devices, a desktop display, or host audio.

To run the image as one container with one volume and no Compose, the way a hosting service does, read [Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting).

## Prerequisites

- Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with Linux containers and Docker Compose.
- Enough disk for the full image plus the `/data` volume. Models, managed runtimes, browser outputs, and caches can grow after explicit use; Row-Bot does not promise one fixed capacity figure.
- For public VPS access: Linux, Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer, DNS you control, and a host-managed HTTPS proxy or Tailscale installation.

Release images are built from tagged source in GitHub Actions with the locked dependency set. Native amd64 and arm64 jobs run the isolated authenticated-container smoke before the release manifest is created, and the registry exposes a digest for immutable pins. The smoke uses bounded request timeouts and requires two consecutive readiness samples; it retries only safe GET probes, never repeats a state-changing POST, and limits failure output to redacted container state and log tails.

## Download A Release-Pinned Compose File

You do not need to clone the repository. Choose a released version, create a private deployment directory, and download the Compose file from the same tag:

```bash
export ROW_BOT_VERSION=X.Y.Z
mkdir -p row-bot-docker
cd row-bot-docker
curl -fsSLo compose.yaml \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/docker/compose.yaml"
export ROW_BOT_IMAGE="ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:${ROW_BOT_VERSION}"
docker buildx imagetools inspect "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}"
docker compose -f compose.yaml config
```

Replace `X.Y.Z` with a release that lists the Row-Bot container in GitHub Packages. A source tag can exist without a published container, so confirm the image before starting. Pull requests and manually dispatched container checks verify builds but do not publish them; publishing happens only after a GitHub Release is published. If the registry reports `manifest unknown` for the version you chose, select a release with a container or use [Build From Source](#build-from-source).

Keep `ROW_BOT_VERSION`, the downloaded file, and `ROW_BOT_IMAGE` aligned. The Compose default is `ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:latest`, but an explicit version is easier to audit and roll back. Stable releases also update `latest`; prereleases do not.

For an immutable image pin, replace the tag with the digest published for that release:

```bash
export ROW_BOT_IMAGE='ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot@sha256:RELEASE_MANIFEST_DIGEST'
docker compose -f compose.yaml config
```

## Account Credential Persistence Is Automatic

Headless containers do not have a desktop keyring. On every `docker compose up`, a short-lived, network-disabled initializer creates a random `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` only when the project-scoped `row_bot_secrets` volume is empty. The application receives that volume read-only and uses the key to encrypt ChatGPT/Codex tokens and other owner-entered secrets under `/data/secure-secrets`.

There is no key to create or environment value to set for the normal Compose path. Keep both named volumes for restart, container replacement, upgrade, and rollback, and back up the key separately from `/data`. Advanced unattended deployments can replace the generated key volume with an operator-managed read-only directory as described in [Read-Only Secret Files](#read-only-secret-files).

## First Start And Owner Invitation

Like every Row-Bot, the container sends [install stats](/docs/privacy-safety#install-stats) once a day: a random ID, its version and `docker`, nothing else. To turn them off for this deployment, add `ROW_BOT_INSTALL_COUNT: "0"` to the service's `environment` in `compose.yaml` before the first start, or switch off **Share install stats** in Settings › System › Privacy.

A fresh `up` pulls the image only when it is absent locally, creates the data and encryption-key volumes, initializes the key without network access, and starts the foreground server:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f compose.yaml ps
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz
```

The unauthenticated root shows a neutral connection flow. Create the first invitation from a private terminal; the output is a one-time secret:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \
  row-bot access invite --layout desktop --origin http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

Open the printed URL, review the confirmation, and select **Connect**. Use `--layout compact` for phone presentation. Both layouts grant the same owner authority.

Useful secret-free checks are:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot row-bot access list
docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot row-bot access doctor --host 127.0.0.1
docker compose -f compose.yaml logs --tail 200 row-bot
```

Do not paste invitation URLs, cookies, provider credentials, or unredacted logs into issues or chat.

## Finish Setup And Install Private Knowledge Search

First launch is the same in desktop, source, and Docker installations: answer **How should Row-Bot think?** to choose your first model. Private knowledge search uses **Mixedbread Embed Large v1**, a separate local model for semantic memory and document search, as a 675 MB download you start from Settings → Documents (Setup Center links there). The download requires internet access to Hugging Face and does not upload documents or memories.

In Docker, the downloaded files live in the `/data` cache, so the named volume preserves them across restarts and container replacement. Install it for the recommended semantic search experience. Until then, Row-Bot still works and uses bounded lexical and graph fallback; install the model from [Settings → Documents](/docs/settings/documents) under **Search model files**.

After changing an embedding provider or model, rebuild the document and memory vectors from this screen. A cloud embedding provider is a separate opt-in choice and sends the indexed text to that provider; the recommended default stays local after the initial download.

## Stop, Restart, Reboot, And Replace

Normal stop and start retain the container and named volume:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml stop row-bot
docker compose -f compose.yaml start row-bot
```

`restart: unless-stopped` lets an existing service return when the Docker daemon starts after a host reboot. After every reboot, verify `ps`, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and an existing authenticated browser.

Replacing only the container preserves the same instance identity, settings, sessions, conversations, and selected caches in `/data`:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate row-bot
```

## Multiple Isolated Instances

Use a different Compose project name and host port for each instance. Compose project names isolate the containers, networks, and named data and encryption-key volumes:

```bash
docker compose --project-name row-bot-main \
  -f compose.yaml up -d

ROW_BOT_HOST_PORT=8081 docker compose --project-name row-bot-lab \
  -f compose.yaml up -d
```

Create invitations for `http://127.0.0.1:8080` and `http://127.0.0.1:8081`, respectively. Every project automatically receives its own data and encryption-key volumes. Do not copy one instance's access database or encryption key into another unless you are deliberately restoring that same instance. Each fresh instance has a different identity, so its cookies and owner sessions remain isolated even when the hostname is the same.

## Consistent Offline Backup

Treat a backup as private user data. Stop the service before copying the whole volume so related SQLite files are one consistent set. Use a disposable helper container to create archives; do not use `docker compose cp` for the complete `/data` tree because model caches can contain symbolic links that a Windows host cannot reproduce.

The helper has no network, receives the source volumes read-only, and adds only the capability needed to read every file in the stopped volume:

```bash
backup_dir="$(pwd)/backups/row-bot-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mkdir -p "$backup_dir"
docker compose -f compose.yaml stop row-bot
row_bot_container="$(docker compose -f compose.yaml ps -a -q row-bot)"
docker run --rm \
  --network none \
  --read-only \
  --user 0:0 \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add DAC_READ_SEARCH \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --volumes-from "${row_bot_container}:ro" \
  --mount "type=bind,src=${backup_dir},dst=/backup" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" \
  -c 'set -eu; tar -C /data -czf /backup/data.tar.gz .; tar -C /run/secrets -czf /backup/secrets.tar.gz ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY'
docker compose -f compose.yaml start row-bot
```

Run the final `start` command even if archive creation reports an error. On Windows PowerShell, use `$backupDir = (New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "backups\\row-bot-$((Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ'))").FullName`, `$rowBotContainer = docker compose -f compose.yaml ps -a -q row-bot`, backticks instead of backslashes for line continuation, `$backupDir` in the bind mount, and `$env:ROW_BOT_IMAGE` as the image value. The archive work still runs inside Linux and therefore preserves cache symlinks.

Encrypt and protect both `data.tar.gz` and `secrets.tar.gz` with your normal backup system. Record the image tag and digest beside them. Encrypted server credentials under `/data/secure-secrets` are usable only with the matching `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`; protect both archives. Other credentials supplied through an operator-managed read-only directory need their own recovery procedure.

Test a restore under a different Compose project name and port. This creates a separate named volume and does not overwrite the live instance:

```bash
export ROW_BOT_HOST_PORT=18080
restore_backup_dir="$(cd ./backups/RESTORE_SET && pwd)"
docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml \
  create secret-store-init row-bot
restore_app_container="$(docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml ps -a -q row-bot)"
restore_init_container="$(docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml ps -a -q secret-store-init)"
docker run --rm \
  --network none \
  --read-only \
  --user 0:0 \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add CHOWN \
  --cap-add FOWNER \
  --cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --volumes-from "${restore_app_container}" \
  --mount "type=bind,src=${restore_backup_dir},dst=/backup,readonly" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" \
  -c 'set -eu; tar -C /data -xzf /backup/data.tar.gz'
docker run --rm \
  --network none \
  --read-only \
  --user 0:0 \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add CHOWN \
  --cap-add FOWNER \
  --cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --volumes-from "${restore_init_container}" \
  --mount "type=bind,src=${restore_backup_dir},dst=/backup,readonly" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" \
  -c 'set -eu; tar -C /run/secrets -xzf /backup/secrets.tar.gz'
docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml up -d
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:18080/readyz
docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \
  row-bot access doctor --host 127.0.0.1
```

Set `ROW_BOT_IMAGE` to the recorded image before restoring. On PowerShell, resolve the backup directory with `$restoreBackupDir = (Resolve-Path '.\\backups\\RESTORE_SET').Path`, capture the two container IDs with `$restoreAppContainer` and `$restoreInitContainer`, and use those variables in the same helper commands. Inspect the restored data and authentication before changing any proxy or production route. Remove the isolated project with `docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml down --volumes` only after you have finished the restore test.

## Explicit Upgrade And Rollback

Upgrades are never automatic. The image sets `ROW_BOT_UPDATES=external`, so Row-Bot in a container never downloads updates itself, and Settings › Updates says the host installs them ([Updates](/docs/operations/updates#docker-and-hosts-that-update-row-bot) describes the folder a host updater can use). Take an offline backup, choose the new version or digest, pull it explicitly, recreate, and run checks:

```bash
export ROW_BOT_IMAGE='ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:NEW_VERSION'
docker compose -f compose.yaml pull row-bot
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d row-bot
docker compose -f compose.yaml ps
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz
docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \
  row-bot access doctor --host 127.0.0.1
```

Also verify an existing browser session and a normal streamed response. For rollback, use the previous image digest with its matching pre-upgrade data backup in an isolated project first. Database changes can make an old image incompatible with state already opened by a newer one.

## Read-Only Secret Files

The default stack already provides encrypted persistence for secrets entered in the UI. For centrally managed or pre-provisioned deployments, you can instead keep one allowlisted setting value per file in an absolute private host directory outside the repository. This override replaces the automatic key volume, so the directory must also contain `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`. Download the example override from the same release tag:

```bash
curl -fsSLo compose.secrets.yaml.example \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/docker/compose.secrets.yaml.example"
export ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR=/srv/row-bot/secrets
sudo install -d -o 10001 -g 10001 -m 0700 "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR"
openssl rand -hex 32 | sudo tee \
  "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY" >/dev/null
sudo chown 10001:10001 \
  "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY"
sudo chmod 0400 \
  "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY"
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.secrets.yaml.example config
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.secrets.yaml.example up -d
```

Restrict the host directory to the Docker operator and container UID/GID 10001. The override mounts only `/run/secrets:ro`; it does not put values into Compose environment, labels, command lines, or image layers. Externally managed provider and channel values remain read-only in Settings and are never copied into `/data`.

`ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` is different: it is a 32-byte master key encoded as exactly 64 hexadecimal characters. The default initializer generates it automatically in the project-scoped key volume; the override above makes you its operator. When a desktop keyring is unavailable, Row-Bot uses it to encrypt in-app OAuth tokens and other owner-entered secrets under `/data/secure-secrets`. This allows ChatGPT/Codex and other rotating OAuth credentials to survive a process restart or container replacement without placing the tokens in environment variables. The master key itself remains only in `/run/secrets` and is never copied into `/data`.

Keep the same key for backup, restore, upgrade, and rollback. With no key and nothing saved yet, Row-Bot makes its own key on the data volume ([Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting#the-secret-store-key)); saved secrets with no key stop the start, and an invalid or changed key fails closed and cannot decrypt, replace, or delete existing encrypted records. There is no automatic key rotation. To replace a lost key, reconnect the affected accounts and re-enter secrets after deliberately starting with an empty encrypted secret directory.

## Build From Source

Source builds are opt-in and require a repository checkout. The build override changes only the image source; the base file remains authoritative for runtime and security settings:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot.git
cd row-bot
docker compose \
  -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml \
  -f deploy/docker/compose.build.yaml \
  build row-bot
docker compose \
  -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml \
  -f deploy/docker/compose.build.yaml \
  up -d
```

Record the source revision and resulting image digest before relying on a source build.

## Linux VPS With Host Caddy

This topology uses host networking only in the VPS override. Row-Bot binds `127.0.0.1:8080`; host Caddy terminates HTTPS on ports 80/443 and connects from IPv4 loopback. Nothing publishes container port 8080 externally.

1. Point the dedicated DNS name at the VPS.
2. Allow inbound TCP 80/443 in the host and provider firewalls; do not expose 8080.
3. Install and operate Caddy on the host.
4. Download the release-matched override and Caddy example:

```bash
curl -fsSLo compose.vps.yaml \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/docker/compose.vps.yaml"
curl -fsSLo Caddyfile.row-bot \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/reverse-proxy/Caddyfile.example"
```

Set the exact browser-facing origin and host, then validate the merged configuration:

```bash
export ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL='https://row-bot.example.com'
export ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS='row-bot.example.com'
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml config
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml up -d
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz
```

The override sets `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=127.0.0.1/32` exactly. Replace the example hostname in `Caddyfile.row-bot`, integrate that site block into the host's Caddy configuration, then validate and reload Caddy using the host package's service procedure. Do not broaden proxy trust to a private range or accept caller-supplied forwarding metadata.

The proxy must send `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host` (or `Forwarded`) with every request; the Caddy example does. Row-Bot treats a request that reaches it from loopback with no forwarding headers as coming from the server itself, so a proxy that leaves them out makes every visitor look local.

Create the invitation for the exact HTTPS origin:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml exec row-bot \
  row-bot access invite --layout desktop \
  --origin https://row-bot.example.com
```

From an external browser, confirm the HTTPS connection page, claim the invitation, keep the UI open through a streamed response, and verify its event stream stays connected. Reboot the VPS during a maintenance window and repeat DNS, TLS, readiness, authenticated-session, and streaming checks.

## Host-Managed Tailscale Serve

Tailscale runs on the Linux host, not in the Row-Bot container. Use the VPS override so host Tailscale reaches Row-Bot over exact loopback, but do not install or invoke the Tailscale CLI inside the container.

Set the host's actual private HTTPS name:

```bash
export ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL='https://row-bot-host.example-tailnet.ts.net'
export ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS='row-bot-host.example-tailnet.ts.net'
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml up -d
sudo tailscale serve --bg http://127.0.0.1:8080
tailscale serve status
```

Create an invitation for that exact `https://...ts.net` origin. Tailnet membership supplies private reachability; it does not replace Row-Bot's invitation, session, or revocation controls. The container neither contains nor controls the host Tailscale CLI, Funnel, login, firewall, or route lifecycle.

## Trusted Sessions And Recovery

A trusted browser session lasts up to 30 days. While an authenticated owner UI remains active, the browser checks at startup and every 12 hours. In the final seven days, the server atomically renews that trusted session to 30 days. Temporary 12-hour sessions and migrated legacy sessions never renew.

An inactive trusted browser can still expire after 30 days. If all sessions are lost, recover only from a trusted host terminal or SSH session:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \
  row-bot access invite --layout desktop --origin YOUR_EXACT_ORIGIN
```

Revoked, expired, or device-revoked credentials stay invalid.

## Developer And Headless Boundaries

There are three distinct Developer execution cases:

1. **Row-Bot installed on a host:** Docker Sandbox can use the host's supported Docker runtime when it is available. Local mode remains an explicit workspace choice.
2. **The official Row-Bot application container:** Developer Docker Sandbox is unavailable and fails closed. The image contains no Docker daemon or CLI, and you must not mount the host Docker socket. Local mode can use only a workspace path you explicitly mount into the application container.
3. **An approved Custom Tool inside the application container:** risky approved execution deliberately uses Local mode inside that same container against the selected visible path. It is not a nested Docker sandbox and is not a silent fallback from a requested Docker workspace.

The container has no native tray/window, native desktop Computer Use, physical host microphone or speaker, camera, display server, or GPU by default. Browser-local voice and bundled headless browser automation remain available. Selected local models and runtimes are explicit downloads into `/data`; cache growth depends on what the owner installs and uses.

## Remove The Deployment

Ordinary removal keeps private state:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml down
```

To delete both named volumes and all instance state deliberately, first verify the Compose project and backup, then run:

```bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml down --volumes
```

Those volume deletions remove both private data and the generated encryption key and are not recoverable unless you have a tested backup. External secret directories and backup directories are separate and are never removed by these Compose commands.

## Hosting Row-Bot

Route: /docs/operations/hosting

Run the published Row-Bot image as one container, as a hosting service does: tags, release notes for hosts, settings, the secret-store key, the volume, sizes, memory and updates.

# Hosting Row-Bot

This page is for hosting services, and for anyone who runs the published image the way a hosting service does: one container, one volume and one port, set up with environment variables alone. For Docker Compose on your own computer or server, follow [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker); what this page says about the image applies there too.

Each container is one person's Row-Bot: one owner, signed in from as many devices as they like. It is not a service for several people, and not a boundary between people who don't trust each other.

If a hosting service runs Row-Bot for you, read [Row-Bot In Your Browser](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser) (or [Row-Bot On Railway](/docs/getting-started/on-railway)), [Fix A Hosted Row-Bot](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted) and [What Your Host Can See](/docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see) instead.

## At A Glance

- **Image:** `ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot`, for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`.
- **Command:** the image's own, `row-bot serve`. Start it as the container's first process.
- **User:** uid 10001, gid 10001. A host that starts the container as root gets the same: Row-Bot's first step makes `/data` 10001's and drops to 10001 for good ([Started As Root](#started-as-root)).
- **Volume:** one, at `/data`.
- **Port:** 8080, plain HTTP. HTTPS ends at your proxy.
- **Health:** `/healthz` answers while the process runs; `/readyz` answers 200 once Row-Bot is ready, and 503 while it starts. A check from the container itself (a loopback address, with no `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-*` header) works whatever host names Row-Bot allows; a check through a proxy or from another computer needs a host name Row-Bot knows ([Address And Proxy](#address-and-proxy)).
- **Set-up:** none. There's no init container and no set-up job: `row-bot serve` sets up what it needs as it starts.
- **Logs:** the container output. The setup code and any reason Row-Bot won't start appear there, so show it to the owner.

The image is the whole Row-Bot server: its browser (headless Chromium), and Python and Node.js for tools and MCP servers. It has no GPU, desktop window, screen, microphone or speaker.

To try the shape on your own computer, with a key of its own and the port open only to that computer:

```sh
umask 077
printf 'ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" > row-bot.env
docker run --detach --name row-bot --restart unless-stopped \
  --publish 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 --env-file row-bot.env \
  --volume row_bot_data:/data ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:X.Y.Z
docker logs row-bot
```

The log shows the setup code. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080` and enter it. Keep `row-bot.env` private, and keep a copy apart from the volume.

## Image And Tags

- **`X.Y.Z`** for each release, such as `ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:5.3.2`. One tag covers both architectures.
- **`latest`** moves to each stable release. A prerelease, such as `X.Y.Z-beta.1`, never moves it.
- The image is published when its GitHub release is, so a version tag in the source can exist before its image does. Check it with `docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:X.Y.Z`. To pin the exact build, use the digest from the release ([Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker#download-a-release-pinned-compose-file)).

### Release Notes For Hosts

From 5.3.2 on, each version's notes in [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/releases) end with a **For Hosts** section. It lists breaking changes for hosts, a new recommended size and new host settings, or says "No changes for hosts."

Read it before you offer a new version. Breaking changes for hosts are flagged there, and announced to hosts at least a week before the release that brings them.

## Settings

Everything is an environment variable, set when the container starts. The image already sets the rest (`ROW_BOT_DATA_DIR=/data`, `ROW_BOT_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=server`, port 8080 on every interface), so don't change those.

- [`ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE`](#the-setup-code): optional. The code that makes the first browser the owner, generated by the host for each server.
- [`ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`](#the-secret-store-key): the key that encrypts saved sign-ins and keys, generated by the host for each server and never changed.
- [`ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL`](#address-and-proxy): the exact address people open, set for each server.
- [`ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`](#address-and-proxy): the address ranges of the host's proxy in front of Row-Bot.
- [`ROW_BOT_HOSTED_BY`](#the-hosts-name): optional. Names the hosting service on Row-Bot's own pages.
- [`ROW_BOT_UPDATES`](#updates): `external`, set by the image. Row-Bot never updates itself; the host does.

### The Setup Code

The first person to open a new Row-Bot sees its setup page. Entering the setup code makes that browser the owner; nobody gets in without it.

- **Optional.** A host that sets `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE` generates a new one for each server. It needs 12 to 64 letters or digits. Spaces, dashes and upper or lower case don't matter, and the letters O, I and L count as 0, 1 and 1.
- **Out of the environment.** Row-Bot reads the code as it starts and removes it from its environment, so no program it starts inherits it. It keeps only a salted hash.
- **Printed while nobody owns the server.** Every start prints the code to the container output, and never to Row-Bot's own log files:

  ```text
  ========================================================================
  Row-Bot setup code: ABCD-EFGH-JKMN (open your Row-Bot and enter it)
  ========================================================================
  ```

- **Without the variable,** Row-Bot makes a 12-character code of its own and prints it the same way. Each start makes a new one, and the last one stops working.
- **A code Row-Bot can't use** is ignored with a warning in the log, which never shows the code: one that's too short or has other characters, or one that already signed someone in. While nobody owns the server, Row-Bot then prints a code of its own instead.
- **It works once.** After the owner signs in, later starts print nothing. Leaving the variable as it is changes nothing.
- **Wrong codes.** Five wrong codes from one address pause that address for 15 minutes. Behind a proxy, Row-Bot sees each visitor's own address only when it trusts the proxy ([Address And Proxy](#address-and-proxy)).
- **Recovery.** If the owner loses every signed-in browser, set a new code and restart the container. A recovery code is never printed. The owner opens Row-Bot, chooses **Lost access?** and enters it. It works once, signs that browser in, and signs out every other browser and cancels open invitations. So the owner must be able to change this setting.

Anyone with a terminal in the container can still create a one-time invitation with `row-bot access invite` ([Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access#offline-access-management-and-recovery)).

### The Secret-Store Key

A container has no keychain, so Row-Bot encrypts saved sign-ins and keys itself (model API keys, provider sign-ins, channel tokens, app and MCP sign-ins) in `/data/secure-secrets`, with a 256-bit key.

`ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` gives Row-Bot that key: exactly 64 hexadecimal characters, generated once for each server:

```sh
openssl rand -hex 32
```

- **Out of the environment.** Row-Bot takes the key out of its environment as it starts. Of Row-Bot's processes, only its launcher and its server hold it, in memory. No program they start (a shell, an MCP server, Claude Code, Python, Row-Bot's browser) inherits it. On Linux, both are also non-dumpable, so only root can read the environment they started with.
- **First process.** Anything else started in the container with its variables keeps its own copy of the key, such as an init process (`docker run --init`) or a `docker exec` command. Start `row-bot` as the container's first process, as the image does. The image's own health check starts with an empty environment (`env -i`), so it holds no copy.
- **Off the volume.** The key is never written to `/data`, so a copy of the volume, or a backup of it, holds only encrypted records. The host's settings for the server, and `docker inspect`, still show it.
- **Never printed.** A key that isn't 64 hexadecimal characters stops the start with `Row-Bot didn't start: ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY must contain exactly 64 hexadecimal characters`, without the value.

Row-Bot uses the first key it finds:

1. `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` in the environment.
2. A regular file named `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` (not a symbolic link) in `ROW_BOT_SECRETS_DIR`, which is `/run/secrets` in the image. This is the Compose path, which needs nothing new.
3. Neither: at its first start, Row-Bot makes a key in `/data/secret-store-key/`, readable only by its own user. Anyone with a full copy of the volume, including the host's backups, can then open the saved sign-ins. Row-Bot's own backups (**Settings › Data**) leave the key out.

Row-Bot makes that key only in a container, and only when nothing is saved yet. The desktop app keeps using the computer's keychain.

**Warning: Never change the key, and keep a copy**
Without the key the saved sign-ins can't be opened, and the owner has to enter them all again. Every start checks that the key opens them. If it doesn't, or there are saved sign-ins and no key at all, Row-Bot doesn't start. Nothing is deleted. The container output shows a line starting `Row-Bot didn't start:` that says why, and what to do.

To recover:

- **The key changed:** set it back.
- **Row-Bot made its own key, and the variable is new:** remove the variable, or set it to the contents of `/data/secret-store-key/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`. Once Row-Bot starts with the variable, delete that file: Row-Bot warns while it's still there.
- **The key is lost:** move `/data/secure-secrets` aside and start again. Everything else stays; the owner signs in to providers and apps again.

### Address And Proxy

Row-Bot answers only requests addressed to a host name it knows. By default those are `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`, so every server needs its own address set. Behind an HTTPS proxy, Row-Bot also needs to trust that proxy.

- **`ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL`:** the exact origin people open, such as `https://row-bot.example.com`: a scheme, a host and an optional port, nothing else. Row-Bot adds its host name to the default ones, and through a proxy accepts only this origin.
- **`ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`:** exact host names, separated by commas, with no wildcards. It **replaces** the default list. Row-Bot's own checks reach it at `127.0.0.1`, which works whatever the list holds. `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL` alone is usually enough.
- **`ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`:** the addresses or ranges (CIDR) the proxy connects from, separated by commas. Row-Bot also reads `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXIES`. Only these may tell Row-Bot the visitor's address and scheme.
- **`ROW_BOT_UNTRUSTED_FORWARDED_ACTION`:** what happens to forwarding headers from anyone else. `reject`, the default, refuses the request with `untrusted_forwarding_headers`; `ignore` drops the headers.

Name the proxy in `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, and have it send `X-Forwarded-For` with `X-Forwarded-Proto` (and `X-Forwarded-Host` if it changes the host), or `Forwarded`. Row-Bot then sees each visitor's own address, and knows the browser uses HTTPS. A proxy that leaves those headers out makes every visitor look as if they came from the proxy, or from the server itself when the proxy runs on the same machine, so it must send them on every request. Row-Bot also accepts `X-Real-IP` (Railway) and `CF-Connecting-IP` (Cloudflare) beside them from a trusted proxy, but never takes the visitor's address from those, and refuses them without `X-Forwarded-For`.

Without a trusted proxy, a browser on an HTTPS address can't sign in. With `reject`, Row-Bot refuses the proxy's forwarding headers. With `ignore`, or a proxy that sends none, Row-Bot sees plain HTTP from the proxy's address, and signing in checks that the browser's origin matches exactly. `ignore` also makes every visitor share the proxy's address, so one stranger's wrong setup codes would pause the owner too.

Trust only the proxy's own ranges, never a whole private network. Don't buffer Row-Bot's event stream (`/api/v1/events`, `text/event-stream`). [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access#troubleshooting) explains each error, such as `unexpected_host`.

### The Host's Name

`ROW_BOT_HOSTED_BY` names the hosting service. Row-Bot knows two values, and its pages then use that host's own words:

- **`pikapods`:** the setup page names PikaPods and sends the owner to the pod's **More › Show Logs** for the code, with a **Manage pod** link. **Settings › Updates** says PikaPods installs each new version.
- **`railway`:** the setup page sends the owner to the service's **Variables** for the code, with a **Manage service** link. **Settings › Updates** says the owner updates Row-Bot in Railway ([Railway](#railway)).

Row-Bot ignores any other value, with a warning in its log, and its pages use general words ("in its log", "in its server settings"). Each known host is an entry in Row-Bot's code, links included, so no setting can send the owner anywhere else.

### Install Stats

Like every Row-Bot, a hosted one sends [install stats](/docs/privacy-safety#install-stats) once a day: a random ID, its version and `docker`, nothing else. The owner turns them off in **Settings › System › Privacy**; a host can set `ROW_BOT_INSTALL_COUNT=0` instead.

## The Volume

Everything Row-Bot keeps lives in `/data`: conversations, settings, the encrypted sign-ins, signed-in devices, the workspace, downloaded models and runtimes, and caches. Its home folder is `/data` too.

- `/data` must be writable by uid 10001. A Docker named volume takes that owner from the image; a folder on the host needs `chown 10001:10001`. A volume the host mounts as root works when the container starts as root too ([Started As Root](#started-as-root)).
- Keep the same volume, and the same key, across restarts and updates.
- A copy of the volume is a full copy of the owner's Row-Bot. Treat backups of it as private data.

## Sizes

Measured with full Row-Bot in a container:

| Size | What fits |
|---|---|
| **4 GB memory, 2 cores, 10 GB disk (recommended)** | Everything at once: the local search model, Row-Bot's browser, Python work, MCP servers and local speech-to-text, at a peak of about 3.2 GB with the file cache |
| **2 GB memory (minimum)** | Everything except local speech-to-text, which adds about 600–800 MB |

- **At rest:** about 360–420 MB just started. Idle, it uses about 0.2% of a core with no page open, and up to about 2% with one open.
- **Disk:** the image is about 1.6 GB to download and 6.6 GB unpacked. `/data` reached 1.7 GB in the first hour, with the local search model (641 MB) and speech-to-text (464 MB) downloaded; workspaces and documents grow from there.
- **Out of memory:** the kernel stops the container. Restarted, Row-Bot is ready again within seconds, with its data and sign-ins intact.

## Memory

Row-Bot reads the container's memory limit (cgroup `memory.max`) and keeps, in `/data`, the highest working set it has seen: its use without the file cache the kernel can drop, as Docker and Kubernetes count it. Nothing is turned off on a small server:

- **Row-Bot's browser** closes by itself ten minutes after its last use, when a conversation's idle tabs close anyway, and starts again the next time it's needed, still signed in to sites.
- **Settings › Documents** suggests **Free memory when idle** below 3.5 GB, so the search model unloads between searches.
- **Settings › Voice** marks local speech-to-text "Needs a 4 GB server" below 3.5 GB, and asks before it is chosen. The question's **Use cloud speech-to-text** keeps a cloud speech service under **Listen with** (the one chosen, else one whose key is saved, else Deepgram Nova-3, whose key it then asks for).

If Row-Bot restarts because the server ran out of memory, Home and System Monitor say so, with the server's size, until the owner dismisses it. To fix it, do one of these:

- **Give the server 4 GB.** Resize it where your host manages it: on PikaPods, that's your pod in **My Pods**; on Railway, the service's memory limit in **Settings › Deploy**. Row-Bot keeps its data and sign-ins, and the notice goes once the server is bigger.
- **Use cloud speech-to-text.** In **Settings › Voice**, choose a cloud speech service under **Listen with** (**Deepgram Nova-3**, **AssemblyAI Realtime**, **OpenAI Live Transcribe** or **Gemini Transcribe Live**) and add its key, or talk with Live voice. Local speech-to-text is what doesn't fit beside the rest in 2 GB. Dictate and chat-app voice notes still use local speech-to-text.

## Updates

- **Row-Bot never updates itself in the image.** The image sets `ROW_BOT_UPDATES=external`: Row-Bot runs no update checks or downloads, its agent has no update tool, and **Settings › Updates** says the host installs updates. A program that updates Row-Bot can show its progress there through a shared folder ([Updates](/docs/operations/updates#docker-and-hosts-that-update-row-bot)).
