- **To update,** start the new version's image with the same `/data` volume and the same settings. Conversations, settings, sign-ins and signed-in browsers stay. Read the version's **For Hosts** section first.
- **Going back** is a restore, not a downgrade: a newer version can change data so that an older image can't open it. Go back only with a backup made before the update ([Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker#explicit-upgrade-and-rollback)).
- **For the people on your servers,** the host decides when an update arrives. A host that tests each release first may take some days. On Railway the owner is the host: with Railway's automatic updates on, as the template sets them, each new image installs in the next night's window (02:00–06:00 UTC).

## Started As Root

The image runs as uid 10001. Some hosts start every container as root, for example to mount a volume that root owns (Railway's `RAILWAY_RUN_UID=0`). Started as root inside its own image (`ROW_BOT_CONTAINERIZED=1`, server mode), `row-bot` first:

1. makes `/data` and everything in it 10001's, but only while the top of `/data` isn't 10001's already, so once. It changes links themselves, never what they point to, and leaves alone anything on another file system mounted inside. `/data` becomes readable by its owner only;
2. drops root for good: no other groups, then gid and uid 10001, and checks that root can't come back;
3. makes the image's folders under `/data` again (`tmp` and the caches), which the host's volume hides.

Only then does it read the setup code and the secret-store key, write `/data` or start a program, so everything above (the secrets out of the environment, non-dumpable processes, the health check's empty environment) holds as before. The log says `Started as root in its container: Row-Bot gave /data to uid 10001 and runs as uid 10001` the first time, and `… Row-Bot runs as uid 10001` after that. If any step fails, Row-Bot doesn't start, and the line starting `Row-Bot didn't start:` says why.

A file root adds to `/data` later stays root's, since the top of `/data` is 10001's by then: don't write in `/data` as root, or `chown` what you wrote to `10001:10001`. Root outside a container (`ROW_BOT_CONTAINERIZED` unset) is left as it is.

## Railway

Row-Bot's "Deploy on Railway" template runs the published image in the owner's own Railway account: one service with one volume at `/data`, public over HTTPS at a generated `up.railway.app` address, and an 8 GB, 8 vCPU limit: the Hobby plan's ceiling, billed only by use. Its definition, with the reasons for each value, is `deploy/railway/README.md` in Row-Bot's repository. In short:

- **As root:** `RAILWAY_RUN_UID=0`, because Railway mounts volumes as root ([Started As Root](#started-as-root)).
- **Variables:** `ROW_BOT_HOSTED_BY=railway`, `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL=https://${{RAILWAY_PUBLIC_DOMAIN}}`, a setup code from `${{secret(12, "0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ")}}`, and the proxy's addresses.
- **The proxy:** Railway's edge ends HTTPS and connects from addresses in `100.64.0.0/10`, measured on a real deploy (Railway documents none), so `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=100.64.0.0/10`. It sends `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Real-IP`, and replaces any a visitor sent. Because Railway's `X-Forwarded-For` ends with its edge's own address, Row-Bot takes the visitor from `X-Real-IP`, and only for `ROW_BOT_HOSTED_BY=railway`.
- **No secret-store key in Railway's variables.** Railway disclosed on 21 October 2026 that customers' environment variables may have been decrypted, so Row-Bot makes its key on the volume instead ([The Secret-Store Key](#the-secret-store-key), the third way).
- **No Railway health check, and `PORT=8080`.** Railway's deploy check calls the service as `healthcheck.railway.app`, a host name Row-Bot doesn't allow, so it gets a 400: on a real deploy with `/healthz` set, the deploy hung in DEPLOYING until it was cancelled. It's only used while a deploy goes live, and a service with a volume pauses on every redeploy anyway; if Row-Bot can't start, it exits and Railway shows the deployment as crashed. To add one, set the path to `/readyz` and `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` to the service's own host name and `healthcheck.railway.app`.
- **Updates:** the template uses `latest` and turns on Railway's automatic updates (**Settings › Source › Configure auto updates**, "Update to the latest tag", Overnight, 02:00–06:00 UTC), so each stable release installs by itself the next night. **Settings › Updates** says so and links the service's settings.

## Related

- [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker): Compose, backups, reverse proxies and Tailscale.
- [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access): invitations, sessions and proxy errors.
- [What Your Host Can See](/docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see): the same server from the owner's side.

## Headless Runs (row-bot run)

Route: /docs/operations/headless-run

Run one task with Row-Bot from the command line, with no window or server, for scripts, CI and benchmark harnesses.

# Headless Runs (`row-bot run`)

`row-bot run` gives Row-Bot one task, runs it to the end and exits. There's no window, server or tray. It's for scripts, CI jobs and benchmark harnesses such as Harbor (Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE), which install an agent into a task container, hand it a task and read back what it did.

The task runs as one conversation, with Row-Bot's normal prompts and tools. When the turn ends, Row-Bot can send one follow-up of its own, as the app does. It does this when the reply stopped on its next step, or when the reply names files it says it saved that aren't there.

```bash
row-bot run --task-file task.txt --workspace /app \
  --base-url https://models.example/v1 --model glm-5.3-flash --api-key-env MODEL_API_KEY \
  --approval hands-off --output-dir /tmp/row-bot
```

## What It Never Does

- **No profile access by default.** Each run gets a fresh, empty data folder, which is deleted when the run ends. This holds even when `ROW_BOT_DATA_DIR` is set. Your conversations, memories, settings and keys aren't read or written. `--data-dir DIR` uses a folder you name instead; Row-Bot keeps it, and it's refused while Row-Bot (or its server) has that folder open.
- **No telemetry.** No install-count ping is sent, and `ROW_BOT_INSTALL_COUNT` is set to `0` for the run.
- **No update check.** The updater doesn't run.
- **No server.** No web app, tray, window or remote access starts.
- **No model download.** The first run downloads nothing. If the local embedding model isn't already on the machine, memory search falls back to matching words.
- **No network beyond the model.** With `--base-url`, Row-Bot calls only that endpoint. With a configured provider, it calls only that provider, which also lists its models. The agent's own tools reach the network only when the task asks for it: a shell command, or web search where it's on.
- **No Learning.** Learning never records a headless run. A throwaway folder starts with Learning switched off. A `--data-dir` folder where Learning is on is refused.

## Choosing The Model

**Your own endpoint.** `--base-url` is the endpoint's address, and `--model` is the model's name there.

`--api-style` is the request format the endpoint speaks:

- `chat`: OpenAI Chat Completions (the default);
- `responses`: OpenAI Responses;
- `anthropic`: Anthropic Messages.

For `chat` and `responses`, give the address that ends in `/v1`. For `anthropic`, give the address before `/v1`.

Row-Bot doesn't test the endpoint first. It takes the endpoint at its word that the model can chat and call tools, and the first call shows whether it can.

**A provider Row-Bot knows.** `--model` is `provider:model`, for example:

- `ollama:qwen3:8b` (Ollama at `OLLAMA_HOST`);
- `anthropic:<model>`;
- `openai:<model>`;
- `openrouter:<author>/<model>`.

**The key.** `--api-key-env NAME` names the environment variable that holds the key. Never put the key itself on the command line. Without `--base-url`, it defaults to the provider's own variable, such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.

Row-Bot reads the key, then removes it from its environment before the agent runs anything. Commands the agent starts can't read it. On Linux, other programs running as the same user can't read the environment Row-Bot started with either. The key is kept in memory only, never in a keychain or a file.

## Approvals

Nobody is there to approve an action, so `--approval` decides what happens:

| `--approval` | An action that needs approval |
| --- | --- |
| `ask` (the default) | Refused. It doesn't run, and the agent is told that no person is available to approve it, then carries on without it. The run exits 3. |
| `auto` | Row-Bot's reviewer approves what clearly matches the task. Anything it would ask the person about is refused. |
| `hands-off` | Allowed, and recorded. Used only when you pass it: it can't come from an environment variable. |

Shell command checks, the sandbox and MCP safety work as in the app. Some actions only the person can approve, whatever the level, so a headless run always refuses them. If the agent asks the person a question, it's told that no person is available to answer, and it goes on with the option it recommended.

The trajectory and `summary.json` list each refused action.

### The text a run adds

The model reads Row-Bot's normal prompts. A headless run changes only four lines, the ones that would otherwise send it to a person:

- the result of a refused action;
- the answer to a question;
- the wrap-up at the `--max-rounds` ceiling;
- Row-Bot's own follow-up when a reply stopped on its next step.

`summary.json` and the trajectory's `agent.extra` record these lines as `harness_text`, with their SHA-256. A published result can then say exactly which harness text it ran with.

## Flags

| Flag | What it sets |
| --- | --- |
| `--task TEXT` / `--task-file PATH` | The task. Use `--task-file -` to read it from standard input. |
| `--workspace DIR` | The folder the agent works in. File tools and the shell start here. The default is the current folder. |
| `--model REF` | The model, as above. |
| `--base-url URL`, `--api-style STYLE`, `--api-key-env NAME` | Your own endpoint, and the variable that holds its key. |
| `--context-window TOKENS` | The context window to work within. Older messages are trimmed or summarised to fit. |
| `--max-output-tokens TOKENS` | The longest reply the model may write. |
| `--reasoning-effort LEVEL` | The model's reasoning effort, where it has one (`low`, `medium`, `high`, ...). |
| `--timeout SECONDS` | Stops the run after this long. |
| `--max-rounds N` | The most model rounds the turn may take. The default is 1,000. |
| `--approval LEVEL` | `ask`, `auto` or `hands-off`, as above. |
| `--output-dir DIR` | Where the output files go. |
| `--data-dir DIR` | A data folder to keep, instead of a throwaway one. |

Every flag except `--task`, `--task-file`, `--workspace`, `--approval` and `--data-dir` can also come from an environment variable, `ROW_BOT_RUN_<FLAG>`. For example, `ROW_BOT_RUN_MODEL`, `ROW_BOT_RUN_BASE_URL`, `ROW_BOT_RUN_API_STYLE`, `ROW_BOT_RUN_API_KEY_ENV` or `ROW_BOT_RUN_CONTEXT_WINDOW`.

With `--data-dir`, the run saves its endpoint, context window and workspace in that folder's settings.

## Output

The final answer is printed on standard output. Standard error shows warnings and, if the run didn't finish cleanly, a line saying why.

With `--output-dir`, the folder gets:

- **`trajectory.json`**: the conversation as an [ATIF](https://harborframework.com/docs/trajectory-format) trajectory, Harbor's Agent Trajectory Interchange Format. It has the task, each model reply with its reasoning and tool calls, each tool result tied to its call, and per-reply token counts. `final_metrics` totals every model call in the run, background ones included: prompt, completion and cached tokens, and the cost where the provider reports one.
- **`answer.md`**: the final answer.
- **`summary.json`**: the status, exit code and reason, the model and settings, refused actions, the token and cost totals by purpose, the harness text, and timings.
- **`row-bot.log`**: the run's log.

## Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. |
| `1` | Row-Bot failed. See `row-bot.log`. |
| `2` | The command line is wrong: a flag, the task file, or the key's variable. Nothing was run. |
| `3` | Finished, but at least one action that needed approval was refused, so the answer may be incomplete. |
| `4` | A budget ran out: `--timeout`, or the `--max-rounds` ceiling. This code is also used when the turn stopped because it kept repeating the same action. |
| `5` | The model endpoint failed: it was unreachable, refused the key, hit a rate limit, or the model can't run there. |

## Installing A Pinned Version On Plain Linux

Install from a release tag with the locked dependencies. This needs `git`, `curl` and Python 3.12 or 3.13, which `uv` can download.

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
git clone --depth 1 --branch vX.Y.Z https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot.git /opt/row-bot
cd /opt/row-bot && uv sync --locked --no-dev --python 3.13
/opt/row-bot/.venv/bin/row-bot run --help
```

`--no-dev` leaves out the test tools. The optional extras (voice, designer, browser and others) aren't needed for a headless run. A tool whose extra isn't installed is simply unavailable.

`uv tool install` from git isn't supported yet, because building a wheel needs the web client built first.

## Privacy And Safety

Route: /docs/privacy-safety/

Understand local data, provider calls, credentials, approvals, channels, MCP, plugins, and sharing.

# Privacy And Safety

Row-Bot is local-first: the app and its data live on your machine. Local-first does not mean every feature is offline. Hosted models, web search, browser actions, account tools, channels, MCP servers, plugins, Live voice, cloud speech, and media providers can send data outside the app when you configure and use them.

For how Row-Bot keeps its agent's actions in bounds, and how to report a security problem, read [How Row-Bot Keeps An Agent In Bounds](/docs/privacy-safety/agent-in-bounds).

## Local Data

Conversations, memories, documents, workflows, logs, designs, code folder records, skills, plugins, Buddy assets, and settings are stored in the active local Row-Bot data directory. The desktop Buddy's bubble reuses the selected conversation and does not create a second transcript store. To sit on your windows, the desktop Buddy reads the position and size of the window you are using and where your cursor is; it never reads window titles, app names, contents or pixels, and none of it leaves your computer.

Some things stay on this computer in particular ways:
- **Sign-ins in Row-Bot's browser**: its cookies are kept in the `browser_profile` folder of Row-Bot's data. **Settings › System › Browser and computer use** lists the sites, with **Sign out**.
- **Files Row-Bot sends to your devices**: kept with the conversation, like its other files; a copy of a file too large for a conversation is kept for 7 days, then removed.
- **Pages**: a page runs with no internet and no access to your chats, files or tools.
- **Incognito chats**: nothing in them is read for memory. See [Incognito Chats](/docs/chat/#incognito-chats).

Row-Bot also records how many tokens each model call used, for the context ring and for questions such as "How many tokens did I use this week?". The record holds counts and timings only, never prompts, replies or files, and it stays on this computer; when you ask about usage, the counts go to the conversation's model like any tool result. Counts older than 90 days are removed, and deleting a conversation deletes its counts. See [Context And Usage](/docs/chat/#context-and-usage).

## External Calls

External calls happen when you choose or enable something that needs them: hosted models, subscription providers, API providers, web search, browser automation, account tools, messaging channels, MCP servers, plugin tools, Live voice, cloud speech, and media generation. OpenRouter requests identify Row-Bot as the app making them (its website address and name, in the headers OpenRouter asks apps to send), which lets OpenRouter show Row-Bot in its public app rankings; these headers add no user, prompt or account data.

An installed Row-Bot also keeps itself up to date: about once a day it asks GitHub for a new release and, unless you turn background downloads off, downloads the changed files from GitHub and, when libraries changed, from the Python Package Index and PyTorch. Every file is checked against a published checksum, and update checks and downloads carry no account, usage or personal data. See [Updates](/docs/operations/updates#what-updates-contact).

Row-Bot also contacts these on its own, as Settings › System › Privacy lists: about once a day, while your Claude plan is set up, it asks Anthropic's release location for the newest Claude Code and, when it's newer, installs it while Claude isn't answering; every hour it checks that it can reach the internet (Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1), Ollama and the accounts you connected, while **Check connections every hour** is on in Monitor; model lists update about a minute after start-up and then every six hours when they are older than six hours, only while a cloud provider is connected, and whenever you connect a provider or choose Refresh; and the Apps & Skills catalogs update when you choose Update or turn on their catalog schedule (a model-list refresh also reads OpenRouter's public model list for context sizes, and, at most once an hour, [models.dev](https://models.dev)'s open catalogue of what each model can do: whether it takes tools and images, how much it reads, and what it makes. Row-Bot uses it only where a provider's own list doesn't say; the request carries nothing but itself, and when it fails Row-Bot uses the copy it saved or the one bundled with the release).

### Every Connection At A Glance

| What | Where it goes | When | What it carries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The models you choose | That provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter, Ollama or Row-Bot's own model on this computer, and others) | When a chat, workflow or background job uses the model | Your prompts, files you attach, and tool results for that request |
| Claude with your Claude plan | Anthropic, through your own Claude Code | When a chat uses a Claude plan model | The request. Row-Bot runs Claude Code with its telemetry, error reports and own auto-updates turned off |
| Installing Claude Code | Anthropic's release location (`downloads.claude.ai`), then Claude Code's own installer | When you choose **Use my Claude plan** without Claude Code, or **Update Claude Code**; and about once a day while your Claude plan is set up, to look for a newer version, which Row-Bot installs while Claude isn't answering | Nothing personal; checked against Anthropic's published checksum before it runs |
| Claude's sign-in | Anthropic, through Claude Code's own sign-in | When you sign in to your Claude plan | What you enter in Claude's sign-in. Row-Bot only carries it to Claude Code and keeps none of it |
| Try it free (OpenRouter's free models) | OpenRouter's sign-in page, then OpenRouter and the free model's host | When you choose **Sign in with OpenRouter**, then when a chat uses a free model | The sign-in returns a key of your own, saved like a pasted one. Then your prompts, files you attach and tool results for that request; some free hosts may keep or train on what you send |
| Web search, reading pages, Row-Bot's browser | The search service and the sites involved | When Row-Bot looks something up or browses for you | The search words or the page request |
| Apps and accounts (GitHub, Google, Outlook through Microsoft Graph, X, MCP servers, plugins) | That service | When a tool of the app runs | What that action needs |
| Messaging channels | Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp or your SMS provider | When you or a workflow send through them | The message |
| Speech models | Hugging Face (Whisper), GitHub (Kokoro and the faster speech models), ModelScope (SenseVoice) | When you press **Install** or **Download** in Settings › Voice | Nothing personal; then they run on the computer running Row-Bot. Row-Bot Voice sends your voice only to Row-Bot |
| Cloud speech services | Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI or Google (**Listen with**); ElevenLabs, Cartesia or Google (**Speak with**) | Only once you choose one and its key is saved, while you talk or Row-Bot speaks | Listening: the stretches where you speak. Speaking: the text of each sentence. **Describe a voice**: your description only |
| Live voice | OpenAI, Google or xAI | While you talk with the provider you chose from a chat's Talk menu | Your voice, the chat's recent messages, the agent profile's name and a few related memories (none in an incognito chat), and Row-Bot's answers and progress lines for it to say; for Gemini Live, what you share on camera or screen |
| Install stats | Row-Bot's stats service (Cloudflare) | About once a day | A random ID, the version and the system. See [Install Stats](#install-stats) |
| Finding local model servers | This computer only (127.0.0.1): Ollama's, LM Studio's, vLLM's and llama.cpp's usual ports | When you open **On this computer** in Setup, or choose Check again | A request for the model list; nothing leaves this computer |
| Updates | GitHub, and when libraries change, the Python Package Index and PyTorch | About once a day, and when downloading an update | Nothing personal. See [Updates](/docs/operations/updates#what-updates-contact) |
| Connection checks | Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Ollama and your connected accounts | Every hour, while **Check connections every hour** is on in Monitor | A simple reachability check |
| Model lists | Your connected model providers, OpenRouter's public model list, models.dev's model catalogue (at most hourly) | About a minute after start-up and every six hours when older than six hours, while a cloud provider is connected; and when you connect a provider or refresh | Nothing personal: no prompt, no tokens |
| Apps & Skills catalogs | Each catalog's source | When you update, or on the schedule you turn on | Nothing personal |
| ffmpeg, for video editing | The Python Package Index (`files.pythonhosted.org`) | Once, after you approve its card | Nothing personal; checked against its fingerprint |
| Cua Driver, for computer use | GitHub (the Cua project's releases) | When you choose Install or Repair | Nothing personal; then Cua Driver's own telemetry, described below |
| The browser runtime | Playwright's download servers | When you choose Install browser runtime | Nothing personal |
| Learning's own model calls | Your default model's provider (nothing leaves this computer with a local model) | Only while [Learning](#learning) is on: in quiet hours, when it looks for things to improve, tests a change, or compares a personal-model version or a learning method | Parts of what Learning recorded from your own chats, workflows and goals, and its test tasks |
| Learning's training engine and starting model | PyPI, PyTorch, Hugging Face and GitHub (llama.cpp) | Once, after you agree to the download ask | Nothing personal; every file is checked against its pinned size and fingerprint. The engine's own usage reporting is switched off |
| Training on Hugging Face (Learning) | Your own Hugging Face account | Only if you choose Hugging Face: the sign-in, its price list, and each run you agree to | The training examples that run uses, to private repositories deleted once the model is back on this computer (a finished model that never came back stays in your account, and Learning says so) |
| Other models (Learning) | Hugging Face's public model search and model files | When you search for a model, and when you choose to check one | Your search words. No sign-in or token |
| Download with Row-Bot (llama.cpp) | GitHub (llama.cpp's official releases) and Hugging Face (the Qwen3.8 and Qwen3.5 model files) | When you press **Download** (the button names the size), or **Update** in Settings › Models | Nothing personal; every file is checked against its pinned fingerprint. The model then runs on this computer, offline, and is never sent anything from outside |
| Notifications on a phone | That phone's browser push service: Google (Chrome, Edge on Android), Apple (an installed iPhone app), Mozilla (Firefox) or Microsoft (Edge on Windows) | Only while **Notifications on this device** is on, when Row-Bot starts waiting for you (an approval or a question) | A short notice, end-to-end encrypted for that phone: a title and one line saying what it's about (or only "Row-Bot is waiting for you" with **Show details in notifications** off). The push service can't read it. See [Notifications On A Phone](#notifications-on-a-phone) |

Computer use is a distinct opt-in boundary: Row-Bot works in an app with your real mouse and keyboard while a Stop bar shows on screen, and it asks before the first use of each app in a chat and before paying, sending, deleting or changing settings. Row-Bot downloads the pinned Cua Driver only after an explicit Install or Repair action, verifies the selected archive, and requires the current telemetry disclosure before any executable invocation. The reviewed 0.20.0 upstream telemetry includes pseudonymous identifiers and bounded product, platform, client, tool/outcome, duration/output, aggregate usage, permission, and lifecycle categories; its tagged event builders exclude prompts, tool arguments/results, typed text, screenshots, accessibility trees, app/window names, URLs, paths, raw values, and raw errors. See [Computer Use](/docs/computer-use/) for the full boundary.

Speech on this computer (Kokoro, the voice filter, turn detection and the **Hey Row-Bot** wake word) runs on Microsoft's ONNX Runtime. On Windows, ONNX Runtime has its own usage events (process information, model metadata, errors and timings) that Windows' diagnostic data service may collect. Row-Bot switches them off before any voice model loads, so they are never sent; on macOS and Linux ONNX Runtime has no telemetry. The faster speech models (Moonshine and Nemotron) run on sherpa-onnx's own copy of ONNX Runtime, which is built without Microsoft's telemetry, so Windows' diagnostic data service doesn't collect its events. This is a library's telemetry, not Row-Bot's.

## Learning

[Learning](/docs/learning/) is on from the start, for learning from your corrections, and Home says so once. Reading your past chats, experimental learning and a personal model stay off until you turn them on, and turning Learning off in Settings › Learning stops all of it. While it's on:

- **What it keeps stays on this computer**: its record of how Row-Bot handled your own requests (`learning.db` and the `learning` folder in Row-Bot's data), its test results, the training engine, starting models and your personal-model versions. Secrets are removed before anything is stored. It never records chats with other people, incognito chats, or work Row-Bot does on its own.
- **Its model calls go to your own provider.** Learning looks for things to improve and tests changes with your default model, so those calls go to that model's provider, like your chats do, and carry parts of what Learning recorded. With a local default model, nothing leaves this computer. Its tokens count against the monthly limit you set in Settings › Learning.
- **Downloads ask first.** The training engine and the starting model come from PyPI, PyTorch, Hugging Face and GitHub (llama.cpp) only after you agree, and each file is checked against its pinned fingerprint before it's used.
- **The training engine's telemetry is off.** The engine is built from third-party libraries, some of which would report usage on their own. Row-Bot switches each one's reporting off, and the engine runs behind a network guard that refuses any connection that isn't this computer, so a library that ignored the switch fails instead of sending anything. This is those libraries' reporting, not Row-Bot's; Row-Bot adds none. The engine gets none of Row-Bot's keys, settings or data folder.
- **Hugging Face only if you choose it.** Training there uses your own Hugging Face account. Row-Bot uploads only the training examples a run uses, after you agree to its price, to private repositories it deletes once the model is downloaded and checked (a paid model that wasn't downloaded stays in your account until you delete it there, and Learning says so); never your chat history, memories or files. The sign-in stays in this computer's keychain, and Hugging Face's library runs with its own usage reporting off. Searching for other models contacts Hugging Face only when you search, with no sign-in.
- **Personal models run on this computer**, in Row-Bot's own runner or in Ollama, LM Studio, a llama.cpp server or vLLM here.
- **You stay in control.** Pause, turn off, leave a chat out with **Don't learn from this chat**, or delete learning data at any time. See [Pause, Turn Off Or Delete](/docs/learning/#pause-turn-off-or-delete).

## Install Stats

Row-Bot's only first-party telemetry is **install stats**: once a day it sends a random ID, its version and your system, nothing else, so Row-Bot's maker can see how many installations are in use (the installations reporting in the last 7 and 15 days) and which versions and systems to support. It is on by default, on desktops, servers and Docker alike, and Row-Bot doesn't ask about it; this page and the release notes describe it, and **Settings › System › Privacy** turns it off.

- **What is sent**: exactly `{"schema": 1, "install": "<random ID>", "version": "5.3.0", "os": "windows"}`. The ID is a random 128-bit number made just for this at the first send, never taken from your computer; `os` is `windows`, `macos`, `linux` or `docker`. Nothing else: no IP field, location, account, machine name, prompts, files, tools or models. It is a random ID, not your name, but it is the same ID every day, so it isn't anonymous.
- **When**: shortly after Row-Bot starts (a minute, plus up to an hour so installations don't all send at once), then at most once a day while Row-Bot runs, up to an hour late on purpose. A failed send waits for the next day. It never slows start-up.
- **Where**: over HTTPS from Row-Bot's server process to Row-Bot's stats service, a Cloudflare Worker at `row-bot-count.<account>.workers.dev`.
- **What is kept, and for how long**: the service keeps a keyed hash of the ID (it can't be turned back into the ID) with the day, the version and the system, and deletes it after 35 days. Daily totals of installations reporting in the last 7 and 15 days, by version and by system, and how many installations reported from each country each day, hold no IDs and are kept.
- **What anyone can see**: the service's current totals, the installations reporting in the last 7 and 15 days overall and by system, are public at `/v1/totals`. Nothing else is: not versions, countries, days or anything about one installation.
- **Your IP address**: Cloudflare sees it, as it does for any connection, and works out the country it comes from. Row-Bot's service doesn't store the address or anything else about the request: it only adds one to that country's count for the day, never next to the ID or the installation's records.
- **Turning it off**: switch off **Share install stats** in **Settings › System › Privacy**, or set `ROW_BOT_INSTALL_COUNT=0` (for example on a server or in Docker) before Row-Bot starts. Off stops at once, drops anything pending and stays off through restarts, updates, repairs and restores. On again uses the same ID and sends nothing for the days it was off.
- **Deleting what was sent**: **Delete what was sent…** under **Details** in Settings › System › Privacy turns install stats off and asks the service to delete every record of this installation. Row-Bot proves the request with a deletion secret kept on this computer; the service checks it against the ID and never stores it. Daily totals without IDs stay.

The ID and its deletion secret are kept in `install_count.json` in the Row-Bot data folder. They are never logged or shown, and backups never include them: a restore on this computer leaves them as they are, and a profile restored on another computer counts as a new installation.

## Credentials

Enter credentials only on the relevant Settings page or in the provider sign-in flow. Row-Bot stores secrets in the operating system key store when available and keeps local metadata for status and diagnostics. An explicitly configured server deployment can use a read-only external master-key file to encrypt owner-entered secrets in its persistent data directory; see [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker#read-only-secret-files).

If a hosting service runs Row-Bot for you, read [What Your Host Can See](/docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see).

## Remote Access

Remote Access is single-owner and multi-device. A Tailscale, LAN, SSH, Docker, or reverse-proxy route provides reachability only; each non-local browser still needs a one-time invitation and a revocable Row-Bot session.

Every authenticated interactive browser has full owner authority. Phone/tablet and computer choices select compact or desktop presentation only; device metadata and screen size are not permission boundaries. Row-Bot does not provide guest or multi-user sharing.

Invitation links expire after 10 minutes and work once, but should still be treated like passwords until they expire. Row-Bot stores only hashed invitation and session secrets. Session credentials use HttpOnly cookies and are not placed in URLs.

Prefer Tailscale or HTTPS for remote access. Plain LAN HTTP is unencrypted and does not support a remote browser microphone. For an operator-managed proxy, allow only the canonical browser-facing origin and trust only the exact address that connects from the proxy to Row-Bot. Never resolve a forwarding-header error by trusting every private address or a whole container network.

See [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access) for layouts, lifetimes, revocation, Tailscale ownership, server mode, Docker, and recovery.

### Notifications On A Phone

A phone or computer signed in over HTTPS (Tailscale, a tunnel or a hosted Row-Bot) can turn on **Notifications on this device** in Settings › Devices. It's off until you turn it on, and on an iPhone or iPad it needs Row-Bot added to the Home Screen first.

- **When**: only when Row-Bot starts waiting for you, for an approval or a question.
- **What is sent**: a short notice, through that device's browser push service (Google, Apple, Mozilla or Microsoft, whichever the browser uses): a title of up to 60 characters and one line of up to 120 saying what it's about, such as "Approval needed: Send email to Sam?" or "Row-Bot asked you a question: Which venue?". Tapping it opens the conversation it's about. Secrets such as keys and tokens are removed from the line.
- **Show details in notifications**: on unless you turn it off, in Settings › Devices. Off, every notice says only "Row-Bot is waiting for you". It's one switch for all your devices. Your phone's own lock-screen preview setting decides whether a notice's words show while the phone is locked.
- **How it's protected**: each notice is end-to-end encrypted for that one browser under the Web Push standard (RFC 8291) and signed with Row-Bot's own push key (VAPID, RFC 8292). Only that browser can decrypt it.
- **What is kept**: Row-Bot keeps the device's push address and its encryption keys in `push_subscriptions.json`, its own push key in `push_vapid_key.pem` and, once you change it, the details switch in `push_settings.json`, all in the Row-Bot data folder. Turning the switch off, or signing the device out, stops the notices; a push address the browser drops is forgotten.
- **What the push service sees**: that an encrypted notice was sent to that browser, when, and about how long it is; it can't read it.

## Approvals

Use approvals to review file writes, command execution, browser actions, account actions, channel sends, MCP calls, plugin tools, code folder changes, and other sensitive actions. Deny anything that does not match your request.

Approvals wait until you answer; they no longer expire on their own, unless a workflow step sets its own time limit. Every waiting approval shows in its conversation, in the sidebar's attention indicator and on Overview, with **Approve** and **Deny** in place, so background work can't slip past you. Each tool result records whether approval was needed, given or denied, and a denied action never runs.

Approval level is policy: blocked actions stay blocked, **Ask** waits for you, **Auto**'s reviewer approves only what clearly matches your own request (it never sees tool results, files or web pages, and asks you when unsure), and **Hands-off** runs every action and records it. Some prompts include a short model-written reason for readability, but the underlying approval gate and action details are system-controlled. [How Row-Bot Keeps An Agent In Bounds](/docs/privacy-safety/agent-in-bounds) tells the whole story, including what is not a boundary.

### Activity Log

**Settings › System › Activity** lists every action Row-Bot took with a tool, in chats, workflows, helper agents, goals, channels, Proactive Row-Bot and Developer Studio: when, which tool or app, a short summary, and its outcome with who decided: it ran without needing approval, you approved, the reviewer approved (with its reason), Hands-off allowed it, it was allowed in this chat, you said no, it changed after you approved and didn't run, it was blocked, or it didn't work. Filter by **Needed approval**, **You said no** or **Blocked**, by where it ran, or search; **Export as CSV** saves the list you see as a file. Monitor shows today's count, with a link to the page.

- **What a row holds**: the tool, the words on its approval card or a few reviewed safe details, with keys and tokens removed. Never what a tool read or returned, page text or file contents. An incognito chat's actions are listed, with the summary "In an incognito chat" instead of their words.
- **What it leaves out**: actions you start yourself with a button in the app.
- **Where it's kept**: in `activity.db` in the Row-Bot data folder, on this computer only. Nothing is sent anywhere.
- **For how long**: 90 days, at most 200,000 actions (the oldest go first). Deleting a conversation deletes its actions, its helpers' too, and **Clear activity** deletes them all.
- **Who can change it**: only you, in the app. No tool, agent or workflow can read, change or clear it.
- **Your Always allow rules** live in the same file. Only you make one, from an approval card, and only you switch, edit or delete one; clearing the activity keeps them. See [Always Allow](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#always-allow).

### Programs On This Computer Can't Act As You

On this computer, only Row-Bot's own window, or a browser it opens for you from its tray icon (**Open in Browser**), can change anything. Programs Row-Bot runs for you can look, never approve its actions or change its settings, and a tab you open by typing Row-Bot's address shows **View only on this computer**. See [Programs On This Computer Can't Act As You](/docs/privacy-safety/agent-in-bounds#programs-on-this-computer-cant-act-as-you).

## Sharing Logs Or Screenshots

Before sharing logs, screenshots, documents, thread exports, or review packages, check for names, file paths, account names, message contents, tokens, private documents, or misleading real data.

## Safer Defaults

- Start with local models when privacy matters most.
- Keep channels, MCP, and plugins disabled until needed.
- Keep Computer Use disabled until a local interactive task needs native application control.
- Keep Remote Access off until another trusted device needs it; use the narrowest route and the appropriate layout.
- Use narrow workspaces for file tools.
- Review approvals before external or destructive actions.
- Keep a final human review step before publishing screenshots or docs built from a personal app state.

## How Row-Bot Keeps An Agent In Bounds

Route: /docs/privacy-safety/agent-in-bounds

What Row-Bot's agent can and can't do, why outside text can't approve its own actions, what is not a boundary, and how to report a security problem.

# How Row-Bot Keeps An Agent In Bounds

An assistant that reads your email, browses for you and runs commands is useful because it can act. This page tells, in one place, how Row-Bot keeps those actions in bounds: what it may do on its own, what waits for you, what it never does, and where the limits of that design are. For what stays on your computer and every connection Row-Bot makes, read [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/).

## In Short

- **Actions go through your approval level.** Sending, deleting, paying, most commands and anything outside the workspace wait for you, or for Auto's reviewer, unless you chose Hands-off.
- **Auto's reviewer reads only your words.** It never sees web pages, files, email or tool results, so text an action picked up can't talk it into approving.
- **Outside text is marked as outside.** Web pages, files, mail and app results reach the model fenced off, with an instruction not to follow what's inside.
- **Row-Bot's own data folder is off limits to its tools.** Your conversations, settings and keys live there.
- **Only you can approve.** Programs on this computer, including the ones Row-Bot runs, can look but can't approve, change settings or pair a device.

## What Counts As An Action

Most reading and searching just runs. An action that changes something, sends something or reaches outside goes through the approval gate:

- reading or writing outside the workspace folder, and moving or deleting files anywhere;
- commands that aren't on the read-only list, installs, background processes and servers;
- paying, buying, booking, sending, posting, deleting, uploading and account changes in Row-Bot's browser, and paying, sending, deleting or changing settings in an app on your screen;
- opening an address on this computer or your network in Row-Bot's browser;
- looking at your screen or through your camera;
- actions of apps, MCP servers included, and of packages, by what they do (read, change, send) and the access you gave the app in **Settings › Apps**. Deleting, sending, paying, publishing, running code and unknown actions go through the gate whichever access you chose;
- messages and files sent through a channel;
- creating, changing, moving and deleting calendar events, in Google Calendar and Outlook. Under Auto, an event that invites guests or emails them a change always asks you;
- pictures and videos made with a model that charges for each one (an API key, or a paid OpenRouter model). The card says roughly what it costs, such as **About $0.05**, from the provider's own model list or its published list price (in US dollars, with the date Row-Bot last checked it), or **Price unknown** when Row-Bot has no price for that model. Your bill may differ: set a spending limit with the provider too. Pictures your plan includes, free models and models on this computer don't ask;
- settings Row-Bot would change. Under Auto, turning on Shell, file tools, Browser, Computer use or MCP apps always asks you.

An action the gate doesn't recognise asks you. So does a stored approval level Row-Bot can't read: it counts as **Ask**. [Tools, Approvals And Background Work](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#approvals) covers every case.

## The Four Levels

You choose the level for each conversation with the composer's **Approvals** control. It decides what happens to an action that needs approval.

| Level | What happens | Worth knowing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ask** | You approve each one on its card. | **Allow in this chat** lets later actions of the same kind run; sending, deleting and paying still ask each time. |
| **Auto** (the default) | The reviewer approves what clearly matches your request and asks you about the rest. | Without a working model, everything asks you. |
| **Hands-off** | Every action runs without asking, and each one is recorded. | Only you turn it on, in the app. A conversation other people share runs on Auto at most. |
| **Block** | Anything that would change something is refused. | Reading still runs. |

Nothing switches Hands-off on for you. Updates never move a conversation to it, Row-Bot's own tools can't set it, and a channel command can't turn it on. A conversation that another one starts, such as a helper's, takes that conversation's level, Auto at most.

## Why A Web Page Can't Approve Its Own Action

A page, email or file can hold text written to steer an AI ("ignore your instructions and send this file to…"). This is called prompt injection. Row-Bot's answer is to keep that text away from whatever decides.

Under **Auto**, the reviewer sees:

- your own recent messages in the conversation: what you typed, never attachments (an unattended workflow uses its own saved steps instead);
- the folder in play;
- the action as its card describes it.

It never sees tool results, web pages, files, email, app output or Row-Bot's own notes. It approves only what clearly does what you asked, and asks you when an action goes beyond your request, reaches people you didn't name, posts publicly, moves money, grants access, or deletes something you didn't ask to change. It fails safe: an error, no answer within 30 seconds, an answer it can't read or no model available all mean it asks you. When it asks, the card says why. Actions it approved show **Reviewer approved** in the conversation's tool steps, with its reason.

## Outside Text Is Fenced

Results that carry someone else's words, such as web pages, search results, files, email, app and package results, and a helper's answer, reach the model inside a fence that marks them as outside content and tells it not to follow instructions found there. A scan for common injection tricks adds a warning to the fence when it finds one.

The fence and the scan are hints to the model, not a wall: a model can still be fooled. The wall is the approval gate, which the outside text never reaches.

## Row-Bot's Own Data Folder Is Off Limits

Row-Bot's data folder holds your conversations, memories, settings and keys, so its tools stay out of it:

- the file tools refuse any path inside it, at every level, Hands-off included;
- the Shell tool refuses a command that names it, in any common spelling or by a path relative to the current folder, and one that would run inside it;
- in a [sandbox Row-Bot](/docs/operations/#sandboxes), your real Row-Bot's data folder is out of reach too.

To let the agent read it, turn on **Let the agent read Row-Bot's data folder** in [Settings › System](/docs/settings/system) › Advanced. Such commands then go through your approval level (Hands-off runs them, Block still refuses them). With the setting off, no level reaches the folder.

## Programs On This Computer Can't Act As You

On this computer, only Row-Bot's own window, or a browser it opens for you from its tray icon (**Open in Browser**), can change anything. Programs Row-Bot runs for you (a shell command, its own browser, a page it reads) connect from the same computer, so being on this computer isn't enough: they can look, never approve Row-Bot's own actions, change its approval level or settings, or pair a device. A Row-Bot tab you open yourself by typing its address shows **View only on this computer** in the sidebar until you open it from the window or the tray.

Your phone and every other device you signed in keep full access, and so does an account you paired in a chat app, for work that started there.

## The Code Sandbox

A code folder can run its commands in a Docker sandbox instead of on this computer ([Code Folders](/docs/developer/#sandbox-modes)). Changes reach your real folder only when you apply them.

The sandbox's network is off by default. When you turn it on, it reaches the public internet only: a small network gate beside it refuses this computer (so a local Ollama or Row-Bot itself), your local network and cloud metadata addresses. See [The Sandbox Network](/docs/developer/#the-sandbox-network-and-prepare-sandbox).

## Things Row-Bot Never Does

- **Types a password, one-time code or card number.** When a page or app asks for one, Row-Bot asks you to enter it.
- **Controls itself, a password manager or a protected system screen** in computer use. Computer use's window pictures stay in memory and are never written to the chat, memory, logs or files.
- **Opens cloud metadata addresses or its own app** in its browser.
- **Sends or changes something in the background.** Proactive Row-Bot's background work only reads; anything that would send or change something goes through the same approval card as a chat.

## What Is Not A Boundary

The approval gate is the boundary. These are not, and the safer habit for each is beside it:

- **Hands-off runs everything.** It still refuses blocked commands, tools you switched off and the data folder (unless you allowed it), but nothing else asks, and workflows don't pause. Use it for work you understand, in conversations you watch.
- **The reviewer is a model.** It can approve an action that matches your words but not what you meant. Use **Ask** for unfamiliar or high-stakes work.
- **The workspace folder is open to the file tools.** Inside it they read, write and copy without asking; moving and deleting ask. Choose a narrow workspace folder.
- **Commands, Row-Bot's browser and apps on your screen run as you.** They have your account's rights on this computer; only a code folder's Docker sandbox isolates commands. Approvals decide what starts, not what a program does once it runs.
- **Packages and MCP servers that run on this computer aren't sandboxed.** Their code can read files and start programs like any program. Their tools follow your approvals, but add them only from publishers you trust, and keep them off until you need them.
- **There is no list of allowed websites.** A tool that may reach the internet can reach any public site. Addresses on this computer or your network ask first in Row-Bot's browser.
- **There is no single log of every action.** Each conversation's tool steps record what ran and whether it was approved.
- **The fence and the injection scan are hints.** See [Outside Text Is Fenced](#outside-text-is-fenced).
- **A signed-in device is you.** Anyone using your unlocked computer, or a phone you signed in, has full access. Sign out devices you don't use in **Settings › Devices & remote access**.
- **Your model provider sees what you send it.** Prompts, attached files and tool results go to the provider of the model you chose. Use a model on this computer when that matters.

To try a workflow, skill or package before it touches real accounts, use a [sandbox](/docs/operations/#sandboxes): a second Row-Bot on made-up data.

## Reporting A Problem

If you find a security problem, please report it privately, not in a public issue:

- **GitHub**: **Report a vulnerability** on the repository's [Security](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/security) page opens a private advisory only the maintainer can see.
- **Email**: syd@row-bot.ai.

Include the version, your system, the steps to reproduce and what an attacker gains. You'll hear back within 7 days. A confirmed problem with real impact gets a fix in a release and a published GitHub security advisory, with a CVE ID when its impact warrants one, and the reporter is credited unless they'd rather not be. Only the latest release is supported; a critical fix may be brought to an earlier one when practical. The repository's [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/SECURITY.md) has the same policy.

## Past Advisories

| Advisory | Published | Severity | Fixed in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [GHSA-68j6-243q-h2hp](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/security/advisories/GHSA-68j6-243q-h2hp) | 13 Nov 2026 | Low | 5.3.3 |

- **GHSA-68j6-243q-h2hp**: an unreadable tool settings file turned switched-off tools back on and cleared the shell's blocked-commands list.

Related: [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/), [Tools, Approvals And Background Work](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal), [Extensions And Trust Boundaries](/docs/concepts/extensions-and-trust) and [Computer Use](/docs/computer-use/).

## What Your Host Can See

Route: /docs/privacy-safety/what-your-host-can-see

When a hosting service runs your Row-Bot: what the host can reach, what Row-Bot keeps encrypted and where the key lives, and how to protect yourself.

# What Your Host Can See

When a hosting service runs Row-Bot for you, your Row-Bot lives on that company's computer, not yours. This page says plainly what the host can reach, what Row-Bot does to protect your saved sign-ins, and what you can do. It applies to any host. For a Row-Bot on your own computer, read [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/). To start and use a hosted Row-Bot, see [Row-Bot In Your Browser](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser).

## In Short

- **Your host runs the computer.** It can technically read your Row-Bot's disk, and the memory of the running server. That's true of every hosting service, which is why choosing a host is a matter of trust.
- **Row-Bot encrypts your saved sign-ins and keys.** That protects copies of your data, such as backups. It doesn't hide them from the host, which holds the key.
- **Nothing new goes to Row-Bot's maker.** Row-Bot's maker doesn't run your server and has no way into it.
- **You can limit the damage.** Use keys with spending limits and sign-ins you can revoke, so you can cut off access quickly if you ever need to.

## What Your Host Can Reach

- **Your data folder.** Your conversations, memories, documents and files, workflows, settings and logs are ordinary files on the server's disk. So are the cookies of Row-Bot's own browser, which keep it signed in to websites. The host's backups and copies of the disk hold them too.
- **The running server's memory.** It holds whatever Row-Bot is working with, including the sign-ins it's using at that moment.
- **The traffic to your Row-Bot.** Row-Bot speaks plain HTTP inside the host's network, so the HTTPS connection from your browser ends at the host's proxy in front of it.
- **Its own settings for your server.** If the host generated your setup code and the key for your saved sign-ins, it has both.

Whoever can change your server's settings can also sign in: a new setup code and a restart let one browser in, and sign out every other browser. That's how you get back in when you've lost access, and it means your host could too. If you're ever signed out everywhere without doing it yourself, ask your host why.

## What Row-Bot Keeps Encrypted

**Your saved sign-ins and keys:** model API keys, your ChatGPT and other provider sign-ins, channel tokens, and account, app and MCP sign-ins. A hosted server has no keychain, so Row-Bot encrypts each of them itself (AES-256-GCM) and stores them in the `secure-secrets` folder of its data. They're never stored in plain text.

The setup code, invitations and browser sessions are never stored at all: Row-Bot keeps only salted hashes, which can check a code but can't be turned back into one.

Where the key that opens your saved sign-ins lives depends on your host:

- **Your host gives Row-Bot the key** (`ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`, in its settings for your server). The key is never written to the data folder, so a copy of the data folder, or a backup of it, holds only encrypted sign-ins. The host still has the key in its settings.
- **Your host gives none.** Row-Bot makes a key at its first start and keeps it in the data folder (`secret-store-key`), readable only by Row-Bot. Anyone with a full copy of the data folder, including the host's backups, can then open your saved sign-ins. Row-Bot on Railway works this way on purpose ([Railway](#railway), below).

Either way, Row-Bot's own backups (**Settings › Data › Back up now**) leave out both the key and your saved sign-ins.

**Your Claude plan's sign-in** isn't one of them: Claude Code keeps it itself, in its own folder in the server's home (`.claude`), which on a hosted server is part of the data disk. Row-Bot never reads it and its backups leave it out, but the host can reach it like any file on the disk.

## The Key And The Setup Code

- Row-Bot reads the key and the setup code as it starts, then removes them from its environment. The programs it runs for you (shell commands, MCP servers, Claude Code, Python, Row-Bot's browser) never get them, and a command such as `env` can't show them.
- On Linux, Row-Bot's own processes also hide the environment they started with: only the server's administrator (root) can read it.
- Neither appears in Row-Bot's log files. While nobody owns your Row-Bot, the setup code shows only in the server's console output, with a link that signs in with it when the server knows its own address.

This keeps both secrets away from the programs Row-Bot runs. It doesn't keep them from your host, which set them.

## Nothing New Goes To Row-Bot's Maker

- A hosted Row-Bot makes the same connections as any Row-Bot, and no others: see [Every Connection At A Glance](/docs/privacy-safety/#every-connection-at-a-glance). It doesn't check for updates itself; your host installs them (on Railway, each night once automatic updates are on).
- [Install stats](/docs/privacy-safety/#install-stats) count a hosted Row-Bot as `docker`, like any Row-Bot in a container. They don't say who hosts it. Turn them off in **Settings › System › Privacy**.
- The name of your host is used only on your Row-Bot's own pages, and isn't sent anywhere.

What your host itself records, such as its own logs and billing, is up to the host: read its privacy policy.

## Railway

On Railway you run Row-Bot in your own Railway account ([Row-Bot On Railway](/docs/getting-started/on-railway)), and Railway is the host, as above.

- **What Railway can reach:**
  - the service's **volume** (`/data`): your data folder, and the key that opens your saved sign-ins, which lives there;
  - the service's **variables**: the setup code, your Row-Bot's address and its other settings;
  - the service's **logs**: the deploy log and Row-Bot's console output, which shows the setup code and its sign-in link while nobody owns your Row-Bot;
  - the **traffic** to your Row-Bot, since Railway's proxy ends HTTPS in front of it.
- **The key stays on the volume, not in Railway's variables.** On 21 October 2026 Railway [disclosed](https://blog.railway.com/p/security-disclosure-wednesday-october-21st) that customers' environment variables may have been decrypted ([Railway's October Incident](/docs/getting-started/on-railway#railways-october-incident)). So neither **Continue with Railway** nor the template sets `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`: Row-Bot makes its key on the volume at its first start, readable only by Row-Bot, and leaves it out of its own backups. Railway's variables then hold nothing that opens your saved sign-ins, and the setup code in them works only once.
- **Railway's own backups** are on its Pro plan only. They copy the whole volume, the key included.
- **Continue with Railway** ([row-bot.ai/railway](https://row-bot.ai/railway/)) talks only to Railway. Railway's API doesn't accept calls from web pages, so the page's calls pass through a small relay Row-Bot runs on Cloudflare. The relay passes on only the calls the page needs, with your Railway sign-in, and keeps and logs nothing. The sign-in stays in the page while it works and is forgotten once your Row-Bot opens; Row-Bot never stores it, and the relay never reaches your Row-Bot.

## Protect Yourself

- **Give model API keys a spending limit.** Most providers let you set a budget for a key or an account, so a key that leaks can't cost more than that.
- **Prefer sign-ins you can revoke.** A sign-in you can end from the service's own security settings, or a bot token you can regenerate, is quicker to cut off than a password.
- **Keep your own backup.** Choose **Download backup** in **Settings › Data**. It saves a copy on your device, without passwords or sign-ins.
- **Check your devices now and then.** The list in **Settings › Devices & remote access** shows every signed-in phone and computer, and signs one out.

**If your host has a security incident,** assume your saved sign-ins and keys were exposed, and replace them:

1. At each model provider, make a new API key, paste it into Row-Bot (**Settings › Models**, in that provider's sheet), then delete the old key.
2. End Row-Bot's sign-ins at each service you connected (your model plan, accounts, apps), then sign in again from Row-Bot.
3. Make new tokens for your channel bots and enter them in Row-Bot.
4. Sign out any browser you don't recognise in **Settings › Devices & remote access**.

Related: [Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting), for the technical details hosts work with, and [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/).

## Troubleshooting

Route: /docs/troubleshooting/

Resolve setup, model, chat, approval, workflow, design, code folder, Knowledge, Monitor, app, skill, channel, account, catalog, voice, and Buddy issues.

# Troubleshooting

Start with what Row-Bot already tells you. The sidebar's attention indicator appears when something needs you, Overview's **Needs you** lists it, and [Monitor](/docs/monitor/) shows every health check with a one-click fix. You can also ask Row-Bot "what's wrong?": it reads the same checks and gives each fix (see [Ask Row-Bot About Row-Bot](/docs/chat/about-row-bot)). Most issues fall into one of four categories: setup is incomplete, a provider or tool is off, the wrong model is selected, or Row-Bot is waiting for your approval.

## Setup Problems

- If Row-Bot keeps opening setup, finish **How should Row-Bot think?** or choose **Set up later**. Open Setup Center from Overview or the command palette to continue optional setup.
- Check Settings › Models before troubleshooting a conversation.
- Check Settings › System if local files, browser automation, or command execution are involved, and Settings › Devices & remote access for other devices or the public link.
- For native application control, open the Computer Use setup in Settings › System and resolve its driver or operating-system permission status before retrying.

## Model Problems

- Refresh the provider's model list in its sheet in Settings › Models.
- A model marked **Unavailable** in a picker says why; reconnecting its provider usually fixes it.
- Choose a tool-capable model for workflows, designs, code folders, and multi-step tool use.
- For local and custom endpoints, use enough context for Row-Bot's instructions and tool schemas; on smaller computers, give a local model a smaller **Context** in its settings (Settings › Models).
- If reasoning choices are missing, rejected, or reset, use the active model's conditional control or `/reasoning`, then follow [Reasoning Controls](/docs/chat/reasoning-controls#troubleshooting).

- With a local model, if a reply stops with "The response was interrupted", choose **Resume**. Row-Bot already asks the model once more when it writes a tool call its runtime can't read; a second failure shows this card.

## Windows

- **Windows Firewall asks about `Row-Bot Server`** once after an update, because each version runs from its own folder under `versions`. Allow it for private networks; after that it doesn't ask again.
- **Computer use moves your real mouse.** Keep your hands off the mouse and keyboard while it works; if you touch them, it stops and asks "Carry on?". Esc stops it at once.
- **Video editing downloads ffmpeg once**, about 30 MB from the Python Package Index, after you approve its card.

## macOS

- **The first time Row-Bot works in your Documents folder**, macOS asks for permission and the command waits until you answer. This is a known issue.
- **After allowing Screen Recording or Accessibility** for computer use, choose **Check setup** in Settings › System. If it still says a permission is missing, choose **Row-Bot › Quit** and open Row-Bot again: macOS sometimes applies Screen Recording only to a fresh start.
- **If Row-Bot doesn't start after you replaced the app by hand**, macOS may be waiting for you to allow keychain access for the new copy. Look for the keychain dialog and choose **Always Allow**.

## Linux And Docker

- **Linux** runs as a browser app: open the address Row-Bot prints. Computer use and the native window aren't available there.
- **Docker** keeps everything in its data volume; see [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker/) for backups and upgrades.
- **A Row-Bot that PikaPods runs for you:** see [Fix A Hosted Row-Bot](/docs/troubleshooting/hosted) for the setup code, out-of-memory restarts, sign-ins, local models and moving.

## Chat, Tool, And Approval Problems

- Check the model picker, the composer's **Mode** (Agent or Chat only), the conversation's agent profile, its **Approvals** setting, and the enabled tools.
- If an action is waiting, approve or deny it in the conversation, from the sidebar's attention indicator, or from Overview. Approvals wait until you answer.
- If a step shows as skipped, it was denied and did not run.
- If the sidebar says **View only on this computer**, this tab was opened by typing Row-Bot's address, so it can't change anything. Open Row-Bot from its window, or choose **Open in Browser** from its tray icon. See [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/#programs-on-this-computer-cant-act-as-you).
- Ask Row-Bot to explain the last tool result if the transcript is unclear.
- If computer use stopped and asks "Carry on?", you moved the mouse or typed: choose **Carry on** once you have stopped, or **Stop**. "Row-Bot is using the computer in another chat" means another chat is using it: stop that one or wait for it.

## Workflow Problems

- Confirm the workflow is enabled, and that an earlier run isn't still waiting for approval: while one waits, the next scheduled run is skipped.
- Run it once with **Run** before trusting a schedule.
- Check delivery defaults and the channel's status in Monitor.

## Design And Code Folder Problems

- Designs: give a clearer goal, audience and length, and attach references. Exports use the last saved version.
- Code folders: check that the folder is listed under **Working on** in the conversation's details card. On a phone or in a browser, folders are chosen inside Row-Bot's workspace folder; anything outside it is only available from the desktop app's picker.
- Review commands and changes before approving or importing them.

## Knowledge And Monitor Problems

- If Knowledge is empty, turn on memory in Settings › Memory or add documents in Settings › Documents.
- If a memory is wrong, edit, merge or archive it in Home › Knowledge.
- Use Monitor's **Needs attention**, **History** and **Logs** for background issues, and **Copy diagnosis report** when asking for help.

## Apps And Skills

An app that isn't ready shows one status and one fix: the main action on its page in **Settings › Apps**, also offered in Overview's **Needs you**.

| Status | What it means | Do this |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sign in needed** | The app needs a sign-in, or its saved sign-in stopped working. | **Sign in**, or **Sign in again**. |
| **Key needed** | It needs a key or token. | **Add key**. |
| **Finish setup** | Setup stopped before the end, waiting for a setting, the actions to allow, or something it needs to run. | **Continue setup**. |
| **Working…** | Row-Bot is finishing your last change. | Wait a moment. |
| **Needs attention** | The connection failed, or Row-Bot couldn't confirm your last change. | **Fix**, or **Retry**. |
| **Off** | You turned it off. | **Turn on**. |
| **Removed** | A package was removed and its saved data kept. | **Delete saved data** when you no longer need it. |

- **Finishing your last change… Retry**: Row-Bot couldn't confirm that a change finished, for example because it closed part-way. **Retry** checks what happened and never repeats the change.
- **Open _program_, then check again**: the app works with a program on this computer, such as Blender. Open the program and its add-on, then choose **Check again**.
- **Install Docker Desktop, then try again**, or **Docker Desktop isn't running on this computer**: the app runs as a container image. Install or open Docker Desktop, or choose another way to connect on the app's page.
- **Signing in to an app from your phone**: without a public address, the browser ends on a page that doesn't load at `http://127.0.0.1`. Copy that page's whole address and paste it into the sign-in step; see [Sign in from a phone or another computer](/docs/settings/apps/#sign-in-from-a-phone-or-another-computer). If it says the address is from a different sign-in, open the sign-in page from the step again and paste the new address.
- **_App_ needs your own OAuth app to sign in**: the service accepts only an OAuth app you create. Create one at the service, register the callback address the step shows, and paste its **Client ID** (and **Client secret (optional)**, if it has one).
- If Google asks you to sign in every 7 days, your Google app is still in **Testing**; see [Google sign-ins in Testing last 7 days](/docs/integrations/accounts#google-sign-ins-in-testing-last-7-days).
- If an app's tools never appear in chat, check that it is **Ready**, that it is checked in the chat's **+ › Apps**, that the chat's agent profile allows it, and that **Use apps** is on in **Apps › Advanced**.
- Channels and accounts are apps too (for example **Apps › Telegram** or **Apps › Google**); **Open** on the app's page opens their own settings. A stopped channel shows **Restart** in Monitor, and an account whose sign-in expired shows **Reconnect** there.
- Skills need to be in **Your skills** in **Settings › Skills**, turned on, and relevant to the prompt; you can also call one with its slash command.

### Catalogs And Proxies

- **Couldn't update. The last copy is still used.**: the catalog couldn't be reached. Search keeps working with the last copy; choose **Update** again later.
- Behind a proxy, Row-Bot sends catalog updates and **Search online catalogs** through the proxy set in Windows or macOS settings or in the `HTTPS_PROXY` environment variable. It doesn't run automatic proxy configuration (PAC) scripts, so set the proxy's address itself.
- Logos, bundles downloaded from the Registry and app sign-ins connect directly, not through the proxy, so they fail on a network that allows only proxied traffic.

### Windows Connectors, Composio And App Views

- **Windows connectors** appear in **Apps › Advanced › Catalogs** only on Windows builds that have Windows' On-device Agent Registry (Insider build 26220.7344 or later, with **Experimental agentic features** on). Choose **Update** to list them.
- **Composio** isn't searched until you turn on **Use Composio** in **Apps › Advanced › Catalogs** and agree to its disclosure: it is a separate service, with its own account, that keeps requests and results for up to a year by default. Turning it off doesn't remove a Composio connection you made; remove that on its page.
- **App views** show only under a step that succeeded, for an app that has views, while **Show app views in chat** (in **Apps › Advanced**) and **Show views in chat** on the app's page are on and the app is on in that chat. "This view didn't start" or "Views are busy" usually clears with **Open again**.

## Remote Access And Server Mode

- If the browser shows `untrusted_forwarding_headers`, a proxy supplied forwarding metadata from an address Row-Bot does not trust. Restart after enabling a Row-Bot-owned Tailscale route. For another proxy, configure only its exact connecting address or CIDR; do not trust a broad network.
- If the browser shows `unexpected_host`, add the exact canonical browser-facing host and verify the proxy preserves it.
- If a code cannot be used, create it for the exact scheme, host, and port currently used by that browser. Expired, used and stale-route codes must be recreated.
- If Tailscale reports a conflict, Funnel, or an unowned route, inspect that configuration manually. Row-Bot deliberately refuses to reset or overwrite it.
- If a remote microphone is unavailable, use `localhost` or HTTPS, grant browser permission, and install the local voice model explicitly.
- "Disconnected. What you last saw is kept." means the browser lost its connection to Row-Bot: check that Row-Bot is running and the network is up, then **Reconnect**. "Something went wrong. Try again. Details: client_error" is a fault in the app, not the connection; reload the page, and report the details if it happens again.
- Run `row-bot access doctor` for a secret-free server and route safety report.

The full route, authentication, Docker, proxy, and recovery guidance is in [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access).

## Voice And Buddy

- Check that the browser may use the microphone, and which microphone and speaker are chosen in Settings › Voice › Microphone and speaker (or from the headphones button in the voice bar).
- Use Dictate before Talk if you need review. If Talk answers before you have finished, set **When you pause** to **Give me time to think**, or turn on **Push to talk**.
- On a phone, voice stops listening when the screen locks or turns off, or when you switch apps.
- For Live voice or a cloud speech service, check that its key is saved: Settings › Voice says when one is missing.
- If docked Buddy is missing, enable **Show Buddy** in Settings › Buddy. If a torn-off overlay was hidden, use the tray's **Show Buddy** action.
- Drag Buddy itself out of the sidebar in the native Windows or macOS app. Browser/server and phone layouts cannot create the native overlay.
- Use **Open full thread** for microphone controls, complex approvals, attachments, tool traces, and complete conversation history.
- Restart Row-Bot to return Buddy placement to the sidebar dock; a saved hidden preference must still be turned back on.

## Fix A Hosted Row-Bot

Route: /docs/troubleshooting/hosted

Troubleshooting for a Row-Bot that PikaPods or Railway runs for you: a lost setup code, an out-of-memory restart, a sign-in that won't finish, missing local models and moving.

# Fix A Hosted Row-Bot

This page is for a Row-Bot that PikaPods or Railway runs for you; [Row-Bot In Your Browser](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser) and [Row-Bot On Railway](/docs/getting-started/on-railway) explain how each works. For anything else, see [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/).

Problems with the server itself, such as billing, its size, or a server that won't start or can't be reached, are for your host: see Getting Help for [PikaPods](/docs/getting-started/in-your-browser#getting-help) or [Railway](/docs/getting-started/on-railway#getting-help).

## Lost The Setup Code

**Before anyone has signed in,** Row-Bot prints the code every time it starts. In PikaPods, open your pod's **More › Show Logs** and look for "Row-Bot setup code". If it has scrolled away, restart the pod and it's printed again. On Railway, the code is the value of `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE` in your service's **Variables**, and the deploy log shows it too.

What the page says:

- **"That code doesn't match."** Copy the whole code from the log again. After a few wrong tries the page says how many are left: five wrong codes pause sign-in for 15 minutes, and the page counts down the time.
- **"This code has already been used or has expired."** Change the setup code in your pod's settings in PikaPods and restart the pod, or on Railway set a new `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE` in the service's **Variables** and deploy the change. Then enter the new code.
- **"Row-Bot is starting."** Wait a few seconds; the page tries again by itself.

**After you've signed in,** a new browser shows **This Row-Bot already has an owner**:

- **If another device is still signed in,** add this browser from there: **Settings › Devices & remote access › Connect a phone or computer**.
- **If no device is signed in any more,** change the setup code in your pod's settings in PikaPods to a new one of at least 12 letters or digits, and restart the pod (on Railway: set a new `ROW_BOT_SETUP_CODE` in the service's **Variables** and deploy the change). Then open your Row-Bot, choose **Lost access?** and enter the new code. It works once, and signs out every other browser. Row-Bot doesn't print this code in the log: you know it because you set it.

## Row-Bot Restarted: Out Of Memory

When Row-Bot runs out of memory, the server restarts it. Home's **Needs you** and Monitor then say "Row-Bot restarted because the server ran out of memory", with your server's size. Your saved data and sign-ins stay. A reply that was running when it stopped may need sending again.

Local speech-to-text uses the most. With the search model and Row-Bot's browser, it needs about 3.2 GB. Do one of these:

- **Make the pod 4 GB in PikaPods,** or on Railway raise the service's memory limit to 4 GB in **Settings › Deploy**. The notice's **How to resize** explains it, and its link to your host (**Manage your pod in PikaPods**, **Manage your service in Railway**) opens the host's own page. The notice goes once the server is bigger.
- **Use cloud speech-to-text.** The notice's **Use cloud speech-to-text** opens **Settings › Voice**: choose a cloud speech service under **Listen with** (such as **Deepgram Nova-3**) and add its key, or talk with Live voice. Dictate and chat-app voice notes still use local speech-to-text.

**Dismiss** hides the notice until it happens again.

On a server under 4 GB, Row-Bot helps you stay within it: **Settings › Voice** marks local speech-to-text **Needs a 4 GB server** and asks before you choose it, and **Settings › Documents** suggests **Free memory when idle** for the search model. Row-Bot's browser also closes by itself ten minutes after its last use. [Hosting Row-Bot](/docs/operations/hosting#memory) has the details.

## A Sign-In That Won't Finish

### ChatGPT

- **"This code expired."** Choose **Get a new code**. It copies the new code too.
- **OpenAI's page didn't open,** because the browser blocked the new tab: choose **Open sign-in page**. The code stays on screen with **Copy**.
- **The code wasn't copied:** the panel says "Enter this code on OpenAI's page and approve." and shows the code to type in.
- **You approved, and closed Row-Bot's tab:** Row-Bot finishes the sign-in on your server by itself. Open Row-Bot again to carry on.
- **You reloaded the page, or started again:** that's fine. The newest sign-in replaces one that was still waiting.

### Grok

xAI's sign-in can only send your browser back to an address on the server's own computer, starting `http://127.0.0.1:56121/`, which your browser can't open. That's expected:

1. Sign in on xAI's page. It ends on a page that doesn't load.
2. Copy that page's whole address from the address bar.
3. Paste it into **Address of the page that didn't load** and choose **Connect with code**.

**"That address isn't from this sign-in"** means it came from an earlier try: copy the address shown after this sign-in and paste it again. **"Grok didn't allow the sign-in"** means xAI turned it down: start it again.

### Your Claude Plan
